Flying fish can leap out of the water and glide through the air on wing-like fins to escape predators. They build up speed underwater, then burst out and stretch their fins to soar for long distances, sometimes over 100 meters. They beat their tail to take off again and keep going.

The electric eel can produce a shock strong enough to stun fish or scare away large animals. Special organs in its body store and release electricity, like living batteries. Despite the name, it is actually a type of knifefish, not a true eel.

The electric ray, also called a torpedo ray, can deliver an electric shock to stun prey or defend itself. Special muscles in its body produce the electricity. People long ago even used these rays to try to treat pain, calling it a natural shock.

The manta ray is the largest ray in the ocean, with a wingspan that can reach over 7 meters. Despite its size, it eats tiny plankton, filtering them out of the water as it glides. Mantas are gentle and curious and have one of the largest brains of any fish.

A stingray has a sharp, venomous barb on its tail that it uses only to defend itself when threatened or stepped on. Most of the time it lies quietly buried in the sand, filtering for clams and small fish. Beachgoers do the stingray shuffle, sliding their feet, to avoid surprising one.

The whale shark is the largest fish in the world, growing up to about 18 meters long. Even though it is huge, it eats tiny plankton and small fish by filtering water through its enormous mouth. Each whale shark has a unique pattern of spots, like a fingerprint.

The basking shark is the second-largest fish and swims slowly near the surface with its huge mouth wide open. It filters tiny plankton from the water rather than hunting. Despite its size and gaping mouth, it is completely harmless to people.

Great white sharks have an incredible sense of smell and can detect a tiny amount of blood from far away. They also sense electric signals given off by other animals using special pores on their snouts. These senses help them find prey even in murky water.

Sharks have tiny jelly-filled pores on their snouts called the ampullae of Lorenzini that detect the faint electric fields all living animals give off. This lets a shark find a fish hiding under the sand or in the dark. It is a sense humans do not have at all.

The hammerhead shark has a wide, flat head shaped like a hammer, with an eye and nostril on each end. This spread-out shape gives it a wider view and a better sense of smell and electric signals. It often uses its head to pin stingrays to the seafloor before eating them.

keywords: how many teeth do sharks have
facts.answer: Sharks constantly lose teeth and grow new ones, sometimes replacing thousands over a lifetime. They have rows of teeth that move forward like a conveyor belt as front teeth fall out. That is why beachcombers sometimes find old shark teeth washed up on the sand.

Megalodon was a giant shark that lived millions of years ago and may have grown up to 18 meters long, far larger than a great white. We know about it mostly from its huge fossil teeth, some bigger than a human hand. It went extinct, but it remains one of the largest predators ever.

Sharks have been swimming in the oceans for more than 400 million years, which means they are older than trees and even older than dinosaurs. They survived several mass extinctions that wiped out many other animals. Modern sharks are descendants of those ancient survivors.

Some sharks must keep swimming so that water flows over their gills and gives them oxygen. If they stopped, they could suffocate. Other sharks can rest on the bottom and pump water over their gills, so not all sharks have to move constantly.

The remora is a fish with a flat sucker on top of its head that it uses to stick onto sharks, turtles, and whales. It hitches free rides and eats scraps of food and parasites off its host. The host usually does not mind, and may even benefit from the cleaning.

Cleaner fish, like the cleaner wrasse, set up cleaning stations on reefs where bigger fish line up to be cleaned. The small cleaner picks dead skin and parasites off the larger fish, even swimming inside their mouths safely. Both sides benefit, so the big fish do not eat their helpers.

Parrotfish use beak-like teeth to scrape algae off coral, swallowing bits of coral rock along the way. They grind it up and poop out fine white sand. A single parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms of sand a year, helping build tropical beaches.

At night, some parrotfish wrap themselves in a bubble of clear slime they make from their own mouths. This mucus cocoon may hide their smell from predators and protect them from tiny biting parasites. In the morning they wriggle out and swim away.

A pufferfish can gulp water to blow itself up into a spiky ball, making it hard for predators to swallow. Many pufferfish also carry a strong poison in their bodies. Even though they look round and cute, they are among the most poisonous animals in the sea.

Male pufferfish of one species make beautiful circular patterns in the sand to attract females. Using only their fins, they carve ridges and valleys into perfect circles up to 2 meters wide. For years divers were puzzled by these patterns before they discovered the tiny artists.

The lionfish is a striking fish with fan-like fins and venomous spines. It is a fierce hunter that gulps prey in one quick motion. In some places where it does not naturally live, it has become an invasive species, eating too many local fish.

The stonefish is the most venomous fish in the ocean and looks just like a lumpy rock on the seafloor. It stays still and waits for prey to swim near. Its venomous spines along its back can cause great pain if someone accidentally steps on it.

The moray eel hides in rocky crevices and has a surprising hidden weapon. It has a second set of jaws deep in its throat that shoot forward to grab prey and pull it back to swallow. This trick is a bit like the alien creature from science fiction movies.

Garden eels live in colonies, poking out of holes in the sandy seafloor and swaying in the current like a garden of plants. They catch tiny food drifting by while keeping their tails anchored in their burrows. If something scary approaches, the whole colony quickly pulls back into the sand.

keywords: how sea turtles find their way
facts.answer: Sea turtles can sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it like a built-in compass to navigate across entire oceans. Females often return to the exact beach where they were born to lay their own eggs, even decades later. Scientists think they remember the magnetic signature of that beach.

The leatherback is the largest sea turtle and can weigh as much as a small car. Instead of a hard shell, it has a leathery, rubbery back with ridges. It mostly eats jellyfish, and its throat is lined with spiky points that help push the slippery prey down.

For sea turtles, the temperature of the sand decides whether eggs hatch into males or females. Warmer nests tend to produce females, while cooler nests produce more males. This means changing temperatures can shift the balance of male and female turtles.

Dolphins use echolocation, sending out clicks and listening for the echoes that bounce back. This lets them build a sound picture of objects and prey, even in dark or cloudy water. They can tell the size, shape, and even what something is made of using only sound.

Dolphins seem to use special signature whistles like names, with each dolphin having its own unique sound. They call to each other using these whistles and can even copy a friend's whistle to get its attention. This is one of the few examples of name-like sounds in animals.

The orca, or killer whale, is actually the largest member of the dolphin family. Orcas are clever hunters that live in family groups called pods and teach hunting tricks to their young. Different pods even have their own calls and food preferences, like cultures.

Orcas are some of the cleverest hunters in the sea and often work as a team. Some make waves to wash seals off ice, while others herd fish into tight balls. Family groups pass down these hunting tricks from older orcas to younger ones.

The sperm whale makes the loudest sounds of any animal, a series of powerful clicks it uses to find food in the deep dark. These clicks are so strong they could be harmful up close. The whale uses them like sonar to hunt squid far below the surface.

Sound travels much faster and farther in water than in air, so whale calls can reach across enormous distances. Some low whale sounds may travel hundreds of kilometers through the ocean. This lets whales stay in touch even when they are very far apart.

Sea otters sometimes hold hands while resting at the surface so they do not drift apart in the current. A group floating together is called a raft. They may also wrap themselves in seaweed called kelp to anchor in place while they nap.

Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open hard shells like clams and sea urchins. An otter often keeps a favorite rock tucked in a flap of loose skin under its arm like a pocket. This makes the sea otter one of the few animals known to use tools.

Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs in a single square inch of skin. Since they have no blubber, this thick fur traps air to keep them warm in cold water. They spend lots of time grooming to keep their coat clean and fluffy.

Kelp forests are underwater woodlands made of giant seaweed that can grow as tall as trees. Giant kelp can grow up to half a meter in a single day, among the fastest-growing living things on Earth. These forests shelter fish, otters, and many other sea creatures.

Sea otters help protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins, which munch on kelp. Without enough otters, urchins can multiply and chew down whole kelp forests, leaving bare patches called urchin barrens. This shows how one animal can keep a whole ecosystem in balance.

Plankton are tiny living things that drift in the ocean, too small or weak to swim against the current. Some are plant-like and make food from sunlight, while others are tiny animals. Even though they are small, plankton are the base of nearly all ocean food chains.

keywords: where does our oxygen come from
facts.answer: Tiny plant-like plankton called phytoplankton make a huge share of the oxygen we breathe, possibly half of all the oxygen on Earth. They float near the surface and use sunlight to make food and release oxygen. So with every other breath, you may be thanking the ocean.

Diatoms are tiny plankton that build delicate shells out of glass-like silica in beautiful geometric shapes. When they die, their tiny glass shells sink and pile up on the seafloor over millions of years. These shells are even used in some toothpastes and filters.

A red tide happens when certain tiny algae suddenly grow in huge numbers, sometimes turning the water red or brown. Some of these blooms release toxins that can harm fish, birds, and even people who eat affected shellfish. Warm water and extra nutrients can trigger these blooms.

Sometimes ocean waves glow blue at night because of tiny bioluminescent plankton called dinoflagellates. When the water is disturbed by waves or a swimmer, the plankton flash with blue light. This creates a magical glow along the shoreline that looks like liquid stars.

Ocean currents are like giant rivers of water moving through the sea, driven by wind, the Earth's spin, and differences in temperature and saltiness. They carry warm and cold water around the planet, shaping weather and climate. Sea creatures and even drifting objects ride these currents for thousands of miles.

The Gulf Stream is a powerful warm current that flows up the eastern side of North America and across toward Europe. It carries warm water from the tropics, helping keep parts of Europe milder than they would otherwise be. It moves more water than all the world's rivers combined.

A slow, worldwide flow called the ocean conveyor belt moves water around the whole planet over hundreds of years. Cold, salty water sinks in some regions and warm water rises in others, linking all the oceans. This grand loop helps spread heat and nutrients across the globe.

Tides are the daily rise and fall of the sea, caused mostly by the pull of the Moon's gravity. As the Earth spins, different shores pass through the bulges of water the Moon pulls up, giving high and low tides. The Sun's gravity also adds to the effect.

When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, their gravity combines to create especially high and low tides, sometimes called spring tides. The biggest of these are nicknamed king tides. They can flood low coastal areas and reveal parts of the seabed normally hidden underwater.

The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the highest tides in the world, with the water level changing by up to 16 meters between high and low tide. That is taller than a four-story building. So much water moves in and out that it could fill a giant stadium many times over.

A tsunami is a series of huge waves usually caused by an underwater earthquake, volcano, or landslide that suddenly moves a lot of water. In the open ocean the waves are low and fast, but they grow tall as they reach shallow coasts. Tsunamis can be very dangerous to people living near the sea.

Rogue waves are surprisingly huge waves that appear without warning in the open ocean, sometimes more than twice as tall as the waves around them. Sailors told stories of them for centuries before scientists proved they are real. They can be powerful enough to damage large ships.

keywords: where does sea salt come from
facts.answer: The ocean is salty mainly because rivers carry tiny amounts of salt and minerals washed from rocks on land into the sea. Over millions of years, that salt has built up because water leaves the ocean by evaporating but the salt stays behind. Underwater volcanoes add minerals too.

keywords: why you float in dead sea
facts.answer: The Dead Sea is so salty that people float easily on top of the water without trying. The extra salt makes the water denser, which pushes swimmers up. It is so salty that almost nothing can live in it, which is how it got its name.

Most of the ocean floor has never been seen by humans up close, and we have better maps of the Moon and Mars than of our own seabed. Only a small fraction has been explored in detail. Scientists discover new ocean species almost every time they explore the deep.

keywords: how much of earth is ocean
facts.answer: Oceans cover about 71 percent of the Earth's surface, which is why our planet looks blue from space. They hold around 97 percent of all the water on Earth. Despite this, most of that vast watery world is still a mystery to us.

The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of the Earth's surface. It is so big that all the land on the planet could fit inside it with room to spare. Its name means peaceful, given by an early explorer who found calm waters.

The Sargasso Sea is a calm part of the Atlantic Ocean that has no land borders, instead being surrounded by ocean currents. It is named for the floating sargassum seaweed that gathers there. Baby sea turtles and eels use this floating seaweed as a nursery.

keywords: where do eels go to breed
facts.answer: European and American eels travel thousands of kilometers to the Sargasso Sea to lay their eggs, then the young drift back to rivers. This long journey was a mystery for centuries, because no one ever saw the eels breed. Scientists still have not watched it happen in the wild.

Salmon are born in rivers, swim out to the ocean to grow, then return to the very same river to lay their eggs. They use smell and the Earth's magnetic field to find their way home. Many leap up waterfalls and swim against strong currents to reach their birthplace.

Every year off South Africa, billions of sardines swim along the coast in one of the biggest animal migrations on Earth, called the sardine run. The swarming fish attract dolphins, sharks, whales, and seabirds that feast together. It is sometimes called the greatest shoal on Earth.

Many fish swim together in tightly packed groups called schools. Moving as one makes it harder for a predator to pick out a single fish and can confuse an attacker. Swimming in a group also helps fish save energy and find food and mates.

When predators attack a school of fish, the fish often swirl into a tight sphere called a bait ball. This swirling motion makes it hard for any one fish to be singled out. Dolphins, sharks, and seabirds may surround the ball and take turns rushing in.

Bluefin tuna are among the fastest fish, able to swim in bursts of over 70 kilometers per hour. Their bodies are sleek and torpedo-shaped, and they can even fold their fins into grooves to slide through water smoothly. They are also one of the few warm-bodied fish.

The sailfish is often called the fastest fish in the ocean and may reach speeds around 100 kilometers per hour in short bursts. It has a long bill like a sword and a tall fin that folds down when it swims fast. It sometimes raises that fin to herd schools of smaller fish.

The swordfish has a long, flat bill shaped like a sword that it uses to slash through schools of fish, stunning them so they are easier to eat. It is a fast and powerful swimmer that can dive deep. Special tissue near its eyes keeps its vision sharp in the cold dark.

The marlin is a large, powerful fish with a long spear-like bill. Blue marlin can grow over 4 meters long and weigh hundreds of kilograms. They are fast hunters that chase fast prey near the surface of warm oceans.

keywords: fish that lays the most eggs
facts.answer: The ocean sunfish can lay more eggs than almost any other animal, possibly hundreds of millions at once. Very few of those eggs survive to become adults, which is why each fish makes so many. The tiny babies look nothing like the giant grown-up sunfish.

The oarfish is the longest bony fish in the world, growing up to about 8 meters long. Its long, ribbon-like silver body and red crest may have inspired old legends of sea serpents. It lives deep in the ocean and is rarely seen alive at the surface.

The hagfish can produce huge amounts of slippery slime in seconds to defend itself. When grabbed, it releases so much slime that it can clog a predator's gills and make it let go. A single hagfish can fill a bucket with slime almost instantly.

The hagfish has a clever trick to clean off its own slime. It ties its body into a knot and slides the knot down to wipe the slime away. It can also tie itself in a knot to get extra force when tearing food.

The lamprey is an ancient jawless fish with a round, sucker-like mouth full of tiny teeth. Some species latch onto other fish and feed on their blood and fluids. Lampreys have been around for hundreds of millions of years, even before dinosaurs.

The horseshoe crab has bright blue blood that is incredibly valuable to medicine. Its blood clots around harmful bacteria, so doctors use it to test that vaccines and medical tools are safe. Horseshoe crabs are also living fossils that have barely changed in hundreds of millions of years.

The horseshoe crab has about ten eyes spread around its body, including some that sense ultraviolet light. Despite its name, it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs. It uses its long, spiky tail to flip itself over if it gets stuck on its back.

The coconut crab is the largest crab that lives on land and can grow nearly a meter across with its legs spread out. It has claws strong enough to crack open coconuts. Although it begins life in the sea, the adult crab would actually drown if it stayed underwater too long.

A hermit crab has a soft, curled belly, so it tucks itself into an empty snail shell for protection. As it grows, it must find a bigger shell and move in. Sometimes a group of hermit crabs will line up by size and swap shells one after another.

Male fiddler crabs have one giant claw and one tiny claw, while females have two small ones. The big claw is used to wave at females and to fight other males, not for eating. From a distance, a male waving his oversized claw looks a bit like he is playing a fiddle.

The decorator crab disguises itself by sticking bits of seaweed, sponge, and small animals onto its shell. This living costume helps it blend into the seafloor and hide from predators. As the crab moves to new areas, it changes its decorations to match its surroundings.

Barnacles are small creatures that glue themselves headfirst onto rocks, boats, and even whales, then build a hard shell around their bodies. They feed by sticking out feathery legs to grab tiny food from the water. The glue they make is one of the strongest natural adhesives known.

Sea sponges are simple animals with no brain, heart, or muscles. They pump water through tiny holes in their bodies to filter out food. Sponges are some of the oldest animals on Earth, and a single sponge can filter thousands of liters of water in a day.

The Venus flower basket is a deep-sea glass sponge with a delicate skeleton made of glassy fibers. Tiny shrimp often live trapped inside it for their whole lives, cleaning and protecting it in return for a safe home. In some cultures the sponge with its shrimp was given as a symbol of lasting togetherness.

The sea pig is a plump, pinkish type of sea cucumber that walks along the deep seafloor on tube-like legs. It eats mud, sorting out tiny bits of food, and often travels in large herds. Despite its odd appearance, it plays an important role cleaning the deep ocean floor.

Sea spiders are long-legged ocean creatures that look like spiders but are not true spiders. Some deep-sea ones grow legs spanning over half a meter. They have such tiny bodies that some of their organs spill into their legs, and many breathe through their skin.

keywords: why deep sea animals get big
facts.answer: Some animals grow much larger in the deep, cold ocean than their shallow-water relatives, a pattern called deep-sea gigantism. The giant isopod and colossal squid are examples. Scientists think cold water, high pressure, and slow growth over long lives may all play a part.

The giant isopod looks like a giant version of the roly-poly bugs found under rocks on land, but it lives deep in the sea. It can grow longer than your forearm. Food is rare in the deep, so it can survive for years without eating.

The light in an anglerfish's lure comes from glowing bacteria that move in to live there. The fish gives the bacteria a safe home and food, and the bacteria give the fish its glow. This kind of helpful partnership between two different living things is called symbiosis.

The cookiecutter shark is a small shark that takes round, cookie-shaped bites out of much larger animals like whales and big fish. It latches on with its lips and spins to scoop out a plug of flesh. It also glows faintly to lure prey close in the dark.

Lanternfish are small glowing fish that may be among the most numerous vertebrates on the planet. They rise toward the surface at night to feed and sink back into the deep by day. Their glow comes from rows of tiny light organs along their bodies.

Every night, countless small ocean animals swim up toward the surface to feed, then sink back down before dawn to hide. This daily up-and-down movement is the largest migration on Earth in terms of the number of animals. It happens in oceans all around the world.

Some deep-sea animals glow softly on their bellies to hide from predators below. By matching the dim light coming from the surface, their silhouette disappears against the brighter water above. This clever trick is called counterillumination.

The firefly squid is a small squid covered in tiny glowing spots that flash blue light. Every spring, huge numbers of them gather along the coast of Japan to lay eggs, lighting up the water like underwater stars. The whole shoreline can sparkle with their glow.

The tiny bobtail squid hides from predators using glowing bacteria stored in a special light organ. At night it glows softly on its underside to blend with moonlight from above, hiding its shadow. Each morning it pushes out most of the bacteria and grows them back by night.

The flashlight fish has glowing organs beneath its eyes that shine with light from bacteria. It can blink the light on and off by covering the organs with a flap of skin. It uses the glow to find food, confuse predators, and signal to other flashlight fish.

Living deep-sea anglerfish are so rarely seen that footage of one swimming was almost unheard of until recent years. Most specimens that scientists study were dead ones caught by accident. The deep sea is so vast and dark that most of its creatures are seldom witnessed alive.

The abyssal plains are vast, flat areas of the deep ocean floor, among the flattest and most remote places on Earth. They lie thousands of meters down in cold darkness. A slow rain of marine snow feeds the strange creatures that live on these wide muddy plains.

Scattered across parts of the deep seafloor are lumpy rocks called manganese nodules that are rich in metals. They grow incredibly slowly, only a few millimeters every million years. They take so long to form that the ones we see today began growing before humans existed.

Seamounts are mountains that rise from the ocean floor but do not reach the surface. There may be more than a hundred thousand of them, and most have never been explored. They create swirling currents that bring up nutrients, making them busy gathering places for sea life.

The longest mountain range on Earth is hidden under the sea. The mid-ocean ridge winds around the planet for over 65,000 kilometers, like the seam on a baseball. It is where new seafloor is created as molten rock rises from inside the Earth.

Cold seeps are spots on the seafloor where chemicals like methane slowly ooze out of the ground. Like hydrothermal vents, they support special communities of life that feed on those chemicals instead of sunlight. Mussels, tube worms, and clams cluster around these seeps in the dark.

In some deep parts of the ocean there are brine pools, which are pools of super-salty water sitting on the seafloor like an underwater lake. The brine is so much denser than normal seawater that it does not mix in. Animals that fall into the brine can be harmed by the extreme saltiness.

Scientists have filmed snailfish swimming deeper than 8,000 meters in ocean trenches, the deepest any fish has been seen. Below a certain depth, the pressure becomes too crushing for any fish to survive. So these snailfish live close to the deepest limit of fish life.

The ocean looks blue because water absorbs the red, orange, and yellow parts of sunlight and reflects the blue back to our eyes. The deeper the water, the more colors are absorbed, leaving only blue. Bits of plankton and sediment can shift the color toward green or brown.

The Bermuda Triangle is an area of the Atlantic Ocean where some ships and planes have gone missing, leading to many spooky stories. Scientists say there is nothing supernatural about it, and the area is no more dangerous than other busy parts of the sea. Bad weather and human error explain most cases.

Sea levels are slowly rising as the planet warms, partly because melting ice adds water to the ocean and partly because warmer water expands and takes up more room. Even small rises can affect low coasts and islands. Scientists track this carefully using tide gauges and satellites.

Mangroves are special trees that grow in salty water along tropical coasts, with tangled roots that rise above the mud. Their roots act like a nursery, sheltering baby fish, crabs, and shrimp. They also protect the shore from storms and waves and store lots of carbon.

Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow seas, forming underwater meadows. Unlike seaweed, they have roots, flowers, and seeds like land plants. These meadows feed animals like turtles and manatees and store large amounts of carbon, helping the planet.

The manatee is a slow, gentle sea mammal nicknamed the sea cow because it grazes on seagrass and other plants. It can eat a huge amount of plants each day. Despite its bulky body, it is a graceful swimmer and is related, surprisingly, to elephants.

The dugong is a relative of the manatee that lives in warm coastal waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It grazes on seagrass meadows, earning the nickname sea cow. Sailors long ago may have mistaken dugongs and manatees for mermaids.

Walruses have long tusks that both males and females use for many tasks, like hauling their heavy bodies out of the water onto ice. The tusks are really overgrown teeth. Walruses also have sensitive whiskers that help them find clams on the dark seafloor.

keywords: how to tell seal from sea lion
facts.answer: Seals and sea lions look similar but have differences. Sea lions have visible ear flaps and can walk on all four flippers, while true seals have only small ear holes and wriggle on land. Sea lions are usually noisier and more playful.

The Weddell seal lives around Antarctica and can dive deep and hold its breath for over an hour while hunting fish under the ice. It keeps breathing holes open in the ice with its teeth. It is one of the southernmost-living mammals on Earth.

The southern elephant seal is the largest of all seals, with big males weighing as much as a small truck. Males have a large, trunk-like nose they inflate to make loud roaring sounds. These seals can dive incredibly deep and stay underwater for long periods while hunting.

Penguins cannot fly through the air, but they fly through the water using their flipper-like wings. Their streamlined bodies and webbed feet make them fast, agile swimmers. Some penguins can dive deep and stay under for several minutes while chasing fish and krill.

The emperor penguin is the largest penguin and the deepest-diving bird, able to dive more than 500 meters and hold its breath over 20 minutes. It lives in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth. Fathers balance their eggs on their feet through the freezing winter.

Puffins are seabirds with colorful beaks, sometimes called clowns of the sea or sea parrots. They can hold many small fish crosswise in their beaks at once thanks to backward-pointing spines on their tongues. They dive underwater using their wings to chase fish.

The frigatebird is a seabird that sometimes steals food by chasing other birds and forcing them to drop their catch. It has a huge wingspan and can stay flying for weeks without landing. Males puff up a bright red throat pouch like a balloon to attract females.

Coral reefs are among the most important ecosystems in the ocean, sheltering a huge variety of life and protecting coastlines from storms. They feed millions of people and support fishing and tourism. Even though reefs cover a tiny part of the sea, they support an enormous share of ocean species.

Some deep-sea corals are among the oldest living things on Earth, with certain colonies believed to be thousands of years old. They grow extremely slowly in cold, dark water. A single old coral could have been alive since before many ancient civilizations existed.

Once a year, many corals on a reef release their eggs and sperm into the water all at the same time, in an event called mass spawning. The water fills with tiny colorful bundles that look like an underwater snowstorm. This timing, often linked to the Moon, helps the coral make new baby corals.

Deep-sea anglerfish can swallow prey larger than themselves because their stomachs can stretch enormously. Since meals are so rare in the deep, an anglerfish must take whatever it can catch, even big mouthfuls. Its flexible jaws and stretchy belly help it make the most of a rare meal.

The glass octopus has an almost completely see-through body, so you can look right through it. This transparency helps it stay hidden in the open water where there is nowhere to hide. Only its eyes, gut, and nerves are visible inside its clear body.

The blue-ringed octopus is small enough to fit in your hand but carries enough powerful venom to be very dangerous. When threatened, it flashes bright blue rings as a warning to stay away. It is usually shy and only bites if it feels trapped.

keywords: how many suckers does an octopus have
facts.answer: An octopus has eight arms lined with hundreds of suckers, sometimes over a thousand in total. Each sucker can taste and touch, so an octopus can sense its surroundings just by holding things. The arms are strong and flexible and can even regrow if one is lost.

Squid move by jet propulsion, sucking water into their bodies and then shooting it out fast to zoom backward. This lets them dart away from danger quickly. Some squid can even shoot out of the water and glide briefly through the air to escape predators.

Squid and octopuses can squirt a cloud of dark ink to confuse predators and cover their escape. The ink can act like a smokescreen or form a blob that distracts the attacker. While the predator is fooled, the animal jets away to safety.

Some cuttlefish put on a dazzling light show before catching prey, sending waves of color rippling across their skin. This display may mesmerize or distract the prey just long enough to grab it. They can also flash one pattern toward a mate and a different one toward a rival at the same time.

Sea slugs, also called nudibranchs, are some of the most colorful animals in the ocean, decorated in bright patterns. Their vivid colors often warn predators that they taste bad or are toxic. Some even steal stinging cells from the jellyfish they eat and use them for their own defense.

Some sea slugs eat algae and keep the algae's food-making parts alive inside their own bodies. This lets the slug make energy from sunlight, almost like a plant. One kind looks so much like a tiny green sheep that it is nicknamed the leaf sheep.

The blue dragon is a small, beautiful blue sea slug that floats upside down on the ocean surface. It eats stinging creatures like the Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its body. This means the tiny blue dragon can deliver a powerful sting of its own.

The giant clam is the largest living clam and can grow over a meter wide and weigh hundreds of kilograms. It does not snap shut on swimmers as old stories claimed. It feeds partly by filtering water and partly from tiny algae living in its colorful flesh, like coral does.

Scallops have dozens of tiny blue eyes lining the edge of their shells, which they use to sense light and movement. They can swim by quickly clapping their shells together to shoot through the water. This bursting motion helps them escape predators like sea stars.

A pearl forms when a tiny irritant, like a grain of sand, gets stuck inside an oyster. To protect itself, the oyster coats the irritant in layers of a smooth, shiny material, building up a pearl over time. Most natural pearls take years to grow.

Abalone are sea snails with beautiful, rainbow-colored shells lined with shiny mother-of-pearl. They cling tightly to rocks with a strong muscular foot and graze on algae. Their shimmering shells are used to make jewelry and decorations.

The cone snail is a beautiful but dangerous sea snail that hunts with a tiny harpoon-like tooth loaded with powerful venom. It shoots the harpoon to paralyze fish, then swallows them whole. Some of its venom is being studied to make new medicines for pain.

A baby sea otter, called a pup, is so fluffy that it floats like a cork and cannot sink. The mother often leaves the pup floating on the surface while she dives for food, sometimes wrapping it in kelp so it does not drift away. The pup's dense fur keeps it warm and buoyant.

Dolphins cannot fully fall asleep, because they have to keep coming up for air. Instead, they let one half of their brain sleep at a time while the other half stays awake to breathe and watch for danger. They often keep one eye open while resting.

Whales are mammals and must hold their breath when they dive, since they breathe air like us. Some, like the beaked whale, can hold their breath for more than two hours. They breathe out through a blowhole on top of their heads, making a spray when they surface.

Baleen is made of keratin, the same material as your fingernails and hair. The fringed plates hang from a whale's upper jaw and act like a strainer to catch tiny food. As the whale grows, its baleen keeps growing too, just like fingernails.

The barreleye fish has bright green, tube-shaped eyes that can rotate inside its transparent head. The green color may help it tell the difference between faint sunlight from above and the glow of bioluminescent prey. By looking up through its clear head, it spots food drifting overhead.

The deep-sea dragonfish can produce red light, which is rare because most deep animals cannot see red. This gives the dragonfish a kind of secret searchlight that its prey cannot detect. It also has see-through teeth and a glowing lure to attract victims.

The black swallower is a small deep-sea fish that can swallow prey larger than itself, sometimes more than twice its own length. Its stomach stretches enormously to hold the giant meal. Sometimes it eats so much that the food cannot digest fast enough.

The telescopefish has large, tube-shaped eyes that point upward to spot the silhouettes of prey against the faint light above. It hangs almost motionless in the deep, dark water, waiting to strike. Its huge mouth can grab prey nearly as big as itself.

The tripod fish stands on the seafloor using three long, stiff fin rays like the legs of a tripod. It faces into the current and waits for tiny food to drift into its outstretched front fins. Standing still saves energy in the food-poor deep sea.

A sea pen is a soft, feather-shaped sea animal that anchors itself in the muddy seafloor and waves gently in the current. It is actually a colony of many tiny creatures living together. Some sea pens glow when touched, lighting up the dark deep.

The basket star is a relative of the sea star with many arms that branch again and again into thousands of tiny curling tips. At night it spreads these arms wide like a net to catch tiny drifting food. By day it curls up into a tight ball to rest.

Brittle stars have slim, flexible arms that let them crawl across the seafloor faster than most sea stars. If a predator grabs an arm, the brittle star can snap it off and grow a new one later. Despite having no eyes, some seem to sense light through their whole bodies.

Feather stars are relatives of sea stars with feathery arms they use to catch food drifting in the water. Some can swim by waving their arms gracefully, while others stay anchored on the seafloor. Their ancient relatives, called sea lilies, have lived in the oceans for hundreds of millions of years.

Not all coral lives in warm, sunny waters. Deep-sea corals thrive in cold, dark water far below where sunlight reaches. Instead of relying on algae for food, they catch tiny particles drifting by, slowly building reefs that shelter deep-sea life.

The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest ocean, and much of it is covered by floating sea ice. Animals like polar bears, seals, and walruses depend on this ice. Underneath, special algae grow on the bottom of the ice, feeding the food chain in the cold sea.

The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica and is one of the coldest and stormiest oceans on Earth. Its chilly waters are full of krill that feed whales, seals, and penguins. A powerful current flows all the way around Antarctica, circling the entire continent.

The Antarctic icefish has clear, almost colorless blood because it has no red blood cells. The freezing, oxygen-rich water around Antarctica lets it survive without them. It is the only known vertebrate with no red blood, making it truly one of a kind.

Many polar fish have special antifreeze proteins in their blood that stop ice crystals from forming inside their bodies. This lets them swim in water cold enough to freeze most animals. Without this natural antifreeze, they would turn to ice.

In the ocean food chain, tiny plankton are eaten by small creatures, which are eaten by bigger fish, and so on up to top predators like sharks and orcas. Energy passes up the chain from sunlight to plankton to the largest hunters. Every level depends on the ones below it.

keywords: what is at the top of the ocean food chain
facts.answer: An apex predator is an animal at the very top of the food chain that few or no other animals hunt. In the ocean, orcas and large sharks are apex predators. Their presence helps keep the whole ecosystem in balance by controlling the numbers of other animals.

A keystone species is an animal whose role is so important that the whole ecosystem depends on it. Sea otters are a keystone species because they keep urchins in check and protect kelp forests. Remove a keystone species, and the entire habitat can change dramatically.

Sea foam forms when seawater filled with bits of algae, salt, and other natural materials gets churned up by waves and wind. The mixing traps air into bubbles, creating frothy foam on the shore. Most sea foam is harmless and is just a sign of busy, living seawater.

Most ocean waves are created by wind blowing across the water's surface, pushing it into ripples that grow into waves. As a wave reaches shallow water near shore, the bottom slows down while the top keeps moving, so it tips over and breaks. The bigger the wind and distance, the bigger the waves.

A rip current is a strong, narrow flow of water that rushes away from the beach back out to sea. It can pull swimmers away from shore quickly. Experts say if caught in one, you should not fight it directly but swim sideways along the beach until you escape its pull.

With ordinary scuba gear, most divers stay above about 40 meters because deeper diving becomes very dangerous. Special equipment and training let some divers go much deeper, but the pressure and gases are risky. To reach the deepest trenches, people must use sturdy submarines.

A submersible is a small submarine built to dive very deep and explore the ocean floor. Its walls must be extremely strong to resist the crushing pressure. Famous submersibles have carried explorers all the way down to the deepest point in the Mariana Trench.

In 2012, filmmaker James Cameron piloted a special submersible all the way to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, almost 11,000 meters down. He was only the third person ever to reach that depth and the first to do it alone. He found that even the deepest ocean holds life.

In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first people to reach the bottom of the Mariana Trench in a vessel called the Trieste. They were amazed to see signs of life at such crushing depths. Their dive proved that creatures can survive even in the deepest part of the ocean.

Scientists explore the deep sea using ROVs, which are underwater robots controlled from a ship by a long cable. ROVs carry cameras, lights, and robotic arms to collect samples without putting people in danger. They have discovered many new deep-sea creatures.

Whales help keep the ocean healthy, partly through their waste. Whale poop is rich in nutrients that feed tiny plankton near the surface, which in turn feed many other animals and produce oxygen. By diving deep to eat and surfacing to breathe and poop, whales spread nutrients around the sea.

The ocean soaks up huge amounts of carbon dioxide from the air, helping to slow down warming. Tiny plankton take in carbon as they grow, and some of it sinks to the deep when they die. This makes the ocean one of the planet's most important helpers in balancing the climate.

As the ocean absorbs extra carbon dioxide, the water slowly becomes more acidic. This can make it harder for animals like corals, clams, and snails to build their shells and skeletons. Scientists study ocean acidification to understand how it affects sea life.

A lot of plastic ends up in the ocean, where it can harm sea animals that mistake it for food. Currents gather floating plastic into large areas, the biggest known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Much of the ocean plastic also breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics.

Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic smaller than a grain of rice that float throughout the ocean. They come from larger plastic breaking down and from things like clothing fibers. Sea animals often swallow them by accident, and scientists are studying their effects on ocean life.

Fishing nets and gear that are lost or thrown away keep drifting in the ocean and trapping animals long after they are abandoned. This is called ghost fishing. Sea turtles, seals, fish, and seabirds can get tangled, so cleanup groups work to remove this ghost gear.

Flatfish like flounder and sole lie flat on the seafloor with both eyes on the top of their heads. They are not born that way; as a baby flatfish grows, one eye slowly moves to join the other on the same side. This lets them hide in the sand while watching for food and danger.

A flounder can change the color and pattern of its skin to match the sand or gravel it lies on. It can even mimic a checkerboard pattern placed beneath it. This camouflage hides it from predators and helps it ambush passing prey.

The archerfish hunts insects by shooting a powerful jet of water from its mouth to knock them off plants above the surface. It can aim accurately even though it must correct for the way water bends light. When the insect falls into the water, the archerfish gulps it down.

Mudskippers are fish that can crawl across mud and even climb roots using their strong front fins. They breathe partly through their skin and the lining of their mouths, so they can stay out of water for a while. They live where land and sea meet, like mangrove mudflats.

Some fish, like the climbing perch, can survive out of water for a time and even wriggle across land to find a new pond. They gulp air and use special breathing organs. This ability helps them when their home water dries up or gets crowded.

Lungfish can breathe air using simple lungs in addition to gills, which lets them survive when their water disappears. Some bury themselves in mud and form a slimy cocoon, sleeping through dry seasons that can last months. They are ancient fish related to the ancestors of land animals.

Fish breathe by pulling water in through their mouths and pushing it out over their gills. The thin, feathery gills pull oxygen out of the water and into the fish's blood. This is why most fish cannot survive long out of water, where their gills collapse and dry out.

Many fish have a gas-filled organ called a swim bladder that helps them float at the right depth without sinking or rising. By adding or removing gas, a fish can stay steady in the water with little effort. Sharks lack one and must keep moving or use their large oily liver to help stay afloat.

Fish can sense sound and movement in the water using a special row of sensors along their sides called the lateral line. This lets them feel vibrations, helping them swim in schools, avoid predators, and find prey. Many fish also have inner ears to detect sound.

keywords: why some deep fish are red
facts.answer: Many deep-sea animals are red, which seems odd until you remember that red light does not reach the deep ocean. Without red light to reflect, a red animal appears black and is nearly invisible to predators. So in the deep, red is one of the best camouflage colors.

Many open-ocean fish have shiny, silvery sides that act like mirrors. By reflecting the surrounding water, they make themselves hard to see from the side, blending into the blue. This natural mirror trick helps them hide where there is nowhere else to take cover.

Many ocean animals are darker on top and lighter on the bottom, a pattern called countershading. From above, the dark back blends with the deep water below, and from below, the pale belly blends with the bright surface. This makes the animal harder to see from both directions.

keywords: why fish lay so many eggs
how many eggs do fish lay
facts.answer: Many fish lay huge numbers of eggs, sometimes thousands or millions at once. So many eggs and babies are eaten by predators that only a few survive to grow up. By laying lots of eggs, fish make sure at least some of their young make it.

Some fish build nests to protect their eggs. Sticklebacks glue together bits of plant to make a tunnel nest, while some catfish dig pits in the sand. Certain fish guard their eggs fiercely, fanning fresh water over them until the babies hatch.

keywords: fish that carry eggs in mouth
facts.answer: Some fish protect their eggs and babies by carrying them inside their mouths, a behavior called mouthbrooding. The parent does not eat while doing this so it will not swallow its own young. When danger passes, the babies swim out, then rush back into the parent's mouth if threatened.

The male jawfish carries a cluster of eggs in his mouth to keep them safe and clean until they hatch. He gently rolls them around so they get fresh, oxygen-rich water. He goes hungry during this time, fully focused on protecting his future babies.

Sea turtles are reptiles and breathe air, but they can hold their breath for a long time underwater. While resting, some can stay submerged for hours. They come to the surface to take a breath, then dive again to feed and swim.

Sea turtles look like they are crying because they have special glands near their eyes that release extra salt from their bodies. Since they drink seawater and eat salty food, they need a way to get rid of all that salt. The salty tears keep their bodies balanced.

The green sea turtle is unusual because adults mostly eat seagrass and algae, making it one of the few plant-eating sea turtles. Its plant diet is even thought to give its body fat a greenish tint, which is how it got its name. Young green turtles eat more small animals before switching to plants.

Some sharks lay eggs inside tough, leathery cases that protect the baby shark as it grows. People sometimes find empty cases washed up on beaches and call them mermaid's purses. Other sharks give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

Pahoehoe is a kind of runny lava that cools into smooth, wrinkly skin that looks like coils of rope or folds of cake batter. Its Hawaiian name is pronounced 'pa-hoy-hoy.' It forms when lava is hot and fluid enough to keep flowing as its surface stiffens.

Aa (said 'ah-ah') is a rough, jagged kind of lava that hardens into sharp clinkers and broken rubble. It is so spiky that walking on it barefoot would make you say 'ah! ah!' The name comes from Hawaiian, and aa moves more slowly and stiffly than smooth pahoehoe lava.

A lava tube is a natural tunnel left behind when a river of lava crusts over on top while the molten rock inside keeps draining away. When the flow stops, an empty cave is left underground. Some lava tubes are big enough to walk through, and explorers find them on Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Pillow lava forms when lava erupts underwater and the cold sea instantly chills its surface into rounded, pillow-shaped blobs. New lava keeps squeezing out and making more pillows that pile up like a stack of cushions. Most of Earth's lava actually erupts this way along undersea ridges.

A shield volcano is wide and gently sloped, like a warrior's shield lying on the ground. It is built by runny lava that flows far before hardening, so it spreads out instead of piling up steeply. Mauna Loa in Hawaii is a giant shield volcano.

A stratovolcano, also called a composite volcano, is a tall, steep cone built from layers of lava and ash stacked over many eruptions. These are the classic pointy mountains like Mount Fuji and Mount St. Helens. They often erupt explosively because their thick lava traps gas.

A cinder cone is the simplest volcano: a steep little hill built from blobs of lava that shot into the air, hardened, and rained back down as cinders. They usually form quickly, sometimes in just weeks or months. Paricutin in Mexico grew from a flat cornfield into a cinder cone.

A caldera is a huge bowl-shaped pit that forms when a volcano empties its magma chamber and the ground above caves in. Calderas can be miles wide, far bigger than a normal crater. Crater Lake in Oregon sits inside a caldera left when a mountain collapsed.

A supervolcano is a volcano capable of an eruption thousands of times larger than an ordinary one, blasting out enough material to change the global climate. Yellowstone in the United States sits on one. The good news is that supereruptions are extremely rare, happening only every tens of thousands of years.
Magma is hot, melted rock deep below the ground. It is a thick, glowing soup of liquid rock mixed with crystals and gas. When magma reaches the surface and pours out, we give it a new name: lava.
Magma and lava are the same melted rock, just in different places. While it is still underground, it is called magma. Once it erupts and flows out onto the surface, it is called lava.

Lava is incredibly hot, usually between about 700 and 1,200 degrees Celsius (1,300 to 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit). That is hot enough to glow bright orange and melt many metals. The hottest lavas are runny and bright, while cooler ones are darker and stickier.

A volcanic bomb is a blob of lava that is hurled into the air during an eruption and spins as it flies, often cooling into a rounded or twisted shape before it lands. Some are as small as a tennis ball, but others are bigger than a car. They can be thrown hundreds of meters from the vent.

Volcanic ash is not soft like campfire ash; it is made of tiny shattered pieces of rock and glass blasted from a volcano. The jagged bits can scratch eyes and clog airplane engines, which is why flights are grounded during big ash clouds. Ash can travel for thousands of kilometers on the wind.

Pumice is a volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it can actually float on water. It forms when frothy lava cools quickly, trapping the bubbles inside. People use pumice stones to scrub rough skin off their feet.

Obsidian is natural glass made when lava cools so fast that crystals have no time to grow. It is usually shiny black and breaks into razor-sharp edges. Ancient people chipped obsidian into knives and arrowheads sharper than steel.

Basalt is the most common volcanic rock on Earth and covers most of the ocean floor. It is dark, fine-grained, and forms when runny lava cools. The black sand beaches of Hawaii are made of crushed basalt.

Granite is a hard, speckled rock that forms when magma cools slowly deep underground, giving its crystals time to grow big enough to see. It is made mostly of quartz, feldspar, and mica. Granite is used for kitchen counters and famous monuments like Mount Rushmore.

Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens. If it cools fast on the surface, like lava, it makes fine-grained rock; if it cools slowly underground, it makes coarse, crystal-filled rock. The word 'igneous' comes from a Latin word for fire.

Sedimentary rock forms when bits of sand, mud, shells, and other material pile up in layers and get pressed together over a very long time. Many sedimentary rocks show stripes, which are stacked layers of the past. Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rock.

Metamorphic rock is rock that has been changed by intense heat and pressure deep inside the Earth without fully melting. The squeezing and baking rearrange its crystals into new patterns. Marble forms from limestone, and slate forms from mudstone this way.

The rock cycle is the never-ending way rocks change from one type into another. Melting, cooling, weathering, squeezing, and heating can turn igneous into sedimentary into metamorphic and back again. A single rock's atoms may have been many different rocks over millions of years.

Marble is a metamorphic rock made when limestone is squeezed and heated deep underground. The change turns it into a smooth, swirly stone that can be polished to a shine. Sculptors have carved marble into famous statues for thousands of years.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mostly from the shells and skeletons of tiny sea creatures piled up on ancient ocean floors. Because it dissolves slowly in water, limestone is where most caves form. The Great Pyramids were built partly from limestone.

Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made of sand grains cemented together over time. Its color depends on the minerals gluing it, ranging from tan to deep red. Many desert canyons and arches, like those in Utah, are carved from sandstone.
Slate is a metamorphic rock that splits easily into flat, thin sheets. It forms when mudstone is squeezed by pressure. People use slate for roofs, floor tiles, and old-fashioned chalkboards.

Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth and comes in many colors, from clear to purple to pink. It is hard enough to scratch glass. Quartz crystals vibrate at a steady rate, which is why they help watches keep accurate time.

Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz that gets its color from tiny amounts of iron and natural radiation in the rock. It often grows inside hollow rocks called geodes. People have prized amethyst as a gemstone for thousands of years.

A geode is a plain-looking round rock that hides a treasure inside: a hollow space lined with sparkling crystals. They form when mineral-rich water slowly fills a bubble or cavity in rock, leaving crystals behind. You cannot tell a geode is special until you crack it open.

Diamond is the hardest natural material on Earth, made of pure carbon squeezed under enormous pressure deep in the planet. Natural diamonds form over a billion years far underground and are brought up by special volcanic eruptions. Because they are so hard, diamonds are used to cut and grind other materials.

The Mohs scale ranks mineral hardness from 1 to 10, with talc being the softest at 1 and diamond the hardest at 10. A mineral can scratch anything softer than itself. Your fingernail is about 2.5, and a steel knife is around 5.5 on the scale.
Talc is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale, ranking just 1, and you can scratch it with your fingernail. It feels slippery and soapy to the touch. Ground-up talc is used to make talcum powder.

A mineral is a single natural substance with a specific chemical makeup and a neat crystal structure, like quartz or salt. A rock is a mixture of one or more minerals stuck together, like a fruitcake made of different ingredients. So minerals are the building blocks, and rocks are what they build.

Plate tectonics is the idea that Earth's outer shell is broken into giant pieces called plates that slowly slide around. These plates carry the continents and oceans on top of them. Where plates meet, they build mountains, open oceans, and trigger earthquakes and volcanoes.

A tectonic plate is one of the huge slabs that make up Earth's rigid outer layer. There are about a dozen big plates and several smaller ones. They move only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Subduction is when one tectonic plate slides down underneath another and sinks into the hot mantle. As the plunging plate melts, it feeds magma to volcanoes above. Subduction zones create deep ocean trenches and powerful earthquakes.

A hotspot is a place where a plume of hot rock rises from deep in the mantle and burns through the plate above, making volcanoes. The plate keeps moving over the fixed hotspot, so a chain of volcanoes forms over time. The Hawaiian Islands are a trail left by one hotspot.

A mid-ocean ridge is a giant chain of underwater mountains where two plates pull apart and new ocean floor is born. Magma rises into the gap and hardens into fresh crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, mostly hidden under the sea.

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground caused when rocks along a fault snap and release built-up energy. The energy travels outward as waves that make the surface tremble. Most earthquakes happen near the edges of tectonic plates.

A fault is a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock can slip past each other. When they suddenly slide, the jolt causes an earthquake. The San Andreas Fault in California is one of the most famous faults in the world.

The Richter scale and similar magnitude scales measure how strong an earthquake is. Each step up the scale means the shaking is about ten times bigger and releases roughly 32 times more energy. So a magnitude 6 quake is far more powerful than a magnitude 5.

A seismograph is an instrument that detects and records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake. It traces wiggly lines that get bigger when the shaking is stronger. Networks of seismographs around the world help scientists locate quakes.

A tsunami is a series of enormous ocean waves usually triggered by an underwater earthquake, landslide, or volcanic eruption. In deep water the wave is barely noticeable, but it slows and piles up huge as it nears the shore. Tsunamis can travel as fast as a jet plane across the open ocean.

The mantle is the thick layer of hot rock between Earth's thin crust and its metal core. It makes up most of the planet's volume. Although it is solid rock, over long times it slowly flows like very stiff putty, which moves the plates above.

The crust is Earth's thin, rocky outer skin where we live. Compared to the whole planet it is incredibly thin, like the peel on an apple. Ocean crust is thinner and denser than the thicker continental crust under land.

Earth's core is a ball of mostly iron and nickel at the planet's center. The outer core is liquid metal, while the inner core is solid even though it is hotter, because crushing pressure keeps it from melting. The swirling liquid core creates Earth's magnetic field.

Earth is built like an onion with layers: the thin crust on the outside, the thick rocky mantle below, then the liquid outer core, and finally the solid inner core. The deeper you go, the hotter and denser it gets. The center is as hot as the surface of the Sun.

Heat from Earth's core makes the mantle slowly churn like the blobs in a lava lamp, with hot rock rising and cooler rock sinking. This slow flow, called convection, drags the tectonic plates along on top. It is the engine behind moving continents.

Pompeii was a Roman city buried under ash when the volcano Vesuvius erupted in the year 79. The ash preserved buildings, streets, and even the shapes of people for nearly 2,000 years. Today visitors can walk through the rediscovered city.

Mount Vesuvius is a volcano near Naples, Italy, famous for burying Pompeii in 79. It is still active and is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes because so many people now live nearby. It last erupted in 1944.

Krakatoa was a volcano in Indonesia whose 1883 eruption was one of the loudest sounds in recorded history, heard nearly 5,000 kilometers away. The blast destroyed most of the island and caused deadly tsunamis. It threw so much ash into the sky that sunsets around the world turned strange colors for years.

Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted in 1980 with a giant sideways blast that flattened forests for miles. The whole top of the mountain slid away in the largest landslide ever recorded. The eruption reshaped the landscape and is closely studied by scientists.

Mount Fuji is Japan's tallest mountain and a famous stratovolcano with a near-perfect cone shape. It is considered active but last erupted in 1707. Many people climb it each summer, and it appears in countless Japanese paintings and poems.

Mauna Loa in Hawaii is one of the largest volcanoes on Earth by volume. It is a shield volcano built by runny lava over hundreds of thousands of years. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it rises higher than Mount Everest.

Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from its base on the seafloor to its peak, taller than Mount Everest from base to summit. Much of it is hidden underwater. Its clear, high summit is home to powerful telescopes.

Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the world's most active volcanoes and has erupted almost continuously in recent decades. Its runny lava often flows in glowing rivers that visitors can watch from a safe distance. Native Hawaiian stories connect it to the volcano goddess Pele.

Mount Etna on the island of Sicily in Italy is Europe's tallest and most active volcano. It has been erupting on and off for hundreds of thousands of years. Its ash actually makes the surrounding soil very fertile for farming.

Yellowstone in the United States is a national park sitting on top of a giant supervolcano. The hidden heat below powers its famous geysers, bubbling mud pots, and steaming hot springs. The colorful hot springs get their rainbow colors from heat-loving microbes.

Old Faithful is a geyser in Yellowstone famous for erupting on a fairly predictable schedule, roughly every 60 to 110 minutes. It shoots boiling water tens of meters into the air. Its reliability is how it earned the name 'Old Faithful.'

A geyser is a hot spring that periodically blasts boiling water and steam high into the air. It works when underground water gets superheated by volcanic rock until pressure forces it out. Geysers are rare and need just the right plumbing of cracks and heat.

A hot spring is a pool or stream of naturally heated water that rises from underground. The heat usually comes from hot rocks left by volcanic activity. Some animals and people bathe in hot springs to stay warm in cold places.

A fumarole is an opening in the ground that puffs out volcanic steam and gases without erupting lava. They often smell like rotten eggs because of sulfur gas. Fumaroles are common around volcanoes and show that heat is still simmering below.

A mud pot is a bubbling pool of hot, gooey mud near a volcano. It forms when volcanic steam and gas mix with a little water and soil, dissolving rock into clay. The thick mud burps and plops as gas bubbles pop through.

A vent is the opening where lava, ash, and gas escape from a volcano. A volcano can have one main vent at the summit or many smaller side vents. Vents are the doorways between the magma below and the surface above.

A crater is the bowl-shaped pit at the top of a volcano around the main vent. It forms from explosions or the collapse of rock around the opening. Some craters fill with water to become lakes, while others glow with lava.

A lava lake is a pool of molten lava that sits in a volcano's crater or vent. The surface forms a thin dark crust that cracks open to show the glowing orange lava beneath. Only a few volcanoes in the world have long-lasting lava lakes.

A pyroclastic flow is a fast, scorching avalanche of hot gas, ash, and rock that races down a volcano's slopes. It can travel faster than a race car and is hotter than an oven, making it the deadliest part of many eruptions. It was a pyroclastic flow that buried Pompeii.

A lahar is a fast-moving river of mud, water, ash, and rock that rushes down a volcano, often when heat melts snow or ice on top. It can flow like wet concrete and bury everything in its path. Lahars can travel for many kilometers beyond the volcano itself.

Tephra is the general name for all the bits of rock thrown into the air during a volcanic eruption, from fine ash to large bombs. The pieces rain down and pile up around the volcano. Studying layers of tephra helps scientists date past eruptions.

Lapilli are small pieces of volcanic rock, roughly pea to walnut sized, that fall from the air during an eruption. The word means 'little stones' in Latin. They are bigger than ash but smaller than volcanic bombs.

A dormant volcano is one that is not erupting now but could wake up and erupt again in the future. Scientists call it 'sleeping' rather than dead. Mount Rainier in Washington is an example of a dormant but still dangerous volcano.

An extinct volcano is one that scientists believe will never erupt again because its magma supply is cut off. Edinburgh Castle in Scotland sits on an extinct volcano. It can be hard to be sure a volcano is truly extinct and not just dormant.

An active volcano is one that is erupting or is likely to erupt again. There are roughly 1,500 active volcanoes on land around the world, plus many more under the sea. About 50 to 70 of them erupt every year.

There are roughly 1,500 potentially active volcanoes on Earth's land, not counting the huge number hidden under the oceans. On any given day, around 20 are usually erupting somewhere. Most ocean-floor volcanoes erupt without anyone ever seeing them.

A volcanologist is a scientist who studies volcanoes to understand how they work and to warn people before eruptions. They sometimes wear heat-resistant suits to collect lava samples up close. Their work saves lives by predicting dangerous eruptions.

Scientists predict eruptions by watching for warning signs like small earthquakes, the ground bulging upward, and changes in volcanic gases. Instruments around a volcano send data day and night. While they cannot give an exact time, these clues often help warn people in time.

Volcanoes erupt because magma underground is lighter than the rock around it and rises toward the surface. As it climbs, dissolved gases form bubbles that expand, building pressure like a shaken soda bottle. When the pressure gets too high, the volcano erupts.

A fissure eruption happens along a long crack in the ground rather than a single vent, sometimes making a 'curtain of fire' as lava fountains out in a row. These can feed huge lava flows. Iceland often has fissure eruptions.

Volcanoes release gases like water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide. Sulfur gases give volcanoes their rotten-egg smell. These gases drive eruptions and, in huge amounts, can even affect the planet's climate.

Volcanic lightning is real lightning that flashes inside the thick ash clouds of some eruptions. The ash particles rub together and build up electric charge, which discharges as lightning. It is sometimes called a 'dirty thunderstorm.'

Pele's hair is thin golden strands of volcanic glass that form when wind stretches droplets of runny lava into hairlike threads. It is named after the Hawaiian volcano goddess Pele. The strands are sharp and delicate.

Pele's tears are small, smooth, teardrop-shaped beads of volcanic glass formed when blobs of flying lava cool quickly in the air. They are often found at the end of strands of Pele's hair. Both are named for the Hawaiian volcano goddess.

A volcanic island is formed when an undersea volcano erupts again and again until it grows tall enough to poke above the ocean surface. Iceland, Hawaii, and many Pacific islands were born this way. New volcanic islands can still appear today.

Surtsey is a volcanic island off Iceland that rose from the sea during eruptions starting in 1963. Scientists protect it so they can watch how plants and animals slowly colonize brand-new land. It is one of the youngest islands on Earth.

Iceland sits right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where two plates pull apart, plus a hotspot, which makes it one of the most volcanically active places on Earth. It has volcanoes, geysers, and hot springs all over. Icelanders even use the underground heat to warm their homes and make electricity.

Geothermal energy is power made from Earth's natural underground heat, often near volcanic areas. Hot water or steam from below can spin turbines to make electricity or heat buildings directly. Iceland and New Zealand use lots of geothermal energy.

Columnar basalt forms when a thick lava flow cools and shrinks, cracking into tall, many-sided columns, often six-sided like a honeycomb. The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is a famous example. From above the columns look like a tiled floor.

Devils Tower in Wyoming is a giant stone tower made of columnar igneous rock that formed underground and was later exposed when softer rock around it eroded away. Its sides have long vertical grooves. It became the first national monument in the United States in 1906.

Volcanic soil is among the most fertile on Earth because volcanic ash and rock are packed with minerals that plants love. That is why many farms thrive near volcanoes despite the danger. Coffee, grapes, and many crops grow well in volcanic soil.

Black sand beaches form when hot lava meets the ocean and shatters into tiny black grains, or when waves grind down dark volcanic rock. They are common near volcanic islands like Hawaii and Iceland. The sand can get very hot in the sun because dark colors absorb heat.
Some rare beaches have green sand made of tiny olivine crystals worn out of volcanic rock. One famous green sand beach is on the Big Island of Hawaii. The grains glitter olive-green in the sunlight.
Olivine is a green mineral common in volcanic rock and deep inside Earth's mantle. When it is gem quality, it is called peridot and used in jewelry. Its color comes from iron and magnesium.

Volcanoes are not only dangerous; they also do helpful things. They create rich farming soil, build new land and islands, provide geothermal energy, and bring up valuable minerals and gemstones. Over billions of years, volcanic gases even helped form Earth's atmosphere and oceans.

A seamount is an undersea mountain, usually a volcano, that rises from the ocean floor but does not reach the surface. There may be over a million seamounts in the world's oceans. They become busy habitats where ocean life gathers.

A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, like bones, shells, or footprints turned to stone. Fossils usually form in sedimentary rock when minerals slowly replace the original material. They are like nature's photographs of ancient life.

Most fossils form when a dead plant or animal is quickly buried by mud or sand before it can rot away. Over thousands of years, minerals seep in and replace the original material, turning it to stone. It takes a rare combination of luck and time for a fossil to form.

A coprolite is fossilized poop from an ancient animal. Even though it is now hard stone, scientists can study it to learn what dinosaurs and other creatures ate. So fossil dung is actually quite valuable to researchers.

Amber is fossilized tree sap that sometimes trapped insects, plants, or even feathers millions of years ago. The sticky sap hardened over time, perfectly preserving whatever got stuck inside. Amber gives scientists a clear window into the ancient past.

Petrified wood is the fossil of a tree where minerals slowly replaced the wood, turning it to stone while keeping the shape of the rings and bark. The process can produce colorful, crystal-filled logs. Arizona's Petrified Forest is full of these stone trees.

Weathering is the slow breaking down of rocks at Earth's surface by water, ice, wind, and living things. Rain, freezing, and plant roots all chip away at rock over time. Weathering turns solid rock into smaller pieces and eventually into soil.

Erosion is the moving of broken-down rock and soil to new places by water, wind, ice, or gravity. Rivers carry sand to the sea, and wind blows dust across deserts. Over millions of years, erosion can carve canyons and wear down whole mountains.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona was carved by the Colorado River cutting down through rock over millions of years. It is over a mile deep and exposes rock layers nearly two billion years old. Its colorful walls are like a giant book of Earth's history.

A stalactite is an icicle-shaped mineral spike that hangs from a cave ceiling. It grows incredibly slowly as drips of mineral-rich water leave behind tiny deposits. A helpful memory trick is that stalactites hold 'tight' to the ceiling.

A stalagmite is a mineral mound that grows up from a cave floor where mineral-rich water drips down and leaves deposits. It rises so slowly it may take thousands of years to grow. To remember it, a stalagmite 'might' reach the ceiling someday.

Most caves form when slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves limestone rock over thousands of years, hollowing out passages and rooms underground. The same dripping water later decorates caves with stalactites and stalagmites. Some caves stretch for many kilometers.

A gemstone is a mineral or rock that is rare and beautiful enough to be cut and polished for jewelry. Diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and sapphires are famous gems. Most gemstones form deep underground under heat and pressure over a very long time.

A ruby is a deep red gemstone and is one of the hardest minerals after diamond. It is a red form of the mineral corundum, colored by tiny amounts of chromium. Fine rubies can be more valuable than diamonds of the same size.

A sapphire is a gemstone usually known for its rich blue color, though it can also be pink, yellow, or other colors. It is made of the mineral corundum, the same mineral that forms rubies. Sapphires are very hard and prized for jewelry.

An emerald is a green gemstone valued for its rich color, which comes from traces of chromium and vanadium. It is a green variety of the mineral beryl. Many emeralds have tiny natural marks inside, which jewelers poetically call a 'garden.'
An opal is a gemstone that flashes a rainbow of colors as it moves in the light. The colors come from tiny spheres inside the stone that bend light. Most of the world's opals come from Australia.
Turquoise is a blue-green mineral that has been used in jewelry for thousands of years. Ancient Egyptians and Native Americans both prized it. Its color comes from copper in the stone.

Calcite is a common mineral that makes up limestone and marble and decorates many caves. A simple test is that calcite fizzes when a drop of acid touches it, releasing carbon dioxide. Some clear calcite even splits light into a double image.

Feldspar is the most abundant group of minerals in Earth's crust, making up over half of it. It is a key ingredient in granite and many other rocks. Crushed feldspar is used to make ceramics and glass.

Mica is a mineral that splits into thin, shiny, see-through sheets, like the pages of a tiny book. It sparkles in many rocks and in some makeup and paint. Long ago, sheets of mica were used as windows in stoves and lanterns.

Pyrite is a shiny golden mineral nicknamed 'fool's gold' because it tricked miners into thinking they had struck it rich. Unlike real gold, pyrite is brittle and has sharp, cube-shaped crystals. Its name comes from a Greek word for fire because it sparks when struck.

Gold is a soft, heavy, shiny metal that does not rust or tarnish, which is why ancient treasures still gleam today. It is so rare and valued that people have searched for it throughout history. Gold is found in veins of rock and as nuggets washed into rivers.
Table salt is actually a mineral called halite. It often forms when ancient salty lakes or seas dry up, leaving behind beds of salt. People mine huge salt deposits and even carve rooms in salt mines.

Coal is a black rock made from plants that grew in swamps hundreds of millions of years ago, then got buried and pressed for ages. Because it formed from living things, it is called a fossil fuel. Burning coal releases the ancient stored energy, but it also pollutes the air.
