Latin, the language of ancient Rome, still shows up in everyday life. Phrases like et cetera, meaning and so on, and per annum, meaning per year, come straight from Latin. Doctors, lawyers, and scientists still use many Latin words today, thousands of years after Rome's peak.

Nubia, including the powerful Kingdom of Kush, was an African civilization south of Egypt along the Nile. The two lands traded, fought, and influenced each other for thousands of years. At one point Nubian kings conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs, becoming known as the Black Pharaohs.

Ramesses the Great was one of ancient Egypt's most powerful pharaohs, ruling for about 66 years and living into his 90s. He built more monuments and statues of himself than almost any other pharaoh. He fathered so many children that he may have had over 100 sons and daughters.

The famous golden burial mask of King Tutankhamun has a long, braided false beard. In modern times, museum workers accidentally knocked the beard off and once glued it back on incorrectly. Experts later carefully fixed the mistake to restore this priceless 3,000-year-old treasure.

Ancient Egyptian scribes wrote mostly in black ink made from soot, but they used red ink for important words, titles, and the starts of sentences. This is one of the earliest examples of highlighting key text. They carried their inks in small pots on a wooden writing palette.

Persepolis was the grand ceremonial capital of the ancient Persian Empire, filled with huge palaces and stone carvings. People from many lands across the empire brought gifts to the Persian king, shown in detailed wall carvings. Alexander the Great later conquered and burned the city.

The ancient Persian Empire built a famous highway called the Royal Road, stretching over 2,500 kilometers. Royal messengers riding in relays could carry news along it in about a week, a journey that would take ordinary travelers months. This fast communication helped hold the huge empire together.

Music was important in ancient Egypt for festivals, temples, and everyday fun. People played harps, flutes, drums, and rattles called sistrums. They also clapped wooden hand-shaped clappers to keep the beat, and many of these instruments have been found in tombs.

Ancient Greek pottery was often beautifully painted with scenes from myths, sports, and daily life. Two main styles were black figures on a red background and later red figures on a black background. These vases are like illustrated storybooks that tell us a great deal about Greek life.

The ancient Romans regularly counted their citizens in an event called a census to know how many people they had for taxes and the army. This was a major undertaking across the huge empire. The idea of a census is still used by governments around the world today.

One leading idea about how the pyramids were built is that workers dragged stone blocks up long earthen ramps. As the pyramid grew taller, the ramps grew with it. There are different ramp theories, such as straight ramps or ramps that spiraled around the pyramid, and experts still debate which was used.

The ancient Egyptians cut and shaped enormous stone blocks using copper tools, stone hammers, and lots of patience. To split hard rock, they sometimes drove wooden wedges into cracks and soaked them with water so they would swell and break the stone. It was slow, skilled work without iron or steel tools.

The ancient Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples were making rubber thousands of years before it was known in Europe. They mixed sap from rubber trees with juice from another plant to create a bouncy, durable material. They used it for balls, sandals, and waterproof items.

Before they had large wooden ships, ancient Egyptians made boats by tying bundles of papyrus reeds together. These light reed boats floated well and were used for fishing and traveling on the Nile. Similar reed boats are still built in some parts of the world today.

Shops in ancient Rome often had painted signs or carved symbols above their doors to show what they sold, since many people could not read. A picture of a goat might mean a dairy, and a boot might mark a shoemaker. This is a very old form of the shop signs and logos we still use.

Not everyone in ancient Egypt could afford a fancy mummification with all the rituals. There were cheaper versions for ordinary people that used less expensive methods and simpler wrappings. The poorest were often just buried in the dry desert sand, which sometimes preserved their bodies naturally.

Long before they invented the careful mummification process, ancient Egyptians buried their dead in the hot, dry desert sand. The dry conditions naturally dried out and preserved the bodies. Seeing these preserved bodies may have inspired Egyptians to develop true mummification later on.

Ancient Rome had a kind of early newspaper called the Acta Diurna, meaning daily acts. It was carved or written on boards and posted in public places for citizens to read. It shared news about court cases, government decisions, and important events in the city.

Besides black kohl, ancient Egyptians made green eye makeup from a ground-up mineral called malachite. Wearing eye paint was partly for beauty but also linked to protection and the gods. Both rich and poor Egyptians, men and women, wore this colorful makeup.

The Giza plateau near modern Cairo holds three great pyramids, several smaller ones, and the Great Sphinx. The three big pyramids were built for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure. Together they form one of the most famous ancient sites in the world.

There were several types of gladiators in ancient Rome, each with different weapons and armor. The retiarius fought with a net and trident like a fisherman, while the murmillo carried a large shield and sword. These different styles made the fights more exciting for the crowds.

The smooth Egyptian pyramids did not appear all at once; builders learned by trial and error. The Bent Pyramid actually changes angle partway up, probably because builders realized it might collapse if they kept the steep slope. These early attempts taught them how to build the perfect Great Pyramid.

The Step Pyramid of Djoser is the oldest large stone pyramid in Egypt, built about 4,700 years ago. It was designed by a famous architect named Imhotep, who stacked stone platforms to form giant steps. This first pyramid was the model that later led to the smooth-sided pyramids.

Imhotep was an ancient Egyptian genius who designed the first pyramid, the Step Pyramid of Djoser. He was also a doctor, writer, and advisor to the pharaoh. He was so admired that long after his death, Egyptians worshipped him almost like a god of wisdom and healing.

The ancient Etruscans, who lived in Italy before Rome rose to power, made some of the world's first false teeth. They used gold bands to attach replacement teeth, sometimes from animals or other people. This early dental work was passed on to the Romans who came after them.

The Etruscans were a civilization that lived in Italy before and during the early rise of Rome. They were skilled metalworkers, traders, and tomb builders, and they greatly influenced Roman culture. Much of their language is still not fully understood, leaving many of their secrets a mystery.

Ancient Egyptians wrote numbers using picture symbols, with different signs for one, ten, a hundred, and so on up to a million. A single tally mark meant one, a coiled rope meant a hundred, and a tadpole stood for one hundred thousand. They wrote bigger numbers by drawing more of these symbols.

Farmers in ancient Mesopotamia dug networks of canals to carry water from the rivers to their dry fields. This irrigation let them grow plenty of food in a hot land. Managing the water and storing surplus grain helped these early communities grow into the world's first cities.

The Narmer Palette is a famous carved stone slab from ancient Egypt over 5,000 years old. Although palettes were used for grinding eye makeup, this one is special because its carvings may record the uniting of Upper and Lower Egypt into one kingdom. It is one of the earliest historical documents from Egypt.

Ancient Egypt was once two separate kingdoms, Upper Egypt in the south and Lower Egypt in the north. They were united into one country around 5,000 years ago. To show he ruled both, the pharaoh wore a double crown that combined the white crown of the south and the red crown of the north.

The ancient Romans loved wine but almost always mixed it with water before drinking. Drinking wine straight was considered the habit of barbarians and heavy drinkers. They sometimes also added spices, honey, or even seawater to flavor it.

Ancient Egyptians wore light clothing made of linen, which is woven from the flax plant, to stay cool in the hot climate. White linen was the most common, and the finer and whiter it was, the wealthier the wearer. Most people wore simple, lightweight garments that left arms and legs free.

Some ancient Maya gently shaped the soft heads of babies by pressing them between boards over time. This gave the skull a longer, flatter shape that they considered beautiful and noble. The practice did not harm the babies, and similar customs appeared in several ancient cultures.

Children in ancient Rome played many games we would recognize today, such as marbles, hopscotch, and ball games. They also played with dolls, toy soldiers, and hoops that they rolled with sticks. Some Roman children even kept pet birds and dogs just like kids do now.

In a quarry in Aswan, Egypt, there is a giant obelisk still attached to the bedrock because it cracked while being carved. If finished, it would have been the largest obelisk ever made. Lying there unfinished, it gives us clues about how Egyptians cut and shaped these huge stones.

Writing was probably first invented not for stories but to keep track of trade and goods. Early Mesopotamian records counted things like sheep, grain, and jars of oil. Only later did people use writing to record laws, religion, and tales, which changed human history forever.

Reading hieroglyphs can be tricky because they were written in different directions. The clue is which way the animals and people face: you usually read toward the front of the figures. So if the birds look to the left, you start reading from the left side.

Most ordinary people in ancient Rome lived in crowded apartment buildings called insulae, sometimes several stories tall. The upper floors were cheapest, cramped, and most dangerous in case of fire or collapse. The ground floors were nicer and often had shops at the front.

keywords: ancient egypt afterlife fields of reeds
facts.answer: Ancient Egyptians believed that if a person passed the test of the heart, they could reach a paradise called the Field of Reeds. It was imagined as a perfect version of Egypt, with rich farmland and plenty of food. There the dead would live happily and work peaceful land forever.

Egyptians were often buried with small figures called shabti, meant to do work for them in the afterlife. People believed that when the gods called the dead to do labor, the shabti would magically come to life and answer instead. Some wealthy people were buried with hundreds of these little helpers.

keywords: ancient roman empire bread and circuses
facts.answer: To keep the people of Rome happy and calm, leaders provided free grain and grand public entertainment, a policy summed up as bread and circuses. The free bread fed the poor, and the games and races kept crowds amused. Politicians used this to win popularity and avoid unrest.

The ankh is a famous ancient Egyptian symbol shaped like a cross with a loop on top. It represented life and was often carried by gods in Egyptian art, held up to a person's nose to give the breath of life. Today the ankh remains one of the most recognized symbols of ancient Egypt.

Brewing beer is one of the oldest human crafts, going back over 5,000 years in Mesopotamia and Egypt. Ancient people wrote hymns that doubled as beer recipes. Some scientists even think the desire to make beer may have helped encourage early people to start farming grain.

Ancient Egyptians stored grain in large dome-shaped buildings called granaries to save food between harvests. Careful records were kept of how much was stored and given out. This stockpiling helped the country survive bad years when the Nile flood was too low to grow enough food.

Roman roads were built in careful layers to last a long time. Workers dug a trench, then added layers of large stones, gravel, sand, and finally tightly fitted paving stones on top. The roads were curved slightly in the middle so rainwater would drain off the sides.

Ancient Egyptians sometimes placed decorated masks over the faces of mummies. These masks showed an idealized, youthful version of the dead person so their spirit could recognize their body. The most famous example is the dazzling gold mask of King Tutankhamun.

The Fertile Crescent is a curved region in the Middle East where some of the world's earliest farming began over 10,000 years ago. Its rich soil and rivers let people grow wheat and barley and raise animals. Settling down to farm here led to the first villages, cities, and civilizations.

Ancient Egypt was divided into local regions called nomes, a bit like states or counties. Each nome had its own governor and even its own local gods and symbols. This organized system helped the pharaoh manage the long, narrow country stretched along the Nile.

keywords: ancient roman empire numbers no zero problem
facts.answer: The ancient Romans had no symbol for zero, which made arithmetic clumsy and hard. To do calculations, they often used a counting board or an abacus instead of writing sums out. The handy zero we use came from India and reached Europe long after Rome's peak.

The abacus is one of the oldest calculating tools, used by ancient civilizations including the Babylonians, Romans, and Chinese. By sliding beads along rods or moving counters, people could add and subtract quickly. Skilled abacus users can still calculate faster than some people using a calculator.

keywords: ancient egypt mummified pets buried with owners
facts.answer: Some ancient Egyptians loved their pets so much that they had them mummified and buried alongside them. Pet cats, dogs, monkeys, and birds have been found in tombs. The Egyptians hoped to be reunited with their animal friends in the afterlife.

keywords: ancient roman empire fast roads spies
facts.answer: The ancient Romans used a network of agents and informers to gather information across their vast empire. Messages could travel fast on the famous Roman roads using relays of riders. Knowing what was happening in distant provinces helped emperors keep control and respond to threats.

Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest known volcano in the solar system, rising about 22 kilometers (13.6 miles) high. That's nearly three times taller than Mount Everest. Its base is so wide it would cover the entire state of Arizona.

Valles Marineris on Mars is a system of canyons over 4,000 kilometers long, stretching as far as the distance across the United States. In places it is 7 kilometers deep, far deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon. It is one of the largest canyons in the whole solar system.

Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron-rich dust that has rusted, just like an old nail turns orange. The rust is iron oxide, the same chemical that makes blood and some rocks red. Winds spread this reddish dust all over the planet.

Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, keeping the surface around 465 degrees Celsius. That's hot enough to melt lead.

A day on Venus is longer than its year. Venus spins so slowly that one full rotation takes about 243 Earth days, while it orbits the Sun in only about 225 Earth days. So a single Venusian day lasts longer than a Venusian year.

Venus spins backwards compared to most other planets, a motion called retrograde rotation. On Venus the Sun would appear to rise in the west and set in the east. Scientists think a giant collision long ago may have flipped it over.

Mercury has wild temperature swings because it has almost no atmosphere to hold in heat. The daytime side can reach about 430 degrees Celsius, while the night side drops to around minus 180 degrees Celsius. That's one of the biggest temperature ranges of any planet.

Even though Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, it has frozen water hidden in deep craters near its poles. Sunlight never reaches the bottoms of these craters, so the ice stays frozen. Spacecraft have detected this surprising ice from orbit.

Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has raged for at least 350 years. It is so big that two or three Earths could fit inside it. The storm has been slowly shrinking over the past century but remains the largest in the solar system.

Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system, so big that all the other planets could fit inside it with room to spare. It is more than 1,300 times the volume of Earth. Despite its size, it spins faster than any other planet, finishing a day in about 10 hours.

Saturn's rings are made mostly of countless chunks of ice and rock, ranging from tiny grains to pieces as big as houses. The rings are very wide but surprisingly thin, often only about 10 meters thick. They shine because the ice reflects sunlight.

Uranus rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees, so it basically rolls around the Sun like a ball. This means its poles take turns facing the Sun, giving it extreme seasons that each last about 21 Earth years. Scientists think a massive collision knocked it over long ago.

Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, reaching speeds up to about 2,100 kilometers per hour. That's faster than the speed of sound on Earth. These supersonic winds whip around the cold, blue planet.

Neptune and Uranus look blue because of methane gas in their atmospheres. Methane absorbs red light and reflects blue light back into space. Neptune's blue is a bit deeper than Uranus's, possibly due to an extra unknown ingredient.

Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects. It shares its region with many icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt. Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon.

Pluto has a giant heart-shaped region on its surface named Tombaugh Regio, after Pluto's discoverer Clyde Tombaugh. The left side of the heart is a smooth plain of frozen nitrogen ice. NASA's New Horizons spacecraft photographed it in 2015.

keywords: what is the sun made of
facts.answer: The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen, with about three quarters of its mass being hydrogen and most of the rest helium. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that makes the Sun shine. Tiny amounts of heavier elements are also present.

keywords: how much of solar system is the sun
facts.answer: The Sun contains about 99.8 percent of all the mass in the solar system. Everything else, including all the planets, moons, asteroids, and comets, makes up only the remaining tiny fraction. Its gravity holds the whole solar system together.

keywords: how long sunlight to reach earth
facts.answer: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth. That means when you look at the Sun, you are seeing light that left it more than 8 minutes ago. Light travels at about 300,000 kilometers per second.

keywords: what kind of star is the sun
facts.answer: The Sun is a star, just like the ones we see at night, but it looks bigger and brighter because it is so much closer to us. It is a medium-sized yellow dwarf star. Many stars in the universe are far larger or smaller than the Sun.

keywords: why does the moon change shape
facts.answer: The Moon seems to change shape because we see different amounts of its sunlit side as it orbits Earth. The Moon doesn't make its own light; it reflects sunlight. The cycle from one full moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.

keywords: why we always see same moon face
facts.answer: We always see the same side of the Moon because it is tidally locked to Earth, meaning it rotates once for every orbit it makes. The far side was a mystery until spacecraft photographed it in 1959. The far side is not actually dark; it gets just as much sunlight.

The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters per year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow. This happens because of the way the Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans. Over millions of years this adds up to a big distance.

Scientists think the Moon formed when a Mars-sized object smashed into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. The collision flung debris into space, which clumped together to make the Moon. This idea is called the giant impact hypothesis.

The footprints left by astronauts on the Moon could last for millions of years. The Moon has no wind or rain to erase them. They will only disappear slowly from tiny meteorite impacts and space dust over very long timescales.

keywords: why does the moon cause tides
facts.answer: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, creating bulges of water that we experience as high tides. As Earth rotates, different places pass through these bulges, giving most coasts two high and two low tides each day. The Sun's gravity also affects tides, but less than the Moon's.

The asteroid belt is a region between Mars and Jupiter filled with millions of rocky objects called asteroids. Despite the movies, the asteroids are usually millions of kilometers apart, so it is mostly empty space. Together they don't even add up to the mass of the Moon.

Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is classified as a dwarf planet. It makes up about a quarter of the entire belt's mass. Scientists believe Ceres may have a salty ocean hidden beneath its surface.

Comets are like dirty snowballs made of ice, dust, and rock left over from the early solar system. When a comet gets close to the Sun, the ice turns to gas and forms a glowing tail. The tail always points away from the Sun because of the solar wind.

keywords: comet tail points away from sun
facts.answer: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, no matter which direction the comet is traveling. This happens because the solar wind and sunlight push the gas and dust away from the Sun. So sometimes a comet's tail actually leads in front of it as it heads away.
Halley's Comet is the most famous comet and returns near Earth about every 76 years. It last appeared in 1986 and is expected back in 2061. People have recorded sightings of it for over 2,000 years.

A meteor is the streak of light we see when a space rock burns up in Earth's atmosphere, which people call a shooting star. If a piece survives and lands on the ground, it is called a meteorite. Before it enters the atmosphere, the rock is called a meteoroid.

Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through the trail of dust left behind by a comet. The tiny dust grains burn up in our atmosphere, creating many shooting stars in one night. The Perseids in August and the Geminids in December are among the most popular showers.

keywords: what galaxy do we live in
facts.answer: We live in a spiral galaxy called the Milky Way, which contains an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars. From inside it, the band of the Milky Way looks like a faint, milky stripe across the night sky. Our Sun is just one ordinary star in one of its spiral arms.

The Andromeda Galaxy is heading toward our Milky Way and the two will likely merge in about 4 to 5 billion years. Even so, the stars are so far apart that almost none will actually crash into each other. The two galaxies will eventually form one giant galaxy.

keywords: how many stars in the universe
facts.answer: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches. Scientists estimate there are at least a billion trillion stars, and possibly far more. Each of those stars could have its own planets.

A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. They form when very massive stars collapse at the end of their lives. Because no light gets out, black holes are invisible and we detect them by their effects on nearby matter.

The first-ever photo of a black hole was released in 2019, showing the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87. It looks like a fiery orange ring around a dark center. The image was made by linking telescopes around the world into one Earth-sized observatory.

A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers. It is a measure of distance, not time, even though it has the word year in it. Stars are so far away that astronomers use light years instead of kilometers.

The closest star to our Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light years away. Even though that sounds close in space terms, it would take a current spacecraft tens of thousands of years to get there. It is a small, dim red dwarf star.

Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star so enormous that if it replaced our Sun, it would swallow up Mercury, Venus, Earth, and even Mars. It is nearing the end of its life and will one day explode as a supernova. You can see it as a bright reddish star in the Orion constellation.

A supernova is the gigantic explosion of a dying star, which can briefly shine brighter than an entire galaxy. These blasts scatter elements like iron and gold into space, which later form new stars and planets. Many of the atoms in your body came from ancient supernovas.

A neutron star is the incredibly dense leftover core of a massive star that exploded as a supernova. Just one teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth. They can spin hundreds of times per second.

A constellation is a pattern of stars that people long ago imagined as a picture in the sky, like a hunter or a bear. There are 88 officially recognized constellations. The stars in a constellation usually aren't actually close together; they just look that way from Earth.

Polaris, the North Star, stays almost still in the sky while other stars appear to circle around it. This is because it sits nearly above Earth's North Pole. For centuries sailors used it to find north and navigate at night.

The northern and southern lights, called auroras, happen when particles from the Sun hit gases high in Earth's atmosphere. The collisions make the gases glow in greens, reds, and purples. They appear mostly near the North and South Poles where Earth's magnetic field guides the particles.

The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers above Earth and circles the planet roughly every 90 minutes. That means astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises and sunsets every day. It has been continuously occupied by people since the year 2000.

Astronauts float in space not because there is no gravity, but because they are in constant free fall around Earth along with their spacecraft. This falling together creates the feeling of weightlessness. Gravity is actually still quite strong up at the space station.

Yuri Gagarin of the Soviet Union became the first human in space on April 12, 1961. He orbited Earth once in his Vostok 1 spacecraft, a flight that lasted about 108 minutes. His journey opened the era of human spaceflight.

On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon during NASA's Apollo 11 mission. He was joined by Buzz Aldrin, while Michael Collins orbited above in the command module. Armstrong's famous words were one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.

keywords: how many people walked on the moon
facts.answer: Only 12 people have ever walked on the Moon, all American astronauts during the Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972. No human has returned to the Moon's surface since then. NASA's Artemis program plans to send astronauts back, including the first woman.

Space is silent because there is no air to carry sound waves. Sound needs a material like air or water to travel through, and space is mostly empty. So even a huge explosion in space would make no noise.

Planets stay in orbit around the Sun because of a balance between the Sun's gravity pulling them inward and their forward motion through space. Without gravity, they would fly off in straight lines. Without their speed, they would fall straight into the Sun.

Jupiter and Saturn are called gas giants because they are made mostly of hydrogen and helium gas with no solid surface to stand on. If you tried to land, you would just sink deeper into thicker and thicker gas. Their cores may be small and rocky deep inside.

Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because they contain a lot of icy materials like water, ammonia, and methane along with hydrogen and helium. The ices aren't frozen solid like an ice cube, but exist as hot, dense fluids inside. They are smaller than the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn.

Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are called terrestrial planets because they have solid, rocky surfaces. They are smaller and closer to the Sun than the giant outer planets. Earth is the largest of the four rocky planets.

Jupiter has the most known moons of any planet, with over 90 confirmed and counting. Its four largest, called the Galilean moons, were discovered by Galileo in 1610. They are named Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

Europa, one of Jupiter's moons, has a smooth icy surface covering a deep, salty ocean that may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. Because of this hidden ocean, scientists consider it one of the best places to search for alien life. Its surface is crisscrossed with cracks.

Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active world in the solar system, with hundreds of erupting volcanoes. Jupiter's powerful gravity squeezes and stretches Io, heating its insides. Its surface is splattered with yellow, orange, and red sulfur.

Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and it even has rivers and lakes. But those lakes aren't water; they are made of liquid methane and ethane. Titan is one of the most Earth-like worlds in some ways.

Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, shoots giant geysers of water and ice into space from its south pole. These plumes come from an underground ocean of liquid water. That hidden ocean makes Enceladus another exciting place to look for life.

Mars has two small, lumpy moons named Phobos and Deimos, which look more like potatoes than round worlds. They may be captured asteroids. Phobos is slowly spiraling toward Mars and will eventually break apart or crash into the planet.

keywords: is earth the only planet with life
facts.answer: As far as we know, Earth is the only planet with life. It sits in the just-right zone where water can stay liquid, and it has a protective atmosphere. Scientists are searching other worlds like Mars and Europa for signs of life, but none have been found yet.

The habitable zone, sometimes called the Goldilocks zone, is the region around a star where it is not too hot and not too cold for liquid water to exist. Earth sits comfortably inside the Sun's habitable zone. Scientists look for planets in other stars' habitable zones when searching for life.

An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Astronomers have confirmed thousands of them, and there are likely billions more in our galaxy. Some are giant gas worlds, while others are rocky and Earth-sized.

One main way scientists find exoplanets is the transit method, which watches for a tiny dip in a star's brightness when a planet passes in front of it. Another method detects a star's slight wobble caused by an orbiting planet's gravity. Most exoplanets are too small and far to photograph directly.

The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, according to scientists. It began with an event called the Big Bang, when everything expanded from an incredibly hot, dense state. The universe has been expanding and cooling ever since.

The Big Bang is the leading scientific explanation for how the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. It wasn't an explosion in space but the rapid expansion of space itself from a tiny, hot point. Everything we see today grew from that beginning.

The universe is expanding, meaning galaxies are moving farther apart over time. It is space itself stretching, like dots drawn on a balloon spreading apart as it inflates. This discovery helped scientists figure out the universe had a beginning.

Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, formed from a swirling cloud of gas and dust around the young Sun. Scientists figured this out by measuring radioactive atoms in very old rocks and meteorites. The whole solar system formed around the same time.

Earth has seasons because it is tilted about 23.5 degrees on its axis. As Earth orbits the Sun, different parts get more direct sunlight at different times of the year. It is the tilt, not Earth's distance from the Sun, that causes the seasons.

Even though you can't feel it, Earth is spinning very fast. At the equator, the surface moves at about 1,670 kilometers per hour. Earth also races around the Sun at roughly 107,000 kilometers per hour.

The sky looks blue because sunlight is made of all the colors, and Earth's air scatters the blue light more than other colors. This scattering spreads blue light across the whole sky. At sunset the light passes through more air, scattering away the blue and leaving reds and oranges.

Space looks black because it is mostly empty and has almost no air to scatter light, unlike Earth's sky. Stars and the Sun shine, but the space between them stays dark. Even in the daytime, an astronaut in space sees a black sky full of stars.

keywords: how big is the sun compared to earth
facts.answer: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth. You could line up about 109 Earths across the face of the Sun. And if the Sun were hollow, more than a million Earths could fit inside it.

The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, hot enough to vaporize any material we know. But the Sun's core is far hotter, around 15 million degrees Celsius. That extreme core heat powers the fusion that makes the Sun shine.

Solar flares are sudden bursts of energy and light from the Sun's surface. They can release as much energy as millions of nuclear bombs in just a few minutes. Strong flares can affect satellites, radio signals, and power grids on Earth.

Sunspots are darker, cooler patches on the Sun's surface caused by strong magnetic activity. They look dark only because they are cooler than the bright areas around them. Sunspots come and go in a roughly 11-year cycle.

The solar wind is a constant stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun in all directions. It travels through the whole solar system at hundreds of kilometers per second. Earth's magnetic field protects us from most of it, but it also helps create the auroras.

keywords: why earth has a magnetic field
facts.answer: Earth has a magnetic field created by the movement of liquid iron in its outer core. This invisible field acts like a giant shield, deflecting harmful particles from the Sun. Without it, our atmosphere could be slowly stripped away into space.

Mars once had rivers, lakes, and possibly even oceans of liquid water billions of years ago. Spacecraft have found dried-up riverbeds and minerals that only form in water. Today Mars is a cold desert, but its watery past makes it a top place to search for ancient life.

Several robotic rovers have explored Mars, driving across its surface and studying rocks and soil. Curiosity landed in 2012 and Perseverance landed in 2021, carrying tools to search for signs of ancient life. Perseverance even brought along a tiny helicopter named Ingenuity.

Ingenuity was a small helicopter that became the first aircraft to fly on another planet when it lifted off on Mars in 2021. Flying on Mars is tricky because the air is very thin, so its blades had to spin extremely fast. It flew dozens of times before its mission ended.

Mars can have enormous dust storms that sometimes grow to cover the entire planet for weeks or months. These storms can block out sunlight and make the sky hazy and orange. One giant storm in 2018 ended the mission of NASA's Opportunity rover.

Jupiter has rings, but they are faint and made of tiny dust particles, so they are hard to see. They were discovered by the Voyager 1 spacecraft in 1979. All four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, have rings.

All four giant planets in our solar system have rings, not just Saturn. Saturn's rings are by far the brightest and most spectacular. Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune have much fainter, darker rings that are difficult to spot.
Saturn has the most known moons in the solar system, with more than 140 confirmed. Many were discovered recently by powerful telescopes. Its largest moon, Titan, is bigger than the planet Mercury.

There are several recognized dwarf planets in our solar system, including Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea, and Makemake. Dwarf planets are round like regular planets but haven't cleared other objects out of their orbits. Astronomers think many more may exist far out in the solar system.

Eris is a distant dwarf planet about the same size as Pluto but even more massive. Its discovery in 2005 helped lead astronomers to reconsider what counts as a planet. Eris is so far away that it takes about 558 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.

The Kuiper Belt is a vast ring of icy objects beyond Neptune's orbit. It is home to Pluto and many other dwarf planets and comets. It is similar to the asteroid belt but much larger and made of icy bodies instead of rock.

The Oort Cloud is a giant spherical shell of icy objects thought to surround our entire solar system far beyond the planets. It is believed to be the source of long-period comets. It is so distant that no spacecraft has ever reached it.

Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to orbit the Sun once, so it hasn't even completed one full orbit since it was discovered in 1930. Its orbit is very stretched out, sometimes bringing it closer to the Sun than Neptune. Pluto is so far away that the Sun looks like just a very bright star from there.

keywords: how many planets in solar system
facts.answer: Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Before 2006 there were nine, but Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet. The four inner planets are rocky and the four outer ones are giants.

In order from the Sun, the planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. A popular memory trick is My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos. The first four are rocky and the last four are gas or ice giants.

Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system, only a little bigger than Earth's Moon. It is also the closest planet to the Sun. A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days because it zips around the Sun so quickly.

Mercury is the fastest planet, racing around the Sun at about 47 kilometers per second. That speed is why the Romans named it after their swift-footed messenger god. It completes a full orbit in only 88 Earth days.

Venus is the brightest planet in our night sky and is often called the morning star or evening star. It shines so brightly because thick clouds reflect a lot of sunlight. After the Moon, Venus is usually the brightest natural object in the night sky.

Venus is sometimes called Earth's twin because it is almost the same size and made of similar rocky material. But the two are wildly different in other ways. Venus has a crushing, super-hot atmosphere that makes it the most hostile planet for life.

keywords: why is earth called blue planet
facts.answer: Earth is nicknamed the Blue Planet because oceans cover about 71 percent of its surface, making it look blue from space. The first whole-Earth photo, called the Blue Marble, was taken by Apollo 17 astronauts in 1972. No other planet we know has so much liquid water on its surface.

The Moon is about 384,400 kilometers from Earth on average. That's far enough that all the other planets in the solar system could fit in the gap between Earth and the Moon. It took the Apollo astronauts about three days to travel there.

Jupiter spins faster than any other planet, finishing one day in just under 10 hours despite being the biggest planet. Its fast spin causes it to bulge out at the equator. The rapid rotation also helps drive its powerful storms and colorful bands.

keywords: how long is a day on saturn
facts.answer: A day on Saturn lasts only about 10.5 hours because it spins so quickly. This fast rotation flattens the planet slightly so it bulges at its middle. A year on Saturn, however, lasts about 29 Earth years.

Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun, located about 4.5 billion kilometers away. It is so distant that sunlight there is hundreds of times dimmer than on Earth. Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to complete one orbit.

Neptune is special because it was the first planet found through mathematics rather than just looking. Astronomers noticed Uranus wobbling in its orbit and calculated that an unseen planet's gravity must be tugging on it. In 1846 they pointed a telescope where the math predicted, and there was Neptune.

keywords: only spacecraft to visit uranus neptune
facts.answer: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, flying past them in the 1980s. It gave us most of the close-up photos we have of these distant ice giants. No mission has returned to either planet since then.

Stars twinkle because their light passes through Earth's moving atmosphere, which bends and wobbles the light on its way to our eyes. Planets usually don't twinkle as much because they appear as small disks rather than tiny points. Above the atmosphere, in space, stars shine steadily.

Stars come in different colors depending on their temperature. The hottest stars glow blue or white, medium ones like our Sun look yellow, and the coolest stars shine red. So a star's color tells astronomers how hot it is.

The Sun is actually white, but it often looks yellow or orange from Earth because our atmosphere scatters away some of its blue light. From space, astronauts see the Sun as bright white. Scientists call it a yellow dwarf star anyway.

Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in the galaxy, making up the majority of all stars. They are small, cool, and dim, which is why we can't easily see them without telescopes. They also burn their fuel slowly and can live for trillions of years.

Stars are born inside giant clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Gravity pulls the material together until the center becomes so hot and squeezed that nuclear fusion begins. That fusion lights the star up and starts its long life.

How a star dies depends on its size. Medium stars like our Sun puff up into red giants and then shed their outer layers, leaving a small hot core called a white dwarf. The most massive stars explode as supernovas and may become neutron stars or black holes.

A white dwarf is the small, hot, leftover core of a medium-sized star like our Sun after it has died. It is incredibly dense, packing nearly the mass of the Sun into something the size of Earth. White dwarfs slowly cool and fade over billions of years.

In about 5 billion years, our Sun will run low on fuel and swell into a huge red giant, possibly engulfing Mercury, Venus, and maybe Earth. Then it will shed its outer layers and leave behind a white dwarf. Don't worry; this is billions of years away.

A pulsar is a fast-spinning neutron star that beams out radio waves like a lighthouse. As it rotates, the beam sweeps past Earth, so we detect regular pulses of energy. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times every second.

At the center of our Milky Way galaxy is a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A-star. It has about 4 million times the mass of the Sun. Most large galaxies are thought to have a supermassive black hole at their center.

Galaxies come in different shapes. Spiral galaxies like the Milky Way have swirling arms, elliptical galaxies look like fuzzy egg-shaped balls of stars, and irregular galaxies have no clear shape. The universe contains billions of galaxies of all these types.

keywords: how many galaxies in the universe
facts.answer: Astronomers estimate there are at least 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, and possibly many more. Each galaxy can hold millions to trillions of stars. That makes the total number of stars almost unimaginably large.

Dark matter is a mysterious substance that scientists believe makes up most of the matter in the universe, yet we can't see it. We know it's there because its gravity affects how galaxies move. Scientists are still trying to figure out exactly what it is.

Dark energy is a mysterious force that scientists think is causing the universe to expand faster and faster. It seems to make up most of the energy in the universe. Like dark matter, no one yet knows exactly what it is.

The observable universe, the part we can see, stretches about 93 billion light years across. We can only see this far because light from more distant regions hasn't had time to reach us yet. The whole universe may be even larger, perhaps infinite.

The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits Earth and has taken some of the most stunning pictures of space ever seen. Being above the atmosphere lets it see clearly without the blur that affects telescopes on the ground. It has helped scientists make countless discoveries.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, is the most powerful space telescope ever built. It sees in infrared light, letting it peer through dust and look back at some of the earliest galaxies in the universe. It sits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.

Telescopes in space can see more clearly than those on the ground because they are above Earth's atmosphere, which blurs and blocks some light. Space telescopes can also detect kinds of light, like ultraviolet and infrared, that the atmosphere absorbs. That's why missions like Hubble and Webb are so valuable.

keywords: why is it hard to breathe in space
facts.answer: There is no air to breathe in space because it is almost a complete vacuum, nearly empty of any gas. Without a spacesuit or spacecraft, a person could not survive there. Astronauts carry their own oxygen supply wherever they go.

A spacesuit is like a personal spaceship that protects astronauts in the harsh environment of space. It provides oxygen, keeps the right pressure and temperature, and shields against radiation and tiny space debris. Modern spacesuits are heavy on Earth but feel weightless in space.

To leave Earth and reach space, a rocket must go very fast to overcome Earth's gravity, reaching what is called escape velocity, about 40,000 kilometers per hour. Rockets burn enormous amounts of fuel to reach such speeds. Going to orbit takes a bit less speed than escaping Earth completely.

Rockets work by pushing hot gas out the back at high speed, and this push sends the rocket forward in the opposite direction. This follows Newton's law that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Rockets can work in space because they don't need air to push against.

GPS works using a network of satellites orbiting Earth that constantly send out signals. Your phone or device listens to several of these signals and uses the tiny time differences to calculate exactly where you are. It takes signals from at least four satellites to pinpoint your location.

Space junk is human-made debris orbiting Earth, including broken satellites, old rocket parts, and tiny flecks of paint. Millions of pieces zoom around at thousands of kilometers per hour. Even a small piece can damage a spacecraft because it moves so fast.

Scientists explore Mars to learn whether life ever existed there and to understand how planets like Earth form and change. Mars is the most Earth-like planet we can easily reach. Studying it also helps prepare for the possibility of humans visiting one day.

keywords: how long to get to mars
facts.answer: A spacecraft typically takes about seven to nine months to travel from Earth to Mars. The exact time depends on the positions of the two planets in their orbits. The best launch windows come about every 26 months, when Earth and Mars line up well.

Mars is much smaller than Earth, with a diameter only about half of ours. Its surface area is roughly equal to all the dry land on Earth. Because it is smaller, its gravity is also weaker, only about 38 percent of Earth's.

Gravity on the Moon is only about one sixth as strong as on Earth. That's why astronauts could bounce and hop around so easily during the Apollo missions. A person who weighs 60 kilograms on Earth would feel like just 10 on the Moon.

Your weight would change a lot from planet to planet because each has different gravity. On Jupiter you would feel much heavier, while on Mars you would feel much lighter. The bigger and more massive a planet, the stronger its pull on you.

Jupiter has the strongest gravity of any planet in our solar system because it is the most massive. If you could stand on its cloud tops, you would feel about two and a half times heavier than on Earth. Its powerful gravity also helps protect the inner planets by pulling in some comets and asteroids.

Pluto is freezing cold, with temperatures around minus 230 degrees Celsius. It is so far from the Sun that it receives very little warmth and light. At those temperatures, gases like nitrogen and methane freeze solid on its surface.

NASA's New Horizons spacecraft made the first close-up flyby of Pluto in 2015 after a journey of more than nine years. It revealed Pluto's surprising heart-shaped feature, icy mountains, and frozen plains. The spacecraft then continued on to explore even more distant objects.

The Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn for 13 years, from 2004 to 2017, sending back incredible images of the planet, its rings, and moons. It dropped a probe called Huygens onto the moon Titan. At the end, Cassini dove into Saturn on purpose to avoid contaminating its moons.

Empty space is extremely cold, with a background temperature of about minus 270 degrees Celsius, just a few degrees above absolute zero. But near a star or in direct sunlight, things can also get very hot. Without air to spread heat, temperatures depend heavily on whether you are in sunlight or shadow.

Absolute zero is the coldest temperature possible, about minus 273 degrees Celsius, where atoms stop moving as much as they can. Nothing in the universe can get colder than this. The empty space between galaxies is only a few degrees warmer than absolute zero.

You couldn't stand or walk on Jupiter because it has no solid surface. It is a giant ball of gas that just gets thicker and hotter the deeper you go. Anyone trying to land would simply sink and be crushed by the enormous pressure.

keywords: jupiter could have been a star
facts.answer: Jupiter is sometimes called a failed star because it is made of the same gases as the Sun, mostly hydrogen and helium. But it is far too small to start nuclear fusion in its core. To become a real star, it would need to be about 80 times more massive.

Mars is a cold world, with an average temperature of about minus 60 degrees Celsius. On a warm summer day near the equator it might reach a comfortable temperature, but nights plunge far below freezing. Its thin atmosphere can't hold in much heat.

Mars has a very thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide, with less than one percent the air pressure at Earth's surface. The thin air means liquid water can't easily stay on the surface, and it provides little protection or warmth. Humans visiting Mars would need spacesuits to breathe.

Living on Mars would be very challenging because of its thin, unbreathable air, freezing temperatures, and harmful radiation. Future explorers would need sealed habitats, spacesuits, and a supply of oxygen and water. Scientists and engineers are studying how it might one day be possible.

About 66 million years ago, a giant asteroid roughly 10 kilometers wide slammed into Earth near what is now Mexico. The impact caused massive fires, tsunamis, and a cloud of dust that blocked the Sun for years. This event is thought to have wiped out the dinosaurs.

Near-Earth objects are asteroids and comets whose orbits bring them close to Earth's path around the Sun. Scientists track thousands of them to watch for any that might come dangerously close. So far, none pose a known threat in the near future.

In 2022, NASA's DART mission deliberately crashed a spacecraft into a small asteroid to test if we could change its path. The impact successfully nudged the asteroid into a slightly different orbit. It was the first real-world test of defending Earth from a dangerous asteroid.

Venus is wrapped in a thick layer of clouds made largely of sulfuric acid, which hide its surface from view. These clouds reflect most of the sunlight, making Venus very bright in our sky. They also help trap heat, making it the hottest planet.

The air pressure on the surface of Venus is about 90 times greater than on Earth. That is similar to the crushing pressure nearly a kilometer deep in our oceans. Early spacecraft that landed there were crushed and stopped working within an hour or two.

Mercury is covered in craters from countless impacts by asteroids and comets over billions of years. Because it has almost no atmosphere and little geological activity, these craters never get erased. Its surface looks a lot like our cratered Moon.

The Caloris Basin on Mercury is one of the largest impact craters in the solar system, about 1,550 kilometers wide. It was formed by a massive collision long ago. The crash was so powerful that it created jumbled terrain on the exact opposite side of the planet.

Earth's atmosphere has several layers. The troposphere is closest to the ground where weather happens, followed by the stratosphere which holds the ozone layer, then the mesosphere, thermosphere, and finally the exosphere that fades into space. The higher you go, the thinner the air becomes.

Space is generally said to begin at the Karman line, about 100 kilometers above Earth's surface. There is no hard boundary; the air just keeps getting thinner with height. Above this line, the air is too thin for normal aircraft to fly.

Planets and stars are round because their own gravity pulls everything toward the center equally, shaping them into spheres. Smaller objects like asteroids don't have enough gravity to do this, so they stay lumpy. Earth is actually slightly squished at the poles because it spins.

Earth is not a perfect sphere; it bulges slightly at the equator and is a little flattened at the poles. This happens because the planet spins, pushing material outward at the middle. Scientists call this slightly squashed shape an oblate spheroid.

Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge spinning cloud of gas and dust. Most of the material collapsed to the center and became the Sun, while the leftovers clumped together to form the planets. The cloud's spin is why the planets all orbit in roughly the same direction and plane.

keywords: why do all planets orbit the same direction
facts.answer: Almost all the planets orbit the Sun in the same direction because they formed from the same spinning cloud of gas and dust. They inherited that swirling motion from the original disk. Most planets also spin in that same direction, though Venus and Uranus are odd exceptions.

keywords: the moon is not made of cheese
what is the moon made of
facts.answer: Despite the old joke, the Moon is not made of cheese; it is made of rock and dust. Its surface has a powdery gray layer called regolith, created by countless tiny impacts. Astronauts brought back hundreds of kilograms of Moon rocks for scientists to study.

keywords: why no air on the moon
facts.answer: The Moon has almost no atmosphere, which is why its sky is always black even in daytime and why there is no weather. With no air to trap heat, its temperatures swing wildly between scorching days and freezing nights. The lack of air is also why sound can't travel there.

keywords: why is the moon different sizes
facts.answer: The Moon sometimes looks bigger or smaller because its orbit around Earth is not a perfect circle. When the full moon is at its closest point, it appears larger and brighter and is nicknamed a supermoon. The Moon also looks bigger near the horizon, but that is actually an optical illusion.

keywords: how many moons does earth have
facts.answer: Earth has just one natural moon, simply called the Moon. It is unusually large compared to its planet, the fifth-largest moon in the entire solar system. Some other planets, like Jupiter and Saturn, have dozens of moons each.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun, sitting just the right distance away for liquid water and life. It is the largest of the four rocky inner planets. So far it is the only place in the universe known to support living things.

Uranus has a pale blue-green color because of methane gas in its atmosphere, which absorbs red light and reflects blue and green. Its color is fairly plain and featureless compared to the swirling bands of Jupiter and Saturn. Uranus is the coldest planet in the solar system.

Uranus is the coldest planet in the solar system, with temperatures dropping to around minus 224 degrees Celsius. Surprisingly, it is even colder than Neptune, which is farther from the Sun. Scientists think Uranus may have lost most of its internal heat long ago.

Scientists think it may rain diamonds deep inside Neptune and Uranus. The intense heat and crushing pressure squeeze carbon atoms together until they form solid diamonds. These diamonds may sink slowly toward the planets' cores.

keywords: how long is a year on neptune
facts.answer: A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years, since it is so far from the Sun and has such a long orbit to travel. Neptune was discovered in 1846 and completed its very first full orbit since discovery in 2011. A single Neptune day, however, is only about 16 hours.

keywords: how many earths fit in jupiter
facts.answer: Jupiter is so enormous that about 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. Across its widest part you could line up roughly 11 Earths. Yet Jupiter is much lighter for its size than Earth because it is made of gas.

keywords: why is saturn famous for rings
facts.answer: Saturn is famous for having the brightest and most beautiful rings in the solar system. They are so large and shiny that you can see them through a small backyard telescope. Scientists are still debating exactly how and when these rings formed.

keywords: how many rings does saturn have
facts.answer: Saturn's rings are organized into several main groups, labeled with letters like A, B, and C in the order they were discovered. Each main ring is actually made of thousands of thinner ringlets. Gaps between them, like the Cassini Division, are carved by the gravity of nearby moons.

Astronauts sleep by strapping themselves into sleeping bags attached to the wall so they don't float around and bump into things. There is no up or down in space, so they can sleep in any orientation. Many wear eye masks because the Sun rises every 90 minutes on the space station.

Astronauts can grow up to a few centimeters taller while in space. Without gravity squeezing them down, the spaces between the bones in their spine stretch out. Once they return to Earth, their height goes back to normal.

Astronauts eat specially prepared foods, often dried or packaged so they don't make crumbs or spill in weightlessness. They add water to many meals to rehydrate them. Salt and pepper come as liquids so the grains don't float away and get into equipment.

keywords: how astronauts use the bathroom in space
facts.answer: Going to the bathroom in space requires special toilets that use airflow, like a vacuum, instead of water to pull waste away. Astronauts strap themselves down so they don't float off. On the space station, water from urine is even recycled into clean drinking water.

keywords: why is the milky way called that
facts.answer: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way because from Earth it appears as a faint, milky band of light stretching across the night sky. That glow comes from billions of distant stars too far to see one by one. The name comes from a Greek word meaning milky circle.

keywords: can you see the milky way
facts.answer: You can see the Milky Way with your own eyes, but only from dark places far from city lights. It appears as a hazy, cloudy band stretching across the sky. Light pollution from cities hides it from many people today.

keywords: why can't i see stars in the city
facts.answer: Light pollution is the brightening of the night sky from artificial lights like streetlamps and buildings. It makes it hard to see stars in cities, sometimes hiding all but the brightest few. Going to a dark rural area reveals thousands more stars.

The telescope was invented in the early 1600s in the Netherlands, and Galileo soon built his own to study the sky in 1609. With it he discovered Jupiter's moons, craters on the Moon, and the phases of Venus. The telescope transformed how we understand the universe.

Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who used a telescope in the early 1600s to make groundbreaking discoveries. He spotted four moons orbiting Jupiter, mountains on the Moon, and the phases of Venus. His observations supported the idea that Earth orbits the Sun, not the other way around.

In the 1500s, the astronomer Copernicus proposed that the Sun, not Earth, sits at the center of the solar system. This idea, called the heliocentric model, was shocking at the time because people believed Earth was the center of everything. Later observations proved Copernicus was right.

keywords: why don't we feel earth moving
facts.answer: We don't feel Earth spinning and racing around the Sun because everything around us, including the air, moves along with it at the same steady speed. It's similar to riding in a smooth car or plane where you don't feel the motion. Only changes in speed, not steady motion, can be felt.

Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun, not exactly 365. To keep our calendar in line, we add an extra day, February 29, almost every four years, which we call a leap year. Without leap years, the seasons would slowly drift out of place over time.

keywords: why does the moon look bigger near the horizon
facts.answer: The Moon looks bigger when it is near the horizon, but this is actually an optical illusion called the Moon illusion. The Moon is the same size whether high or low; our brains just judge it as larger when we compare it to trees and buildings. You can test this by measuring it with your thumb.

keywords: why do we see different stars in different seasons
facts.answer: We see different stars in different seasons because Earth orbits the Sun, so at night we face different parts of space throughout the year. The constellations visible in winter are different from those in summer. Over a full year, the whole circle of stars passes through our night sky.

The zodiac is a band of 12 constellations that lie along the path the Sun appears to travel through the sky over a year. Ancient peoples gave them names like Leo the lion and Scorpius the scorpion. The Sun passes in front of each of them at different times of the year.

Orion is one of the easiest constellations to spot, named after a hunter in Greek mythology. Its most famous feature is Orion's Belt, a row of three bright stars in a line. The constellation also contains the glowing Orion Nebula, where new stars are being born.

The Big Dipper is a well-known group of seven bright stars shaped like a ladle or pan. It is actually part of a larger constellation called Ursa Major, the Great Bear. The two stars at the end of its bowl point toward the North Star.

The Southern Cross, or Crux, is a small but famous constellation visible from the Southern Hemisphere. It appears on the flags of several countries including Australia and New Zealand. People in the south use it to help find the direction of the South Pole.

Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky, sometimes called the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major, the big dog. It looks so bright partly because it is fairly close to us, only about 8.6 light years away. It is actually two stars orbiting each other.

Astronomers measure the distance to nearby stars using a method called parallax. They observe how a star seems to shift slightly against the background when viewed from opposite sides of Earth's orbit. The bigger the shift, the closer the star is.

keywords: why is venus called morning and evening star
facts.answer: Venus is often the first starlike point to appear after sunset or the last to fade before sunrise, so people call it the evening star or morning star. It is actually a planet, not a star. Because its orbit is inside Earth's, Venus always appears near the Sun in our sky.

keywords: can you see planets without a telescope
facts.answer: You can see five planets without a telescope: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. They look like bright stars but usually don't twinkle the way real stars do. People have watched these wandering lights move across the sky since ancient times.

The word planet comes from a Greek word meaning wanderer. Ancient sky watchers noticed that planets slowly moved against the background of fixed stars, as if wandering across the sky. The other stars seemed to stay in the same patterns night after night.

keywords: solar system in motion around galaxy
facts.answer: Our entire solar system orbits the center of the Milky Way galaxy, carrying the Sun and planets along at about 800,000 kilometers per hour. Even at that speed, one trip around the galaxy takes about 225 million years. The last time the Sun was in its current spot, dinosaurs were just beginning to appear.

Space is almost entirely empty, with vast distances between stars and even larger gaps between galaxies. The bits of matter we see, like stars and planets, make up just a tiny fraction of the universe. Most of space is a near-perfect vacuum with hardly any atoms in it.

The cosmic microwave background is faint leftover light from the early universe, dating to about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. It fills all of space and is the oldest light we can detect. Studying it has taught scientists a great deal about how the universe began.

keywords: how do we know what stars are made of
facts.answer: Scientists can tell what stars are made of by carefully studying their light. When starlight is split into a rainbow of colors, certain dark lines reveal which elements are present. This clever technique is called spectroscopy.

keywords: why is the sun important for earth
facts.answer: The Sun is essential for life on Earth because it provides the light and heat that keep our planet warm enough for liquid water. Plants use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis, forming the base of nearly all food chains. The Sun's gravity also keeps Earth in its life-friendly orbit.

Plants capture energy from sunlight and use it to turn water and carbon dioxide into food and oxygen, a process called photosynthesis. Nearly all life on Earth depends on this, either by eating plants or eating animals that eat plants. So the energy in most food originally came from the Sun.

Jupiter's enormous gravity helps protect the inner planets by pulling in or flinging away many comets and asteroids that might otherwise threaten Earth. Some scientists call it a cosmic vacuum cleaner. In 1994, astronomers watched a comet smash into Jupiter rather than wandering toward us.

On Mars, sunsets appear blue, the opposite of Earth's reddish sunsets. This happens because the fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters light differently than Earth's air does. Rovers have photographed these eerie blue Martian sunsets.

keywords: highest mountain on earth vs space
facts.answer: Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level on Earth, reaching about 8.8 kilometers. While that's huge for our planet, it's tiny compared to Mars's Olympus Mons, which is more than twice as tall. Earth's own active geology keeps its mountains from growing as enormous.

Measured from its base on the ocean floor to its peak, the Hawaiian volcano Mauna Kea is actually taller than Mount Everest, at over 10 kilometers. Most of it is hidden underwater. Its summit is also home to some of the world's best telescopes because of the clear, dark skies.

Astronauts train underwater because floating in a giant pool feels similar to the weightlessness of space. They practice spacewalks and repairs in full suits inside huge water tanks. This helps them get used to moving and working without the pull of gravity.

A spacewalk is when an astronaut leaves the spacecraft to work outside in space, wearing a protective suit. Astronauts do spacewalks to repair equipment, build structures, or run experiments. They stay attached by tethers so they don't float away.

keywords: how many countries have sent humans to space
facts.answer: Only a few countries have launched their own humans into space using their own rockets, including Russia, the United States, and China. Many other countries have sent astronauts up aboard these rockets. Hundreds of people from dozens of nations have now traveled to space.

Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union became the first woman in space in 1963. She orbited Earth 48 times during her three-day mission. It would be about 20 years before another woman flew to space.

Before humans went to space, scientists sent animals to see if it was safe. Fruit flies, monkeys, and dogs were among the first space travelers. A dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth in 1957.

keywords: why we send robots to space
facts.answer: Scientists send robotic probes to explore places that are too dangerous or too far for humans. Robots can survive extreme heat, cold, and radiation, and they don't need food or air. Spacecraft like rovers and orbiters have explored every planet in our solar system.

The Mariner spacecraft were among the first probes to explore other planets in the 1960s and 1970s. Mariner 2 made the first successful flyby of Venus in 1962. Mariner 10 became the first spacecraft to visit Mercury.

keywords: why does the sun look bigger than other stars
facts.answer: The Sun looks much larger and brighter than other stars only because it is incredibly close to us compared to them. Other stars are trillions of kilometers away, so they appear as tiny points of light. If our Sun were that far away, it would look like just another faint star.

Light travels at about 300,000 kilometers per second, the fastest speed in the universe. Nothing can travel faster than light. Even at that incredible speed, light from distant stars can take thousands or millions of years to reach us.

keywords: looking into space is looking back in time
facts.answer: When you look at distant stars and galaxies, you are actually seeing light that left them long ago, so you're looking into the past. Some stars you see may have already died. The farther away an object is, the older the light is by the time it reaches you.

Scientists think some of Earth's water may have arrived from comets and asteroids that crashed into the young planet billions of years ago. These icy visitors could have delivered water that helped fill the oceans. Some water also came from inside Earth itself.
Every planet spins around an invisible line through its center called its axis. This spinning is what gives planets their days and nights. Earth's axis is tilted, which is what gives us our seasons.

Space missions are expensive because rockets, spacecraft, and the technology to survive in space all require advanced engineering and years of careful work. Everything must be tested thoroughly because mistakes in space can't easily be fixed. Still, space exploration has led to many inventions we use on Earth.

Many everyday inventions came from technology developed for space exploration. Memory foam, scratch-resistant lenses, water filters, and improved camera sensors all have roots in space research. These useful spinoffs benefit people who never leave Earth.

keywords: why mars has the biggest volcano
facts.answer: Mars has the biggest volcanoes partly because, unlike Earth, its surface doesn't shift around on moving plates. On Earth, plates slide over hot spots, so a volcano can only grow so big before moving away. On Mars the volcano sits in place for ages, letting lava pile up into a giant mountain.

Earth is the only planet known to have plate tectonics, where its outer shell is broken into giant moving pieces. These shifting plates build mountains, cause earthquakes, and recycle the surface over time. Other rocky planets seem to have a single solid shell instead.

keywords: how big is the asteroid belt
facts.answer: The asteroid belt stretches across a huge region between Mars and Jupiter, but its asteroids are spread incredibly far apart. If you flew a spacecraft through it, you would likely never see one nearby. Movies that show asteroids packed close together aren't realistic.

Vesta is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt and the brightest asteroid as seen from Earth. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited and studied it in 2011. Vesta has a giant crater near its south pole from an ancient collision.

Centaurs are icy objects that orbit the Sun between Jupiter and Neptune, behaving like a mix of asteroids and comets. They were named after the mythical creatures that were part human and part horse. Their orbits are often unstable and can change over time.

The Moon appears gray because its surface is covered in rock and dust that reflects sunlight in a fairly colorless way. Up close, astronauts described the Moon's dust as gray, like fireplace ashes or charcoal. From Earth it can look slightly yellow because of our atmosphere.

The Moon is covered in craters made by asteroids and meteorites smashing into it over billions of years. Because the Moon has no air, water, or weather, the craters never wear away. Some of the biggest craters are visible from Earth as the Moon's darker patches.

The dark patches you can see on the Moon are huge plains of ancient hardened lava called maria, which is Latin for seas. Early astronomers thought they looked like oceans, though they hold no water. The lighter areas are older, more heavily cratered highlands.

Many cultures see shapes in the Moon's surface, like the famous man in the Moon or a rabbit. These imagined pictures come from the pattern of dark maria and lighter highlands. Because the same side of the Moon always faces us, everyone sees the same patterns.

keywords: how big is the universe getting
facts.answer: The universe is not only expanding but speeding up its expansion over time. Distant galaxies are racing away from us faster and faster. Scientists think a mysterious force called dark energy is driving this acceleration.

keywords: why can't we travel to other stars easily
facts.answer: Traveling to other stars is extremely hard because the distances are so vast. Even the nearest star beyond the Sun is over four light years away, and our fastest spacecraft would take tens of thousands of years to reach it. New kinds of propulsion would be needed for such journeys.

Astronomers have found many exoplanets that are roughly Earth-sized and orbit in their star's habitable zone. Some could possibly have liquid water and the right conditions for life. So far we don't know if any truly resemble Earth, but the search continues.

TRAPPIST-1 is a small, cool star about 40 light years away that has seven rocky planets orbiting it. Several of these planets sit in the zone where liquid water might exist. It is one of the most exciting planetary systems scientists have found for studying possible life.

Hot Jupiters are giant gas planets, similar in size to Jupiter, that orbit extremely close to their stars. They zip around in just a few days and are scorching hot. Their discovery surprised scientists, who hadn't expected huge planets so near their suns.

Rogue planets are planets that don't orbit any star and instead drift alone through the galaxy. They may have been flung out of their original solar systems long ago. Without a star to warm them, these wandering worlds are cold and dark.

Although space is silent because it has no air, spacecraft can detect radio waves and other signals from planets and stars. Scientists sometimes convert these signals into sounds we can hear, creating eerie space tunes. These aren't real sounds traveling through space, but they help us understand cosmic activity.

keywords: how long is a day on mars
facts.answer: A day on Mars is only slightly longer than a day on Earth, lasting about 24 hours and 39 minutes. Scientists call a Martian day a sol. This similarity makes Mars feel a bit familiar compared to other planets.

keywords: how long is a year on mars
facts.answer: A year on Mars is almost twice as long as an Earth year, lasting about 687 Earth days. This is because Mars is farther from the Sun and takes longer to complete its orbit. Mars has seasons like Earth, but each one lasts roughly twice as long.

keywords: how long is a year on different planets
facts.answer: A year is the time a planet takes to orbit the Sun, and it varies wildly. Mercury's year is just 88 Earth days, while Neptune's year lasts about 165 Earth years. The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year.

keywords: how long is a day on different planets
facts.answer: A day is how long a planet takes to spin once, and it differs greatly from planet to planet. Jupiter spins fastest, finishing a day in under 10 hours, while Venus takes 243 Earth days. Earth and Mars have similar day lengths of about 24 hours.
Mercury has no moons at all. Being so close to the Sun, its gravity competes with the Sun's powerful pull, making it hard to hold onto a moon. Venus is the only other planet with no moons.

Mercury and Venus are the only two planets in our solar system with no moons. Earth has one, Mars has two, and the giant outer planets each have dozens. Scientists think being close to the Sun made it hard for Mercury and Venus to keep moons.

keywords: why planets orbit in a flat plane
facts.answer: The planets all orbit the Sun in roughly the same flat plane, like marbles rolling around on a tabletop. This is because they formed from a flat, spinning disk of gas and dust. Pluto's orbit, however, is tilted noticeably out of this plane.

Some scientists and companies dream of mining asteroids for valuable metals like iron, nickel, and even gold and platinum. A single metal-rich asteroid could contain more of some metals than have ever been mined on Earth. Reaching and mining them, though, would be very challenging.

Psyche is an unusual asteroid thought to be made largely of metal, possibly the leftover core of an early planet. NASA launched a spacecraft to study it up close. Learning about Psyche may help scientists understand what planet cores are like.
