Jupiter has colorful stripes because of bands of clouds blowing in different directions at high speeds. Lighter bands are rising clouds, while darker belts are sinking ones, made of different chemicals. The planet's fast spin stretches these clouds into long stripes around it.

Jupiter has powerful auroras at its poles, far brighter and bigger than Earth's northern lights. They glow because of charged particles guided by Jupiter's strong magnetic field. Several other planets, including Saturn, also have auroras.

Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet, about 20,000 times stronger than Earth's. This huge magnetic field creates intense radiation belts around the planet. Spacecraft visiting Jupiter need special shielding to survive the radiation.

Saturn has a giant six-sided storm, shaped like a hexagon, swirling around its north pole. Each side of this hexagon is longer than the width of Earth. Scientists are still studying why this strange geometric shape forms.

keywords: why is space called the final frontier
facts.answer: Space is sometimes called the final frontier because it is the vast unknown that humans have only just begun to explore. After exploring Earth's land and seas, space remains the next great region to discover. There is far more out there than we could ever explore in a lifetime.

keywords: why doesn't the sun burn out fast
facts.answer: The Sun won't burn out for a very long time because it has a huge supply of hydrogen fuel and uses it slowly through nuclear fusion. It is about 4.6 billion years old and has roughly 5 billion more years to shine. So the Sun is only about middle-aged.

Stars like the Sun make their energy through nuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms are squeezed together to form helium. This process releases enormous amounts of energy as light and heat. It happens in the star's super-hot, high-pressure core.

keywords: how big is the sun's gravity
facts.answer: The Sun's gravity is incredibly strong because it is so massive, about 28 times stronger at its surface than Earth's gravity. This powerful pull keeps all the planets, asteroids, and comets in orbit around it. Its gravity reaches across the entire solar system.

A coronal mass ejection is a giant burst of charged gas, called plasma, flung out from the Sun. These eruptions can send billions of tons of material racing through space. If one hits Earth, it can cause stunning auroras but also disrupt satellites and power systems.

keywords: how the sun affects weather in space
facts.answer: Activity on the Sun, like flares and solar storms, creates what scientists call space weather. Strong space weather can disturb satellites, GPS, radio signals, and even power grids on Earth. Scientists monitor the Sun closely to give warnings about big solar storms.

keywords: why earth has an ozone layer
facts.answer: Earth's ozone layer is a region high in the atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays. Without it, this radiation would harm plants, animals, and people. The ozone layer acts like sunscreen for the whole planet.

An adult human body has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 300, but many of these fuse together as we grow. The skull alone is made of 22 separate bones held together by jagged seams called sutures.

The smallest bone in your body is the stapes, found deep inside your ear. It is shaped like a tiny stirrup and is about the size of a grain of rice. It helps pass sound vibrations to the inner ear so you can hear.
The femur, or thigh bone, is the largest and strongest bone in the human body. It runs from your hip to your knee. Bone for bone, it can support around 30 times the weight of an adult person.

Bones are strong because they combine hard mineral crystals with a tough, flexible protein called collagen. The minerals make bones rigid while the collagen keeps them from snapping easily. This mix makes bone stronger than steel for its weight.

Bone marrow is the soft, spongy tissue inside many of your bones. It is a busy factory that makes new red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Your body produces billions of new blood cells there every single day.

Bones can heal themselves after a break, which most other hard materials cannot do. Special cells build a soft bridge of new tissue across the crack, then harden it into bone. A simple fracture often knits back together in six to eight weeks.
The human body has around 600 muscles. They make up nearly 40 percent of your total body weight. You use about 200 different muscles just to take a single step.

For its size, the masseter, your jaw muscle, is one of the strongest in the body. It can clench your back teeth together with a force of over 90 kilograms. That is the power that lets you crunch hard foods.

The heart is often called the hardest-working muscle because it never takes a break. It beats around 100,000 times a day, every day of your life. Unlike other muscles, it can keep going without ever getting tired.

Smiling and frowning both use lots of facial muscles, and scientists still argue over the exact counts. What is clear is that your face has more than 40 muscles, letting you make thousands of different expressions. That is why your face can show so many feelings.

Some muscles work without you thinking about them, called involuntary muscles. These include the smooth muscles that push food through your gut and the muscle of your heart. They keep working even while you sleep.

keywords: how fast do nerves send messages
facts.answer: Nerve signals can travel through your body at speeds of up to about 120 metres per second, faster than a race car. That is how you can yank your hand away from something hot almost instantly. Messages zip between your brain and body constantly.

The human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, the cells that carry messages. Each neuron can connect to thousands of others, making trillions of links. This web of connections lets you think, remember, and feel.

Your brain is only about 2 percent of your body weight, but it uses around 20 percent of your energy. It is one of the hungriest organs you have. Most of that energy keeps your neurons sending signals.

The brain itself has no pain receptors, so it cannot feel pain directly. This is why surgeons can sometimes operate on a brain while the patient is awake. The headaches you feel come from tissues and blood vessels around the brain, not the brain itself.

Your brain is split into two halves called hemispheres, joined by a thick band of nerve fibres. In general, the left half controls the right side of your body and the right half controls the left side. The two halves constantly share information with each other.
About 60 percent of an adult human body is made of water. Babies are even wetter, at around 75 percent water. Your brain and heart are roughly 73 percent water, while your lungs are about 83 percent.

An average adult has about 5 litres of blood, enough to fill a large soda bottle and a half. Blood makes up roughly 7 to 8 percent of your body weight. Children have less because their bodies are smaller.

If you laid all of an adult's blood vessels end to end, they would stretch about 100,000 kilometres. That is long enough to wrap around the Earth more than twice. Most of that length is made of tiny vessels called capillaries.

Blood is red because of a protein called haemoglobin that carries oxygen inside red blood cells. Haemoglobin contains iron, which turns bright red when it grabs oxygen. Blood low on oxygen looks a darker brick-red, not blue.

keywords: how long red blood cells live
facts.answer: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days before it wears out. Your body then recycles its parts and replaces it. You make around 2 million new red blood cells every second to keep up.

keywords: what do white blood cells do
facts.answer: White blood cells are the soldiers of your immune system. They patrol your blood and tissues hunting down germs, viruses, and other invaders. Some swallow germs whole, while others make special chemicals to destroy them.

Platelets are tiny cell fragments in your blood that help you stop bleeding. When you get a cut, they rush to the spot and stick together to form a plug. They also help build the scab that protects the wound while it heals.

A scab is a natural bandage your body builds over a cut. Platelets and a protein called fibrin form a mesh that traps blood cells and dries into a hard crust. This crust keeps germs out while new skin grows underneath.

A bruise happens when a bump breaks tiny blood vessels under your skin without breaking the skin itself. The leaked blood shows through as a mark. The colour changes from red to purple to green to yellow as your body cleans up the blood.

Your lungs pull air in so your body can grab oxygen and breathe out waste gas called carbon dioxide. Inside are around 300 to 500 million tiny air sacs called alveoli. Spread flat, their surface would cover roughly the size of a tennis court.

An adult at rest breathes about 12 to 20 times a minute, adding up to over 20,000 breaths a day. You barely notice because breathing is mostly automatic. Over a lifetime you take hundreds of millions of breaths.

Scientists are still not certain why we yawn, but one leading idea is that it helps cool down the brain. Yawning is also contagious, meaning seeing someone yawn can make you yawn too. Even reading about yawning can set one off.

A hiccup happens when your diaphragm, the breathing muscle under your lungs, suddenly jerks. This makes you gulp air, and a flap in your throat snaps shut to make the hic sound. Hiccups often start after eating too fast or swallowing air.

A sneeze is your body's way of blasting irritating dust, pollen, or germs out of your nose. The air from a sneeze can shoot out at speeds of around 160 kilometres per hour. You cannot keep your eyes open during a full sneeze.

A cough is a quick burst of air that clears your throat and airways of mucus or things that should not be there. Sensors in your airway trigger the cough automatically. It is one of your lungs' main ways of protecting themselves.

Your heart is a muscular pump about the size of your fist. It squeezes to push blood out to your whole body and then relaxes to fill up again. In a single day it pumps enough blood to fill a large swimming pool.

The heart has four hollow rooms called chambers. The two on top are atria, which receive blood, and the two on the bottom are ventricles, which pump it out. Valves between them act like one-way doors so blood flows in the right direction.

The lub-dub sound of a heartbeat comes from the valves snapping shut. The lub is the valves between the upper and lower chambers closing. The dub is the valves leading out to the body and lungs closing right after.
A resting adult heart usually beats 60 to 100 times a minute. Children's hearts beat faster, often around 70 to 120 times a minute. The smaller you are, the faster your heart tends to go.

The liver is your largest internal organ, sitting on the right side under your ribs. It does over 500 different jobs, including filtering toxins from your blood and storing energy. It is also the only organ that can regrow itself if part is removed.
Your two kidneys are bean-shaped filters about the size of your fist. They clean your blood and turn the waste into urine. Together they filter all of your blood about 30 times a day.

An average adult makes about 1 to 2 litres of urine each day. The colour tells you about hydration: pale yellow usually means well hydrated, while dark yellow can mean you need more water. Your kidneys decide how much water to keep or release.

The spleen is an organ on the left side of your belly that helps clean your blood. It filters out old, worn-out red blood cells and stores some blood as a backup. It also helps your immune system fight certain infections.

The pancreas is an organ behind your stomach with two big jobs. It makes juices that help your gut break down food, and it makes hormones like insulin that control your blood sugar. Without insulin, your body cannot use sugar for energy properly.

Your small intestine is about 6 to 7 metres long, coiled up neatly inside your belly. The large intestine adds another 1.5 metres or so. Together they are much longer than you are tall, but folding lets them fit.

It takes food roughly 24 to 72 hours to travel all the way through your digestive system. Chewing and the stomach do the early work in a few hours. The slow part is the intestines pulling out nutrients and water.

Your stomach makes a strong acid that helps break down food and kill germs. It is acidic enough to dissolve some metals, yet a slimy mucus layer protects your stomach wall. Your body replaces that lining about every few days to stay safe.

Your stomach growls when muscles squeeze gas and fluids through your empty digestive tube. The fancy name for it is borborygmus. It often gets louder when you are hungry because your gut is clearing out to get ready for food.
Saliva, or spit, does more than keep your mouth wet. It starts breaking down food, helps you taste, and protects your teeth from germs. You make about 1 to 1.5 litres of saliva every day.

You have around 2,000 to 10,000 taste buds, mostly on your tongue. They detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savoury. Taste buds wear out and get replaced about every one to two weeks.

keywords: why food tastes bland with cold
facts.answer: Most of what you think is taste is actually smell. Your nose and tongue work together to create flavour. That is why food tastes bland when your nose is stuffed up from a cold.

Scientists estimate humans can tell apart around a trillion different smells. Your nose has millions of smell receptors that send signals straight to your brain. Smells are also strongly linked to memory, which is why a scent can suddenly bring back an old moment.

Your ears pop when the air pressure inside changes, often on a plane or in the mountains. A small tube connects your middle ear to your throat to balance the pressure. The pop is that tube opening to let air move in or out.

Deep in your inner ear are tiny loops filled with fluid that help you keep your balance. When you move or spin, the fluid sloshes and tells your brain which way you are tilting. Spinning fast can confuse them, which is why you feel dizzy afterwards.

keywords: why we get dizzy when spinning
facts.answer: When you spin, the fluid in your inner ear keeps swirling for a moment after you stop. Your brain still thinks you are moving, so the world seems to spin. The dizzy feeling fades once the fluid settles down.

The black circle in your eye, the pupil, changes size to control how much light gets in. In bright light it shrinks to protect your eye, and in dim light it grows wide to gather more light. This happens automatically without you thinking about it.

A blink takes only about a tenth of a second, faster than you can notice. You blink around 15 to 20 times a minute, which adds up to thousands of times a day. Blinking spreads tears to keep your eyes clean and moist.

Eyebrows help keep sweat and rain out of your eyes by steering it to the sides of your face. They also help you show feelings, like surprise or anger, with just a small movement. Humans are very good at reading each other's eyebrows.

Eyelashes act like a dust shield for your eyes. They catch tiny bits of dirt and trigger a fast blink if something gets too close. They also help slow the air around your eyes so they do not dry out as quickly.

You actually make three kinds of tears. Basal tears keep your eyes wet all the time, reflex tears flush out irritants like onion fumes, and emotional tears come when you feel strong feelings. Emotional tears even have a slightly different chemical makeup.
Cutting an onion releases a gas that floats up to your eyes. When it mixes with the water on your eyes it forms a mild acid that stings. Your eyes make reflex tears to wash the irritation away.

Colour blindness means a person sees certain colours differently, most often red and green. It happens when some of the colour-sensing cells in the eye do not work the usual way. It is far more common in boys than in girls.

Your eyes see colour using cells called cones at the back of the eye. Most people have three kinds of cones that detect red, green, and blue light. Your brain blends their signals to create every colour you see.
Your eyes use cells called rods to see in dim light. Rods do not detect colour, which is why things look grey at night. It can take your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to fully adjust to the dark.

Your skin is the largest organ of your body. An adult's skin can cover an area of about 2 square metres and weigh several kilograms. It protects you from germs, helps control your temperature, and lets you feel touch.

Your skin has three main layers. The outer layer, the epidermis, is your waterproof shield. Below it the dermis holds nerves, blood vessels, and sweat glands, and the deepest layer stores fat for warmth and cushioning.

Your skin is always renewing itself, with the outer layer fully replacing about every month. You shed roughly 30,000 to 40,000 dead skin cells every minute. Much of household dust is actually made of these flakes of old skin.

Sweating is your body's air-conditioning system. When you get hot, glands release sweat onto your skin, and as it dries it carries heat away to cool you down. You have millions of sweat glands all over your body.

Fresh sweat is mostly water and salt and barely smells at all. The smell comes from harmless bacteria on your skin feeding on the sweat. Their leftovers create the odour, which is why washing keeps you fresher.

Goosebumps appear when tiny muscles at the base of your hairs pull tight. This is a leftover reflex from our furry ancestors, who would fluff up to look bigger or stay warm. We get them when cold or feeling strong emotions.

Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, which is faster than toenails. Nails grow quicker on your dominant hand and a bit faster in summer. They are made of a tough protein called keratin, the same stuff in your hair.

Hair is made of a strong protein called keratin, the same material as your nails. The part you can see is actually not alive, which is why a haircut does not hurt. New hair grows from living roots tucked under your skin.
The average person has about 100,000 to 150,000 hairs on their head. You naturally lose around 50 to 100 hairs a day, which is completely normal. New hairs grow from the same roots to replace them.

Hair gets its colour from a pigment called melanin made by cells in the roots. As you age, those cells slowly make less melanin, so new hair grows in grey or white. The age this starts is mostly decided by your genes.

Everyone's fingerprints are unique, even identical twins have different ones. They form before you are born, partly shaped by how you moved in the womb. The ridges help you grip objects and feel textures.

Adults usually have 32 teeth in four types. Sharp incisors at the front bite, pointy canines tear, and flatter premolars and molars at the back grind food. Each shape is built for a different job in chewing.

Children grow 20 baby teeth, also called milk teeth, that start coming in around six months old. These fall out one by one starting around age six. Bigger adult teeth then push up to take their place.

The enamel coating your teeth is the hardest substance your body makes, even harder than bone. It protects the softer inside of the tooth from biting and chewing. Unlike bone, enamel cannot grow back once it is damaged.

The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to your large intestine. For a long time people thought it was useless, but it may store helpful gut bacteria. People can live perfectly well without it if it is removed.

The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that sits under your lungs and does most of your breathing. When it tightens and flattens, it pulls air into your lungs, and when it relaxes, air pushes out. A sudden spasm of this muscle causes hiccups.
Shivering is your body's way of making heat when you get cold. Your muscles rapidly tighten and relax, and all that movement warms you up. It happens automatically without you choosing to do it.

Normal body temperature is around 37 degrees Celsius, though it varies a little from person to person. Your temperature is usually lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon. Your brain works hard to keep it steady.

A fever is when your body raises its own temperature to help fight an infection. The extra heat makes it harder for many germs to survive and helps your immune system work faster. So a mild fever is often a sign your body is defending itself.

Germs are tiny living things, too small to see, that can make you sick. The main kinds are bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Not all germs are bad, though, and many bacteria in your body are actually helpful.

Your body is home to trillions of tiny microbes, especially in your gut, and many of them help you. They aid digestion, make some vitamins, and crowd out harmful germs. There may be as many microbe cells in and on you as your own cells.

Your immune system is your body's defence team against germs. It includes white blood cells, your skin, mucus, and even fever. When it beats a germ, it often remembers it so it can fight that germ faster next time.

A vaccine teaches your immune system to recognise a germ without you getting sick. It shows your body a harmless piece or weakened version of the germ. Then if the real germ ever shows up, your body already knows how to fight it.

Antibodies are tiny Y-shaped proteins your immune system makes to fight specific germs. They stick to invaders and either disable them or flag them for white blood cells to destroy. Once your body makes them, it can often remember how for years.

keywords: why we get sick from same cold
facts.answer: You can catch colds over and over because there are hundreds of different cold viruses. Beating one does not protect you from the others. The viruses also change over time, so your body keeps facing new versions.
The human body is made of roughly 37 trillion cells. Each cell is a tiny living building block with its own job. Together they form everything from your skin to your brain.

DNA is like an instruction book stored inside almost every cell of your body. It holds the code that decides things like your eye colour and height. If you stretched out the DNA from one cell, it would be about two metres long.
Chromosomes are tightly coiled packages of DNA inside your cells. Humans usually have 46 of them, arranged in 23 pairs. You get one of each pair from each of your parents.

Stem cells are special cells that can grow into many different types of cells. They act like spare parts, replacing worn-out or damaged cells. Doctors are studying them to help heal injuries and diseases.

Hormones are chemical messengers that travel through your blood to control your body. They manage things like growth, sleep, hunger, and mood. Glands such as the thyroid and pancreas make and release them.

Adrenaline is a hormone your body releases when you feel scared or excited. It speeds up your heart, sharpens your focus, and gives you a burst of energy. This is part of the fight-or-flight response that prepares you to act fast.

The fluttery feeling of butterflies in your stomach comes from adrenaline during nervous or exciting moments. Blood gets pulled away from your gut toward your muscles, which creates that odd sensation. It is a normal sign your body is on alert.

Sleep gives your body and brain time to repair and recharge. While you sleep, your brain sorts memories and your body fixes cells and grows. Without enough sleep, you find it harder to think, learn, and stay healthy.

School-age children usually need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Teenagers need around 8 to 10 hours, and adults need about 7 to 9. Younger bodies and brains need more sleep because they are still growing fast.

Dreams are stories and images your brain creates while you sleep, mostly during a stage called REM sleep. Scientists think dreaming may help process emotions and memories. Most people dream every night even if they do not remember it.

REM stands for rapid eye movement, a stage of sleep when your eyes dart around under your eyelids. This is when most vivid dreams happen and when your brain is very active. You cycle through REM and deeper sleep several times each night.

Melatonin is a hormone that helps tell your body when it is time to sleep. Your brain makes more of it when it gets dark and less when it is light. That is why bright screens at night can make it harder to fall asleep.

Memories are stored as patterns of connections between brain cells. A part of the brain called the hippocampus helps turn new experiences into lasting memories. The more you repeat something, the stronger those connections become.

Forgetting is actually useful because it clears out unimportant details so your brain is not overloaded. Memories you do not use can fade as their brain connections weaken. Things tied to strong emotions or repeated often are easier to remember.

A reflex is a super-fast automatic reaction that protects you, like yanking your hand off something hot. The signal often takes a shortcut through your spinal cord instead of going all the way to your brain first. This saves precious time when you need to react instantly.

Your spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves running down your back inside your spine. It carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body. It also handles some reflexes on its own without waiting for the brain.

Your spine, or backbone, is made of 33 bones called vertebrae when you are born. Some fuse together as you grow, leaving adults with about 26 separate sections. These bones stack up to protect your spinal cord while letting you bend and twist.

keywords: why we get shorter at night
facts.answer: You are actually a tiny bit taller in the morning than at night. During the day, gravity gently squishes the soft cushions between your spine bones. While you sleep lying down, they soak up fluid and puff back up.

Cartilage is a tough but bendy material found in places like your ears, nose, and joints. It is softer than bone and cushions where bones meet so they do not grind. Your ears and the tip of your nose are shaped by cartilage, not bone.

Joints are the places where two bones meet and let your body move. Some, like your knee, work like a hinge, while your shoulder swivels like a ball in a socket. Smooth cartilage and slippery fluid help them move without rubbing painfully.

When you crack your knuckles, you are popping a tiny gas bubble in the fluid that cushions the joint. The pop is that bubble bursting or forming. Despite the old warning, cracking your knuckles does not actually cause arthritis.

Tendons are tough cords that connect your muscles to your bones. When a muscle pulls, the tendon tugs the bone and your body moves. The Achilles tendon at the back of your ankle is the largest and strongest one.

Ligaments are strong, slightly stretchy bands that connect bone to bone at your joints. They hold your bones together and keep your joints stable. A sprain happens when a ligament gets stretched or torn.

The brainstem connects your brain to your spinal cord and controls things you never have to think about. It runs your breathing, heartbeat, and blood pressure. Even while you sleep, it keeps these vital jobs going.

The cerebellum is a wrinkled part at the back of your brain that helps with balance and smooth movement. It fine-tunes actions like walking, catching a ball, or riding a bike. Though it is small, it holds a huge share of your brain's neurons.

Babies cannot walk at first because their muscles, bones, and brain coordination are still developing. They build strength step by step, learning to roll, sit, crawl, and stand. Most babies take their first steps around their first birthday.

You grow taller mainly at soft areas near the ends of your bones called growth plates. New bone forms there, slowly stretching your bones longer. When you finish growing, usually in the teens or early twenties, these plates harden and you stop getting taller.

A growth spurt is a short stretch of time when your body grows quickly. The biggest spurts happen in babyhood and again during the teenage years. During a spurt you may suddenly need bigger shoes and feel extra hungry and tired.

You feel hungry when your stomach and brain decide your body needs more energy. A hormone called ghrelin rises and tells your brain it is time to eat. Once you have eaten enough, other signals tell your brain you are full.

Feeling full happens when your stretched stomach and gut hormones send signals to your brain. These signals take about 20 minutes to arrive, which is why eating slowly helps you notice when you have had enough. A hormone called leptin also helps tell you to stop.

Thirst is your body's way of telling you it needs more water. When your blood gets a little too concentrated, your brain triggers the urge to drink. Drinking before you feel very thirsty helps keep your body running smoothly.

Vitamins are tiny nutrients your body needs in small amounts to stay healthy. They help with things like growing, healing, and turning food into energy. Most come from eating a variety of foods like fruits and vegetables.

Vitamin C helps your body heal wounds and keeps your gums and skin healthy. It is found in foods like oranges, peppers, and strawberries. Long ago, sailors who went without it got a disease called scurvy.

Vitamin D is nicknamed the sunshine vitamin because your skin can make it from sunlight. It helps your body use calcium to build strong bones. You can also get it from foods like fish, eggs, and fortified milk.
Calcium is a mineral that helps build strong bones and teeth. Your body also uses it for your muscles and nerves to work properly. Milk, cheese, leafy greens, and some beans are good sources.

Iron is a mineral your body uses to make haemoglobin, the part of blood that carries oxygen. Without enough iron, you can feel tired and weak. Foods like beans, spinach, and red meat help keep your iron levels up.

Protein is a building-block nutrient your body uses to grow and repair muscles, skin, and more. It is found in foods like eggs, beans, nuts, fish, and meat. Your body breaks it into smaller pieces called amino acids to rebuild what it needs.

Fibre is a part of plant foods your body cannot fully digest, but it is still very useful. It helps food move smoothly through your gut and keeps your digestion healthy. Whole grains, beans, fruits, and vegetables are full of it.

A burp is the way your body lets out air that you swallowed while eating or drinking. Fizzy drinks add even more gas, so they often make you burp more. The air comes back up your food pipe and out your mouth.

Passing gas is a normal part of digestion. Gas builds up when bacteria in your gut break down certain foods and when you swallow air. Most people pass gas around 10 to 20 times a day, which is perfectly healthy.

Mucus, including snot, is a sticky fluid that protects and moistens parts of your body like your nose and lungs. It traps dust, germs, and dirt so they do not get deeper inside you. Your body makes more of it when you are fighting a cold.

Your nose runs when you cry because tears do not all spill out of your eyes. Some drain through tiny tubes into your nose, where they mix with mucus. That extra fluid is what drips out, making your nose runny.

Your nose can run in cold weather even when you are not sick. The cold air dries out your nose, so it makes extra mucus to stay moist. Cold air also makes the water in your breath turn to droplets inside your nose.

When you are cold, your body sends more blood to your core to protect important organs. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your hands and feet, so they feel chilly first. Wearing gloves and warm socks helps keep them comfortable.

Your cheeks turn red when blood vessels near the skin's surface widen and fill with more blood. This can happen from heat, exercise, or strong feelings like embarrassment. The extra blood close to the skin gives a rosy glow.

keywords: why we get pins and needles
facts.answer: That prickly pins-and-needles feeling happens when pressure squeezes a nerve and limits blood flow, like sitting on your foot. The nerve cannot send signals normally for a while. When you move and blood returns, the tingling is the nerve waking back up.

keywords: why we get dizzy when standing
facts.answer: Standing up quickly can make you feel dizzy because gravity pulls blood down toward your legs. For a moment your brain gets a little less blood. Your body fixes it fast, so the dizzy feeling usually disappears within seconds.

Blood pressure is the force of your blood pushing against the walls of your blood vessels. It rises a little when your heart pumps and lowers when it relaxes. Doctors check it because pressure that stays too high can strain your heart over time.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry it back. Arteries have thick walls to handle the heart's strong push. Veins have valves inside that act like one-way gates to stop blood from flowing backward.

Capillaries are the tiniest blood vessels, so thin that red blood cells pass through almost single file. Their walls are super thin, which lets oxygen and nutrients pass into your cells. They connect the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.
When you breathe in, oxygen passes from your lungs into your blood. Red blood cells carry it to every part of your body. Your cells use that oxygen to turn food into the energy they need to work.

You often yawn when you are tired or bored, though scientists are still studying exactly why. One idea is that yawning helps wake your brain up a little by cooling it and shifting blood flow. It may also be a signal that your body is shifting between alert and sleepy states.

The thyroid is a small butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It releases hormones that control how fast your body uses energy. When it works too fast or too slow, it can affect your weight, mood, and energy.

Metabolism is the name for all the chemical processes that keep your body running. It turns the food you eat into energy for everything from breathing to running. Even while you rest, your metabolism is busy keeping you alive.

keywords: why we get tired after eating
facts.answer: Feeling sleepy after a big meal is partly because blood flow shifts toward your digestive system. Certain foods can also nudge your brain toward sleep chemicals. It is a normal, temporary dip in energy.

The bladder is a stretchy bag that stores urine until you are ready to go to the bathroom. As it fills, it stretches and sends a signal to your brain. An adult bladder can hold roughly two cups of liquid before it feels full.

keywords: how we control going to bathroom
facts.answer: You control going to the bathroom using a ring of muscle that stays closed until you decide to relax it. Babies have not learned this control yet, which is why they need diapers. As children grow, their brains learn to manage these muscles.
Muscles often feel sore a day or two after hard exercise. This happens because the workout causes tiny tears in the muscle fibres. As your body repairs them, the muscles grow back a little stronger.

A cramp is when a muscle suddenly tightens and will not relax, causing a sharp pain. It can happen from overuse, dehydration, or not having enough minerals like potassium. Gently stretching the muscle usually helps it loosen up.
When you exercise, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster to deliver it. Your breathing also speeds up to pull in more air. This is why your heart pounds when you run or play hard.

Exercise keeps your heart, muscles, and bones strong and healthy. It also helps your brain by improving mood and focus and making sleep better. Moving your body regularly is one of the best things you can do for your health.
The aorta is the largest artery in your body, leading straight out of your heart. It is about as wide as a garden hose. From there, blood branches out into smaller arteries to reach the rest of you.

Alveoli are millions of tiny balloon-like air sacs deep inside your lungs. This is where oxygen passes into your blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Their thin walls and huge total surface make breathing very efficient.

keywords: why we have a belly button
facts.answer: Your belly button is a scar left from where the umbilical cord connected you to your mother before birth. That cord delivered food and oxygen while you grew in the womb. After birth it is no longer needed, so it is clamped and falls off, leaving the navel.
Before birth, a baby does not breathe air with its lungs. Instead, oxygen comes from the mother's blood through the umbilical cord. The baby takes its very first real breath right after being born.

Your pulse is the throb you can feel where an artery runs close to the skin, like your wrist or neck. Each beat is your heart pushing blood through with a little surge. Counting these beats tells you how fast your heart is going.

Plasma is the pale yellow liquid that makes up over half of your blood. The blood cells float in it like ingredients in a soup. Plasma carries nutrients, waste, and important proteins all around your body.

The cornea is the clear dome at the very front of your eye. It works like a window and also bends incoming light to help you focus. Because it has no blood vessels, it gets oxygen straight from the air.

Behind your pupil is a flexible lens that changes shape to focus light. Tiny muscles squeeze it rounder to see close things and stretch it flatter for far things. This automatic adjusting is called accommodation.

People need glasses when their eyes do not focus light exactly on the back of the eye. If the eye is a little too long, far things look blurry, and if too short, close things blur. Glasses bend light the right amount to fix the focus.

Sound enters your ear as vibrations in the air. Your eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones pass the motion along, and a snail-shaped part called the cochlea turns it into nerve signals. Your brain then reads those signals as the sounds you hear.

Earwax is your ear's built-in cleaning and protecting system. It traps dust and tiny bits of dirt and keeps your ear canal from drying out. The wax slowly moves outward on its own, carrying the trapped debris away.

Very loud sounds can damage the tiny hair cells inside your ear that detect sound. Once those hair cells are harmed, they do not grow back. That is why protecting your ears from loud noise helps your hearing last a lifetime.

keywords: why we get wrinkly fingers in water
facts.answer: Your fingers wrinkle in water because your nervous system tells the blood vessels under the skin to shrink. Scientists think the wrinkles may help you grip wet things better, like tyre treads on a wet road. The skin smooths back out once you dry off.

Pimples form when tiny skin openings get clogged with oil and dead skin cells. Bacteria can grow inside, causing the area to swell and turn red. They are very common during the teenage years because of hormone changes.

keywords: why we get a runny nose with allergies
facts.answer: An allergy is when your immune system mistakes something harmless, like pollen, for a threat. It reacts by causing sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy eyes to flush the substance out. The thing that triggers it is called an allergen.

Histamine is a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. It causes the sneezing, swelling, and itching that come with allergies. Medicines called antihistamines work by blocking it to ease those symptoms.

Headaches can come from many things, like tiredness, dehydration, hunger, or tense muscles in your head and neck. The pain comes from nerves and blood vessels around the brain, not the brain itself. Resting, drinking water, and relaxing often help.

keywords: why we get stitches in our side
facts.answer: A side stitch is a sharp pain in your side that often comes when you run hard. It may happen when the muscles you use for breathing get strained or tired. Slowing down and breathing deeply usually helps it fade.

Pain is your body's warning system. Special nerve endings sense damage or danger and send a signal to your brain that says stop or move away. Although it feels bad, pain helps protect you from getting hurt worse.

An itch is a signal from nerves in your skin telling you something may be irritating it, like a bug or dry skin. Scratching can feel good but may make the itch worse. The itch is partly your body's way of getting you to check and protect your skin.

A mosquito bite itches because of the saliva the mosquito leaves behind when it feeds. Your immune system reacts to that saliva by releasing histamine, which causes the itchy, swollen bump. The reaction is harmless but annoying.

keywords: how the body fights a cut
facts.answer: When you get a cut, your body heals it in stages. First it stops the bleeding with a clot, then it sends white blood cells to fight germs, and finally it builds new skin. The whole process can take days to weeks depending on the size.

Inflammation is your body's response to injury or infection. The area gets warm, red, and swollen as extra blood and immune cells rush in to heal it. So that swelling and redness are signs your body is hard at work fixing the problem.

Anaesthesia is medicine that blocks pain so doctors can do surgery without you feeling it. Some kinds numb just one body part, while others put you into a deep, controlled sleep. Special doctors carefully watch you the whole time to keep you safe.

X-rays are a kind of invisible ray that can pass through soft parts of your body but not through dense bone. On the picture, bones show up white because they block the rays. Doctors use X-rays to spot broken bones and other problems.

An MRI uses strong magnets and radio waves to take detailed pictures inside your body. Unlike X-rays, it is great at showing soft tissues like the brain and muscles. The machine is noisy, but the scan itself does not hurt.

A stethoscope is the tool doctors use to listen to sounds inside your body. It carries the sound of your heartbeat, breathing, and gut up to the doctor's ears. Listening helps the doctor check if everything is working normally.

Antibiotics are medicines that fight infections caused by bacteria. They work by killing bacteria or stopping them from multiplying. They do not work against viruses like the common cold, so they are only used when truly needed.

Doctors say to finish all your antibiotics even if you feel better. Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive, and they may grow back stronger. Over time, this can make some bacteria resistant, meaning the medicine no longer works on them.

A thermometer measures temperature, including your body temperature. Doctors and parents use it to check for a fever. Modern ones can read your temperature from your mouth, ear, forehead, or armpit in just seconds.

A placebo is a pretend treatment with no real medicine, like a sugar pill. Surprisingly, people sometimes feel better just because they believe they are being treated. Scientists use placebos in tests to see if a new medicine truly works.

After you have chickenpox once, your body usually remembers the virus and protects you for life. Your immune system keeps special memory cells ready to fight it. That is why most people only catch chickenpox a single time.

When a blood vessel is cut, your body forms a clot to plug the leak. Platelets clump at the spot, and a protein called fibrin weaves a net to hold everything in place. The clot seals the wound while new tissue heals underneath.

People have different blood types, the main ones being A, B, AB, and O. The type depends on special markers on your red blood cells. Blood types matter a lot when someone needs a blood transfusion, since the wrong type can be harmful.

People with O negative blood are called universal donors because their blood can be safely given to almost anyone in an emergency. Their red blood cells lack the markers that would trigger a bad reaction. This makes O negative blood especially valuable to hospitals.

A blood transfusion gives a person blood from a donor, usually after heavy bleeding or during surgery. Doctors carefully match the blood types so the body accepts it. The donated blood helps carry oxygen until the patient's body recovers.
Anaemia is when you do not have enough healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen well. It can make you feel tired, weak, and pale. A common cause is not getting enough iron in your food.

keywords: what is the heart rate of a hummingbird vs human
facts.answer: Your heart rate changes depending on what you are doing. It slows down when you rest or sleep and speeds up when you run, get scared, or feel excited. This lets your heart match the amount of oxygen your body needs at any moment.

Newborn babies have soft spots on their heads called fontanelles. These gaps let the skull bones move during birth and give the brain room to grow quickly. The soft spots gradually close and harden over the first couple of years.

Baby teeth fall out to make room for larger adult teeth. As an adult tooth pushes up, it dissolves the root of the baby tooth above it. With the root gone, the baby tooth gets wiggly and finally drops out.

Wisdom teeth are the last molars to come in, usually in the late teens or early twenties. They are leftovers from ancestors who needed extra grinding teeth for tough diets. Many people's jaws are now too small for them, so dentists sometimes remove them.

Having two eyes lets you judge how far away things are, which is called depth perception. Each eye sees a slightly different view, and your brain combines them into one 3D picture. This helps you do things like catch a ball or pour a drink without missing.
Two ears help you tell where a sound is coming from. A sound reaches the closer ear a tiny bit sooner and louder than the farther one. Your brain uses that difference to pinpoint the direction.

You have two nostrils, and they actually take turns doing most of the breathing throughout the day. While one does the heavy work, the other rests, then they switch. Having two also gives you a better sense of smell and a backup if one gets blocked.

keywords: what is the tongue made of
facts.answer: Your tongue is a bundle of muscles working together, which is why it can move in so many directions. It helps you taste, talk, chew, and swallow. The tongue is one of the few muscles attached at only one end.

Cuts inside your mouth and on your tongue tend to heal quickly. The mouth has a rich blood supply and saliva that helps protect against germs. This speedy healing is why a bitten tongue usually feels better within days.

You sometimes drool in your sleep because you stop swallowing as often while deeply relaxed. Saliva keeps being made, so it can pool and slip out, especially if you sleep on your side. It is completely normal and harmless.

Swallowing pushes food from your mouth down to your stomach using waves of muscle squeezes. A small flap called the epiglottis covers your windpipe so food does not go down the wrong way. This squeezing is so strong you could even swallow upside down.

keywords: why food goes down wrong pipe
facts.answer: Sometimes food or drink slips toward your windpipe instead of your food pipe. Your body reacts instantly with a strong cough to blast it back out. That coughing fit is your airway protecting your lungs.

The oesophagus is the muscular tube that carries food from your throat down to your stomach. It does not just drop food in; it squeezes it along with waves of muscle. This is why you can swallow even when lying down.

Newborn babies cannot see clearly at first and mostly notice light, shapes, and faces up close. Their vision sharpens quickly over the first months as their eyes and brain learn together. Colour vision and depth perception keep improving through their first year.

Newborn babies sleep around 14 to 17 hours a day. All that sleep supports the huge amount of growing their bodies and brains are doing. They wake often because their tiny stomachs need feeding around the clock.

keywords: how the body warms up when exercising
facts.answer: When you exercise, your working muscles produce heat as a by-product. Your body warms up, then starts sweating to cool itself back down. This is why you feel hot and sweaty during a hard game or run.

keywords: why we feel pain in phantom limb
facts.answer: Some people who lose a limb still feel sensations where it used to be, called a phantom limb. The brain keeps a map of the body and can still sense the missing part. Scientists study this to better understand how the brain pictures the body.

keywords: why skin gets darker in sun
facts.answer: When sunlight hits your skin, special cells make more of a pigment called melanin. The extra melanin darkens your skin into a tan, acting as a built-in sunscreen. It helps protect deeper skin from sun damage, though sunscreen protects even better.
Freckles are small spots where the skin makes extra melanin in one place. Sunlight makes them darker and more noticeable. Whether you get freckles depends a lot on your genes.

The funny bone is not actually a bone at all. The zingy feeling comes from bumping a nerve called the ulnar nerve near your elbow, where it sits close to the skin. The name is a play on the humerus, the upper arm bone.

keywords: why we have an arch in our foot
facts.answer: The curved arch in your foot works like a spring. It absorbs the shock each time your foot hits the ground and helps push you forward when you walk or run. This clever shape supports your whole body weight all day.

keywords: how many bones in the hand
facts.answer: Each of your hands has 27 bones, and each foot has 26. Together your two hands and two feet hold over half of all the bones in your body. All those small bones let your hands and feet move in delicate, precise ways.

Your thumb is opposable, meaning it can reach across and touch each of your other fingers. This lets you grip, pinch, and hold tools with great control. It is one of the features that helps humans build and use so many things.

keywords: how nerves carry pain fast and slow
facts.answer: Pain can travel along two kinds of nerves. Fast nerves carry the sharp, sudden ache that makes you pull away right away. Slower nerves carry the dull throbbing pain that lingers afterward, reminding you to be careful.

The gallbladder is a small pouch under your liver that stores a fluid called bile. Bile helps your body break down fatty foods. When you eat something greasy, the gallbladder squeezes bile into your gut to help with digestion.

Bile is a greenish-yellow fluid made by your liver that helps digest fats. It breaks big globs of fat into tiny droplets so your body can absorb them more easily. Bile also helps carry away certain wastes from your liver.

keywords: how the body makes vitamin from sunlight
facts.answer: Your skin can make vitamin D when sunlight touches it. The sun's rays trigger a chemical change in your skin that produces this important vitamin. Just a little safe sun exposure can help, though too much sun can harm your skin.

A cavity is a tiny hole in a tooth caused by decay. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars and make acid that wears away the tooth's hard surface. Brushing, flossing, and eating less sugar help keep cavities away.

Brushing removes plaque, a sticky film of bacteria that builds up on your teeth. If plaque stays, it makes acid that causes cavities and gum problems. Brushing twice a day helps keep your teeth and gums healthy.

Morning breath happens because your mouth makes less saliva while you sleep. With less saliva to wash them away, bacteria grow and produce smelly gases. Brushing in the morning clears them out and freshens your breath.

Plaque is a soft, sticky layer of bacteria that forms on your teeth, especially after eating. If it is not brushed away, it can harden into a tough crust called tartar. Both can lead to cavities and irritated gums.

keywords: how the body cools the brain
facts.answer: Your brain works best at a steady temperature, so your body has ways to keep it cool. Blood flow and even yawning may help carry heat away. Sweating on your face and scalp also helps prevent your head from overheating.

keywords: why we lose body heat through head
facts.answer: You can lose a lot of body heat through your head, partly because it is often uncovered. Your head has many blood vessels close to the surface that release warmth. Wearing a hat in winter helps trap that heat and keep you cozy.

Special nerve endings in your skin detect heat and cold. They send signals to your brain so you know to put on a coat or move out of the sun. Your body then adjusts things like sweating or shivering to stay comfortable.

The largest muscle in your body is the gluteus maximus, the main muscle in your bottom. It powers movements like standing up, climbing stairs, and jumping. It also helps you keep your body upright while walking.

The uvula is the small dangly piece at the back of your throat. It helps make certain speech sounds and keeps food and drink from going up into your nose when you swallow. It also helps produce saliva to keep your throat moist.

Your voice comes from your voice box, where two small flaps called vocal cords sit. When you push air past them, they vibrate to create sound. Stretching them tighter makes higher sounds and loosening them makes lower ones.

During puberty, the voice box grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker. Longer cords vibrate more slowly, which makes the voice sound deeper. This change is usually bigger and more noticeable in boys.

Most hiccups go away on their own within a few minutes as the diaphragm settles down. Many people try tricks like holding their breath or drinking water to stop them. These tricks may work by changing your breathing pattern to reset the muscle.

Breathing through your nose warms and moistens the air before it reaches your lungs. Tiny blood vessels and mucus inside your nose do this job. Your nose also filters out dust and germs, which is better than breathing through your mouth.

Tonsils are two soft lumps at the back of your throat that are part of your immune system. They help trap germs that enter through your mouth and nose. Sometimes they get infected and swollen, which is called tonsillitis.
Adenoids are a patch of tissue high up behind your nose, similar to tonsils. They help catch germs that you breathe in and are part of your immune defences. They tend to shrink as children get older.

Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped filters spread throughout your body, like in your neck and armpits. They trap germs and help your immune system fight infections. When you are sick, they can swell up as they work hard, which people call swollen glands.

The lymphatic system is a network of vessels that carries a clear fluid called lymph around your body. It helps drain extra fluid from your tissues and fights infections. Think of it as a cleanup and defence network working alongside your blood.

keywords: how the body fights a virus
facts.answer: When a virus invades, your immune system springs into action. White blood cells attack infected cells and your body makes antibodies that target the virus. A fever and tiredness are signs your body is fighting hard.

keywords: why we get a sore throat
facts.answer: A sore throat often happens when a virus or bacteria irritates and inflames your throat. Your throat may feel scratchy, swollen, and painful when you swallow. Resting and drinking warm fluids can help it feel better.

You can lose your voice when your vocal cords get swollen or irritated, often from a cold or too much yelling. Swollen cords cannot vibrate properly, so your voice turns hoarse or disappears. Resting your voice helps the cords recover.

keywords: how the body stays balanced standing
facts.answer: Staying upright is a team effort between your inner ears, your eyes, and sensors in your muscles and joints. They all send your brain information about your position. Your brain quickly makes tiny adjustments so you do not topple over.

Motion sickness happens when your eyes and your inner ears send your brain mismatched messages about movement. For example, reading in a moving car tells your eyes you are still while your ears feel motion. The confusion can make you feel queasy and dizzy.

keywords: how the body makes energy from food
facts.answer: Your cells turn food and oxygen into energy in tiny structures called mitochondria. They break down sugars from your food and release energy your cells can use. Mitochondria are often called the powerhouses of the cell.

Mitochondria are tiny parts inside your cells that make most of their energy. They take in nutrients and oxygen and produce a fuel your cells can use. Busy cells like muscle cells pack in lots of mitochondria.

keywords: why we breathe out carbon dioxide
facts.answer: When your cells make energy, they produce a waste gas called carbon dioxide. Your blood carries it back to your lungs. Then you breathe it out, getting rid of the waste with every exhale.

Your brainstem controls your breathing automatically, even when you are not paying attention. It senses how much carbon dioxide is in your blood and speeds up or slows your breathing to match. That is why you keep breathing while you sleep.

keywords: how the body senses low oxygen
facts.answer: The urge to breathe is mostly triggered by rising carbon dioxide, not by low oxygen. As carbon dioxide builds up, your brain pushes you to take a breath. This is why you cannot comfortably hold your breath for very long.

keywords: why running makes you breathe hard
facts.answer: When you run, your muscles burn through oxygen quickly and make extra carbon dioxide. Your brain notices and tells you to breathe faster and deeper. This brings in more oxygen and clears the waste gas out.

A callus is a patch of thick, hardened skin that forms where there is repeated rubbing or pressure. Your body builds it to protect the area underneath. People often get calluses on their hands or feet from work, sports, or instruments.

A blister is a small bubble of fluid that forms when skin is rubbed or burned. The fluid cushions and protects the damaged skin while it heals underneath. It is best not to pop it, since the skin acts as a natural bandage.

Your skin is a tough, waterproof barrier that keeps germs out and moisture in. It also shields you from sunlight, heat, and cold. As the body's first line of defence, it stops many invaders before they can get inside.

Melanin is the pigment that gives colour to your skin, hair, and eyes. It also acts like a natural shield against the sun's harmful rays. People whose ancestors lived in sunny places often have more melanin in their skin.

keywords: how the body makes new blood cells
facts.answer: Most of your blood cells are made inside your bones, in the soft bone marrow. The marrow constantly produces red cells, white cells, and platelets. Because blood cells wear out, this factory never stops working.
The liver is the largest gland in your body. A gland is an organ that makes and releases helpful substances. Among its many jobs, the liver produces bile to help you digest fats.

Each kidney holds about a million tiny filters called nephrons. They sort out waste and extra water from your blood while keeping the good stuff. The waste becomes urine, and the cleaned blood flows on.

A nephron is one of the tiny filtering units inside your kidney. Each one cleans a small portion of your blood, and together they keep your whole body's blood clean. A single kidney contains around a million nephrons.

Urine gets its yellow colour from a pigment called urochrome that your body makes while breaking down old blood cells. The more water you drink, the paler your urine becomes. Dark yellow urine can be a hint that you need to drink more.

Sugar from your food becomes glucose, a fuel your cells use for energy. The hormone insulin helps move glucose from your blood into your cells. Your body works to keep your blood sugar at a steady, healthy level.

Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas that controls your blood sugar. It acts like a key, letting sugar move out of your blood and into your cells for energy. Without enough working insulin, sugar builds up in the blood.

Diabetes is a condition where the body has trouble controlling blood sugar. It happens when the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well. People with diabetes manage it with healthy habits and sometimes medicine.

keywords: why we need glucose for the brain
facts.answer: Your brain runs almost entirely on glucose, a kind of sugar from your food. It uses a large share of the energy in your body. That is one reason skipping meals can leave you feeling foggy and grumpy.

When you exercise, you create tiny tears in your muscle fibres. Your body repairs them, and over time the muscle grows back thicker and stronger. Rest and good food are just as important as the exercise itself for building muscle.

Warming up gently before exercise gets your blood flowing and loosens your muscles and joints. Warm, limber muscles are less likely to get pulled or injured. It also helps your heart and breathing ramp up smoothly.

keywords: why we feel happy after exercise
facts.answer: Exercise can make you feel cheerful because your body releases chemicals called endorphins. Endorphins help reduce pain and lift your mood. This good feeling is sometimes called a runner's high.

Endorphins are natural chemicals your brain releases that make you feel good and ease pain. You can boost them through exercise, laughing, or eating something you enjoy. They are sometimes called the body's own feel-good messengers.

Dopamine is a brain chemical linked to feeling pleasure and motivation. Your brain releases it when something rewarding happens, like winning a game or enjoying a treat. It helps push you to do things that feel good or useful.

Serotonin is a chemical messenger that helps control your mood, sleep, and appetite. Having balanced serotonin can help you feel calm and content. Sunlight and exercise can help your body make more of it.

Laughing is good for your body as well as your mood. It relaxes your muscles, boosts feel-good chemicals, and can even give your heart and lungs a gentle workout. A good laugh helps reduce stress too.

The mantis shrimp throws the fastest punch in the animal world. Its club-like arm strikes so fast it boils the water around it, creating a flash of light and a tiny shockwave. The blow can crack open crab shells and even break aquarium glass.

Mantis shrimp have the most complex eyes known. Humans see color with three types of receptor, but mantis shrimp have up to sixteen. They can also see ultraviolet light and a special kind of light called polarized light that humans cannot detect at all.

Tardigrades, also called water bears, are tiny creatures that can survive almost anything. They can be frozen, boiled, dried out for years, and even shot into the vacuum of space and still come back to life. They do this by curling into a dried ball called a tun and pausing their bodies.

The axolotl is a salamander that can regrow almost any body part it loses. It can grow back legs, tail, parts of its heart, and even bits of its brain, all without leaving a scar. Scientists study axolotls to learn how healing works.

The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast it shoots out a bubble that pops with a bang as loud as a gunshot. The popping bubble briefly reaches a temperature nearly as hot as the surface of the sun. This snap stuns small fish so the shrimp can eat them.

The electric eel can produce a jolt of around 600 volts, enough to knock down a horse. It uses thousands of special cells in its body like tiny stacked batteries. It zaps prey to stun it and also uses small pulses like radar to sense the world around it.

The bombardier beetle defends itself by mixing chemicals inside its body to create a boiling-hot spray. The liquid shoots out of its rear at near boiling temperature with a popping sound. It can aim the burning spray in almost any direction at attackers.

The immortal jellyfish can turn back into its baby form when it is hurt or old, then grow up again. This life cycle can repeat over and over, so in theory it never has to die of old age. It is one of the only animals known to do this.

The superb lyrebird of Australia can copy almost any sound it hears. It mimics other birds, but also chainsaws, camera shutters, car alarms, and barking dogs with stunning accuracy. Males use this skill to show off and attract mates.

Octopuses can change both their color and the texture of their skin in less than a second to blend into rocks, coral, or sand. They have millions of tiny color sacs in their skin that they squeeze and stretch. Amazingly, they are colorblind, yet still match their surroundings perfectly.

Cuttlefish can send waves of color rippling across their skin like a moving light show. They use this to confuse prey, almost hypnotizing small crabs and shrimp before grabbing them. Their skin can flash these colors even though their eyes cannot see color.

The wood frog can freeze almost solid in winter and still survive. Its heart stops, its breathing stops, and ice fills much of its body. Sugar in its blood acts like antifreeze and protects its cells, so it thaws out and hops away in spring.

The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth. When it dives to catch prey, it can reach speeds over 240 miles per hour. Special bumps in its nostrils help it breathe while diving so fast that the wind would otherwise damage its lungs.

The arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal. Each year it flies from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, a round trip of around 44,000 miles. Over its life it may travel far enough to reach the Moon and back three times.

When attacked, the hagfish releases a tiny bit of slime that instantly expands into buckets of thick goo. The slime clogs the gills of attacking fish, forcing them to flee or choke. A single hagfish can fill a large bucket with slime in seconds.

The star-nosed mole has a strange star of 22 fleshy tentacles on its nose packed with touch sensors. It is nearly blind but feels its way through dark tunnels. It is the fastest-eating mammal, able to find and gulp down food in under a quarter of a second.

Pit vipers, like rattlesnakes, have special pits between their eyes and nostrils that sense heat. This lets them see the warmth of a mouse or rat in total darkness, like having built-in night-vision goggles. They can strike prey accurately with their eyes closed.

The horned dung beetle is one of the strongest animals for its size. It can pull a load over 1,100 times its own body weight, like a person dragging six full double-decker buses. They use this power to fight rivals and roll balls of dung.

When threatened, some sea cucumbers shoot their own sticky guts out through their rear at an attacker. The tangled insides trap or distract the predator while the sea cucumber escapes. Over the next few weeks it simply grows a new set of organs.

The platypus hunts with its eyes, ears, and nose all closed underwater. Instead it uses its rubbery bill to sense the tiny electric signals given off by the muscles of shrimp and worms. It is one of the few mammals that can detect electricity this way.

Some wood ants defend their nest by spraying formic acid at enemies. They can bend their bodies and fire the stinging acid several inches through the air. A whole colony spraying at once can drive off much larger animals.

The archerfish hunts insects above the water by spitting a powerful jet of water to knock them off leaves. It can hit a target several body lengths away and even corrects for the way light bends at the surface. Young archerfish practice until their aim becomes deadly.

Geckos can run up glass and even hang upside down on ceilings. Their toes are covered in millions of tiny hairs so small they grip surfaces using a faint molecular attraction. This lets them stick without any glue and peel off cleanly to take the next step.

Spider silk is one of the toughest materials in nature. Strand for strand it is stronger than steel and can stretch far without snapping. If a spider could spin a strand as thick as a pencil, it could stop a flying jet.

A chameleon's tongue can shoot out faster than a sports car accelerates, often longer than the chameleon's own body. The sticky tip grabs an insect and snaps back in a fraction of a second. The tongue speeds up using stored elastic energy, like a slingshot.

Leafcutter ants are farmers. They cut pieces of leaves and carry them home, but they do not eat the leaves. Instead they use them to grow a special fungus underground, and they eat the fungus, tending their gardens like tiny farmers.

The sperm whale can dive more than a mile deep and hold its breath for over an hour. It hunts giant squid in cold, pitch-black water where the pressure would crush a submarine. Its blood and muscles store huge amounts of oxygen for these long dives.

The honey badger is famous for being fearless and tough. It has loose, thick skin that lets it twist around and bite back even when grabbed. It can survive bites from cobras, recover after passing out from the venom, and keep hunting.

Camels can go a week or more without drinking, then gulp down 30 gallons of water in minutes. Their humps store fat, not water, which they break down for energy. Their bodies also handle big swings in temperature so they sweat very little.

The great frigatebird can stay in the air for weeks without landing. It even sleeps while flying, resting half its brain at a time in short naps of just a few seconds. This lets it cross huge stretches of open ocean.

Dolphins find food in dark or murky water using echolocation. They send out clicking sounds that bounce off objects and listen to the echoes to picture what is around them. They can even tell the difference between a real fish and a fake one this way.

Many bats hunt in total darkness using echolocation. They make high squeaks and listen to the echoes to map the world and find flying insects. Some bats can detect an object as thin as a human hair using only sound.

Owls fly almost silently thanks to special feathers. The front edges of their wings have comb-like fringes that break up the air, and soft fuzz on the surface muffles sound. This lets an owl swoop down on a mouse without being heard.

The kangaroo rat can live its whole life without ever drinking water. It gets all the moisture it needs from the dry seeds it eats. Its kidneys are so good at saving water that its urine is almost a paste.

The sailfish is one of the fastest fish in the ocean, able to swim in bursts up to around 60 miles per hour. It folds down a big sail-like fin on its back to slice through the water. It uses speed to herd and catch schools of smaller fish.

The narwhal is a whale with a long spiral tusk that can reach nine feet, looking like a unicorn horn. The tusk is actually a giant tooth packed with millions of nerve endings. Narwhals may use it to sense changes in the water around them.

The beluga whale has a soft, rounded forehead called a melon that it can change shape to focus sound. This helps it aim its echolocation clicks and find fish under thick Arctic ice. Belugas make so many noises they are nicknamed the canaries of the sea.

The electric ray, sometimes called the torpedo ray, can deliver a strong electric shock to stun fish. Its electric organs make up a big part of its flat, round body. Ancient people even used these shocks to try to numb pain.

The fennec fox has enormous ears compared to its tiny body. The big ears help it hear prey like insects moving under the sand. They also work like radiators, releasing body heat to keep the fox cool in the hot desert.

Jellyfish survive and hunt without any brain, heart, or bones. Instead they have a simple net of nerves spread through their body that senses light, touch, and balance. They are mostly water and have been drifting in the oceans for over 500 million years.

The Antarctic icefish is the only known animal with clear, colorless blood instead of red. It lives in water so cold and oxygen-rich that it can survive without the usual red oxygen-carrying cells. Its heart is large and pumps the thin, see-through blood through its body.

The Pompeii worm lives next to deep-sea vents in some of the hottest water any animal can stand. Its tail rests in water near boiling while its head pokes into cooler water. A fuzzy coat of helpful bacteria on its back may protect it from the heat.

The African lungfish can survive years out of water when its pond dries up. It burrows into the mud, wraps itself in a slimy cocoon, and breathes air with simple lungs. When the rains return and water fills the pond, it wakes up and swims away.

The basilisk lizard can sprint across the surface of water on its back legs, earning the nickname Jesus lizard. It slaps the water fast enough to create tiny air pockets that keep it from sinking. It can dash across a pond before gravity catches up.

The alligator snapping turtle has a pink wormlike piece on its tongue that it wiggles as bait. Fish swim in to investigate and the turtle snaps its powerful jaws shut. It can sit perfectly still on the riverbed, looking like an old rock for hours.

The mimic octopus can pretend to be many other sea creatures. It can shape its body and color to look like a venomous lionfish, a flat sole fish, or a sea snake. It picks which animal to imitate based on which predator is bothering it.

Flying fish leap from the water and glide through the air on wing-like fins to escape predators. They can soar over 600 feet in a single glide and stay airborne for many seconds. To stay up they beat their tail fast against the surface to relaunch.

The male proboscis monkey has a huge drooping nose that can be several inches long. The big nose makes his honking calls louder and deeper, which helps attract mates and warn rivals. Females prefer males with the biggest noses.

The okapi, a relative of the giraffe, has a blue-black tongue so long it can clean its own eyes and ears. The tongue can stretch around 18 inches. The okapi uses it to strip leaves from branches in the rainforest.

The secretary bird hunts snakes by stomping them with its long legs. Its kick is incredibly fast and powerful, hitting prey in a fraction of a second with force several times its own body weight. It can kill venomous snakes before they have a chance to bite.

The thorny devil, a spiky Australian lizard, drinks with its skin. Tiny grooves between its scales pull water from damp sand or dew straight to its mouth, like a network of natural straws. It can soak up moisture even from the ground it stands on.

The spitting cobra can shoot venom from its fangs straight at an attacker's eyes from several feet away. It aims for the face and can cause great pain or blindness if not washed out quickly. It uses this to defend itself without having to bite.

Some pistol shrimp team up with a fish called a goby. The nearly blind shrimp digs and keeps a burrow while the sharp-eyed goby watches for danger. When the goby flicks its tail, the shrimp dives for cover, and both share the safe home.

A starfish can regrow an arm if it loses one to a predator. In some species, a single severed arm with a piece of the center can even grow into a whole new starfish. This makes a starfish very hard to get rid of by cutting it apart.

The horned lizard has a startling defense: it can squirt blood from the corners of its eyes. The stream can shoot several feet and tastes foul to coyotes and dogs, sending them running. It builds the pressure by closing off blood flow from its head.

Vampire bats need a meal of blood every couple of nights or they may starve. A bat that fed well will throw up some blood to share with a hungry friend that missed out. They remember who shared with them and return the favor later.

The naked mole rat barely feels certain kinds of pain and almost never gets cancer. It can live around 30 years, far longer than other rodents, and survive with very little oxygen. Scientists study it to learn about aging and disease.

The tongue-eating louse is a parasite that enters a fish's mouth and replaces its tongue. It attaches where the tongue was and the fish then uses the louse like a tongue to hold food. It is the only known case of an animal replacing a body part of its host.

Male bowerbirds build fancy structures called bowers and decorate them with collections of colorful objects. They arrange berries, flowers, shells, and even bits of plastic by color to impress females. Some sort their treasures so carefully it looks like an art gallery.

The electric catfish of African rivers can deliver a strong electric shock of up to several hundred volts. It uses the jolt to stun prey and defend itself in muddy water. Ancient Egyptians drew pictures of this shocking fish thousands of years ago.

The cone snail is a slow sea snail that hunts with a venom-filled harpoon. It fires the tiny dart from a long tube to spear and paralyze fish in an instant. Its venom is so complex that scientists have turned it into powerful pain medicine.

The glass frog has skin on its belly so clear you can see its heart beating and its insides through it. When it sleeps, it can pull most of its red blood into its liver, making its body even more see-through to hide from predators.

The decorator crab dresses itself in bits of the ocean to hide. It attaches seaweed, sponges, and tiny living creatures to hooks on its shell. The disguise camouflages it so well that predators swim right past, mistaking it for the seafloor.

The antlion larva digs a funnel-shaped pit in loose sand and waits buried at the bottom. When an ant slips in, the antlion flicks sand to make it slide deeper, then grabs it with huge jaws. Its sand traps work like a deadly slide.

Surgeonfish, including the colorful blue tang, carry a sharp, blade-like spine near the tail on each side. It folds flat most of the time but flicks out like a switchblade for defense. A swipe can slice a predator that gets too close.

The frogfish has a built-in fishing rod on its head with a wiggly lure on the tip. It waves the lure to attract curious fish, then opens its mouth so fast it sucks prey in within a few thousandths of a second. It can swallow fish nearly its own size.

The deep-sea anglerfish lives in pitch-black water and dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth. The light comes from tiny bacteria living inside the lure. Prey drawn to the glow swims right into its huge, toothy mouth.

Fireflies make their own light using a chemical reaction in their bodies, and almost none of the energy is lost as heat. This cold light is far more efficient than a regular bulb. Each kind of firefly flashes its own pattern to find a mate.

Dragonflies are among the best fliers of all insects. Each of their four wings moves on its own, so they can hover, fly backward, and turn instantly. They catch over nine out of ten prey they chase, a higher success rate than a lion or shark.
