Hummingbirds can hover in place and even fly backward by beating their wings in a fast figure-eight up to 80 times a second. Their hearts can race over 1,200 beats a minute. To save energy at night, they slow their bodies into a deep sleep called torpor.

Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles to the same forests in Mexico each winter, though no single butterfly makes the round trip. It takes several generations, yet the descendants find the exact same trees. They navigate using the sun and a built-in sense of direction.

The desert ant finds its way home across blank sand by counting its own steps like a pedometer. It combines step counting with the angle of the sun to know exactly how far and which way to walk back. Scientists proved this by changing the length of an ant's legs.

Sea turtles can sense Earth's magnetic field and use it like a map. A turtle returns to lay eggs on the very beach where it hatched, even decades later and thousands of miles away. It reads the magnetic signature of the coast to find the exact spot.

Homing pigeons can find their way back to their loft from hundreds of miles away in unfamiliar places. They use the sun, smells, landmarks, and a sense of Earth's magnetic field. Armies once used them to carry important messages.

Salmon swim out to the ocean as young fish, then return years later to spawn in the exact stream where they hatched. They find the right river partly by remembering its unique smell. They can battle upstream and even leap up waterfalls to get there.

Weaver birds build elaborate hanging nests by knotting and weaving strips of grass with their beaks and feet. A male may build several nests, and females inspect them before choosing a mate. Some build giant shared nests that house hundreds of birds.

The trapdoor spider builds a burrow with a hinged lid made of silk and soil that blends into the ground. It hides underneath holding the door slightly open, then bursts out to grab passing insects. The camouflaged door is nearly invisible from above.

The ogre-faced spider spins a small stretchy net and holds it with its front legs like a tiny fishing net. When prey passes below, it stretches the net wide and snaps it down over the victim. It has huge eyes that give it excellent night vision.

Some assassin bugs pile the dried bodies of insects they have eaten onto their backs as a disguise. The grim backpack hides their shape and confuses predators and prey. It is like wearing a cloak made of leftovers to stay hidden.

The velvet worm hunts by squirting two jets of sticky slime from nozzles beside its mouth. The glue hardens fast and tangles up insects so they cannot escape. The worm then bites the trapped prey and even eats the dried slime to recycle it.

The tiny tarsier has eyes so big that each one is heavier than its brain. The huge eyes give it superb night vision for hunting insects in the dark. It cannot move its eyes much, so it turns its head almost all the way around like an owl.

Some bright pink millipedes defend themselves by oozing cyanide, a deadly chemical, from pores along their bodies. The smell warns predators to stay away. Their flashy colors are a clear signal that eating them would be a terrible idea.

The pangolin is the only mammal fully covered in hard overlapping scales made of the same stuff as your fingernails. When threatened it rolls into a tight ball that even lions struggle to open. It has no teeth and uses a long sticky tongue to slurp up ants.

Sloths move so slowly that green algae grows in their fur, helping them blend into the trees. Whole tiny ecosystems of insects live in a single sloth's coat. They move so little that they only need to come down to the ground about once a week.

The chuckwalla lizard escapes predators by squeezing into a rock crack and then gulping air to puff up its body. Wedged tightly in place, it becomes almost impossible to pull out. A predator usually gives up and goes hungry.

The pufferfish gulps water to blow itself up into a spiky ball several times its normal size when threatened. The sudden, prickly balloon is hard to swallow and scares off attackers. Many puffers also carry a strong poison that makes them dangerous to eat.

A porcupine can have around 30,000 sharp quills covering its body. When threatened it raises them and may back into an attacker so the quills jab in. Tiny barbs on the tips make the quills hard and painful to pull out.

A skunk warns enemies by stamping its feet and raising its tail before spraying a foul-smelling oil. It can hit a target several feet away with good aim. The stink is so strong it can be smelled from far off and clings for days.

When badly frightened, an opossum can flop over and play dead so convincingly that predators lose interest. Its body goes stiff, it drools, and it even releases a rotten smell as if it were already a corpse. This is an automatic reaction, not a choice.

The hognose snake puts on a dramatic show when scared. It first flattens its neck like a cobra and hisses, then if that fails it rolls onto its back, opens its mouth, and pretends to be a stinky dead snake. If you flip it upright, it rolls over again to keep up the act.

Certain Malaysian ants defend their colony by exploding on purpose. When a fight is lost, a worker squeezes until its body bursts, splattering a sticky, harmful liquid over the enemy. The sacrifice protects the rest of the nest.

The bombardier beetle can swivel the tip of its abdomen to aim its hot chemical spray in nearly any direction, even forward over its own head. It fires in rapid pulses rather than one stream. The popping bursts and burning chemicals send most attackers fleeing.

The wolverine is a small but ferocious animal that can take down prey much larger than itself. Its strong jaws and special teeth let it crunch through frozen meat and bone. It will even drive bears and wolves away from a meal.

For its size, the Tasmanian devil has one of the strongest bites of any mammal. It can crush bones with its jaws and eats nearly every part of its prey, fur and all. Its loud screeching at meals gave it the spooky name devil.

The jaguar has the strongest bite of any big cat for its size. Instead of going for the throat like other cats, it often kills by biting straight through the skull. Its powerful jaws can even crack open the shells of turtles and crush bones.

The saltwater crocodile has the most powerful bite ever measured in a living animal. Its jaws snap shut with enough force to crush bone instantly. Yet the muscles that open the jaws are so weak that a person can hold them shut with their hands.

The king cobra is the longest venomous snake, sometimes over 18 feet. One bite delivers enough venom to bring down an elephant or kill many people. It mostly eats other snakes and can rear up to look an adult human in the eye.

The inland taipan of Australia has the most toxic venom of any land snake. A single bite holds enough venom to kill many adults, yet this shy snake almost never meets people and rarely bites. It uses its powerful venom to quickly subdue rats.

The black ghost knifefish makes a weak electric field around its body all the time. When something disturbs the field, the fish senses it, letting it hunt and navigate in muddy water at night. It is like having an invisible bubble of touch around itself.

Sharks have tiny jelly-filled pores on their snouts that detect the faint electricity given off by every living thing's muscles. This lets a shark find a fish hiding under sand or in murky water. They can sense electric signals as small as a battery a thousand miles away in the right conditions.

Honeybees tell each other where to find flowers by doing a waggle dance inside the hive. The direction they waggle points toward the food relative to the sun, and the length of the dance shows how far away it is. It is like a tiny map made of movement.

Bees can see ultraviolet light that humans cannot. Many flowers have hidden ultraviolet patterns, like landing strips, that guide bees straight to the nectar. So a plain-looking flower may be glowing with secret bee signposts.

Dung beetles can roll their ball in a straight line by reading the stars. On clear nights they steer using the glowing band of the Milky Way. They are the only insects known to navigate by the galaxy itself.

Elephants talk to each other using deep rumbles too low for humans to hear, called infrasound. These sounds travel for miles, even through the ground. Elephants can feel the vibrations through their feet and trunk to stay in touch across long distances.

An elephant's trunk has no bones but around 40,000 muscles, far more than a human has in the entire body. It is strong enough to push down a tree yet gentle enough to pick up a single blade of grass. The elephant uses it to breathe, smell, drink, and grab.

A giraffe's heart must pump blood all the way up its long neck to its brain. To do this it has the highest blood pressure of any animal and a huge, powerful heart. Special valves in its neck stop too much blood rushing to its head when it bends down to drink.

A woodpecker can bang its head against a tree thousands of times a day without getting hurt. A spongy skull and a special tongue bone wrapped around its head cushion the blows. That long tongue can curl around the brain like a built-in seatbelt.

Camels are built for sandstorms. They have long double eyelashes, a clear third eyelid to wipe their eyes, and nostrils they can close to keep out blowing sand. Wide, padded feet keep them from sinking into the dunes.

A polar bear's fur is not really white, it is made of clear, hollow hairs that scatter light. Underneath, its skin is black to soak up the sun's warmth. A thick layer of fat keeps it so warm that it can overheat when it runs.

The arctic fox has the warmest fur of any animal and can survive temperatures far below freezing without shivering. Its small ears and short legs lose less heat. In winter its coat turns white for camouflage, then brown in summer.

Reindeer eyes change color with the seasons. In summer the back of the eye is golden, but in the dark Arctic winter it turns deep blue, which helps them see in the long polar nights. They can also see ultraviolet light, making things like fur and urine stand out in the snow.

Mantis shrimp can see and reflect polarized light, a kind of light filtered in one direction. Some send secret signals on their shells using polarized patterns that only other mantis shrimp can read. It is like having a private channel no predator can see.

Scorpions glow a bright blue-green under ultraviolet light. A special substance in their hard outer shell makes them fluoresce. Scientists are not fully sure why, but it may help scorpions sense moonlight to know when to stay hidden.

Most deep-sea animals cannot see red light, so one fish called the dragonfish uses it like a private searchlight. It produces a red glow to spot prey that has no idea it is being lit up. It is like hunting with night-vision goggles no one else owns.

Comb jellies have rows of tiny moving hairs that scatter light into shimmering rainbow waves as they swim. The colors are not made by the animal but by the way light bounces off its beating combs. They are among the largest animals to move using these tiny hairs.

The leaf-tailed gecko of Madagascar looks almost exactly like a dead leaf or piece of bark. Its flattened tail, jagged skin flaps, and matching colors break up its outline so it vanishes against a tree. Some even have fake leaf veins and notches.

Stick insects are masters of disguise, looking just like twigs or leaves. Some even sway gently to mimic a branch moving in the breeze. If a bird grabs one, it can drop a leg and grow a new one later.

The dead leaf butterfly has wings that look like a dried brown leaf when closed, complete with fake veins and a stem-like tail. Sitting still on a branch, it is nearly impossible to spot. When it opens its wings, bright blue and orange suddenly flash to startle predators.

The owl butterfly has huge eyespots on its wings that look like the staring eyes of an owl. When a small bird sees them, it thinks a predator is looking back and flies away. The fake eyes buy the butterfly time to escape.

The four-eyed fish swims at the surface and can see above and below the water at the same time. Each eye is split into two parts, one tuned for air and one for water. This lets it watch for birds overhead and food below all at once.

The deep-sea spookfish is the only animal known to see using mirrors inside its eyes instead of just lenses. The mirrors focus dim light from below, helping it spot the faint glow of prey in the dark depths. It can look up and down at the same time.

The sea sapphire is a tiny ocean creature that can flash brilliant blue and then vanish completely. Stacked crystal layers in its skin bounce light to create the color, and at the right angle it becomes nearly invisible. It is one of the most dazzling animals in the sea.

The male peacock spider, smaller than a fingernail, has a colorful flap on its back that it raises like a peacock's tail. It waves its legs and dances to impress a female. Its tiny body shows off some of the brightest colors in the animal world.

The blue morpho butterfly's wings are not actually blue. They are covered in microscopic scales shaped to bounce blue light back, a trick called structural color. If you got the wings wet or looked very close, the brilliant blue would disappear.

When a pistol shrimp snaps its claw, the collapsing bubble gets so hot it gives off a tiny flash of light. Scientists call this rare effect shrimpoluminescence. It is one of the only times a living animal creates light by popping a bubble.

Electric eels sometimes leap out of the water and press against a large attacker to deliver a stronger shock. Pressing against the target sends more of the jolt into it. Scientists confirmed this after one eel zapped a researcher's arm during an experiment.

The goliath frog is the biggest frog on Earth, growing as long as a house cat and as heavy as a newborn baby. It is strong enough to move rocks weighing as much as itself to build little ponds for its eggs. Despite its size, it cannot croak because it has no vocal sac.

The goliath beetle is one of the heaviest insects in the world, weighing as much as a small apple as a larva. The adults can fly even though they are huge. Their wings beat with a buzz so loud it sounds like a small toy helicopter.

The atlas moth has some of the largest wings of any moth, nearly as wide as a dinner plate. The tips of its wings look like the heads of cobras to scare off predators. It does not eat as an adult, living only a week or two on energy stored as a caterpillar.

The Hercules beetle is one of the longest beetles, with a huge horn nearly as long as the rest of its body. Males use the horns to wrestle and flip rivals off branches. For its size it is incredibly strong, able to carry many times its own weight.

The giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, each one about the size of a dinner plate. The huge eyes gather what little light reaches the deep ocean, helping the squid spot sperm whales hunting it. Few people have ever seen a living giant squid.

The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur. Its heart is about the size of a small car, and its tongue can weigh as much as an elephant. A human child could crawl through its main blood vessel.

The whale shark is the largest fish in the ocean, as long as a school bus, yet it eats mostly tiny plankton. It swims with its huge mouth open, filtering food from gallons of water at a time. Despite its size, it is gentle and harmless to people.

The basking shark is the second-largest fish and cruises near the surface with its enormous mouth wide open. It strains tiny plankton from the seawater that flows through its gills. Even though it can be over 30 feet long, it has no interest in big prey.

The ocean sunfish, or mola, is the heaviest bony fish in the world and can weigh as much as a small truck. It looks like a giant swimming head with fins. A single female may carry hundreds of millions of eggs, more than any other animal with a backbone.

The bumblebee bat is one of the smallest mammals in the world, weighing about as much as a coin and small enough to perch on a fingertip. It hunts tiny insects at dusk. Whole populations are rare, living in just a few caves.

The Etruscan shrew is the smallest mammal by weight, lighter than a coin. Its heart can beat over 1,500 times a minute, and it must eat almost constantly to stay alive. It eats around twice its own body weight in food every day.

The bee hummingbird of Cuba is the smallest bird in the world, barely bigger than a bee. Its eggs are no larger than a coffee bean. It beats its wings so fast that it can hover and sip nectar from many flowers in a single day.

One of the smallest fish in the world is a tiny see-through species from Southeast Asian swamps, smaller than your fingernail. It lives in dark, acidic water where few other fish can survive. You would need a magnifying glass to see it clearly.

Spinner dolphins leap out of the water and spin their bodies several times in the air before splashing down. They may do this to shake off pesky parasites, to communicate, or just for fun. A single dolphin can spin up to seven times in one jump.

Humpback whales work as a team to catch fish using a bubble net. They swim in a circle below a school of fish while blowing bubbles, creating a shrinking wall the fish will not cross. Then the whales swim up through the trapped fish with mouths wide open.

Orcas, or killer whales, are clever team hunters. Some swim together to create a wave that washes seals off ice floes into the water. Different groups have their own special hunting tricks that parents teach to their young, like a family tradition.

Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open hard shellfish. An otter floats on its back, rests a rock on its belly, and bangs a clam against it until it breaks. Many otters keep a favorite rock tucked in a flap of skin under their arm.

New Caledonian crows make and use tools, even bending wire into hooks to fish grubs out of holes. They can solve puzzles with several steps and remember the faces of people who once bothered them. They are among the smartest birds known.

Octopuses are remarkably smart for an animal with no bones. They can open jars, solve mazes, and escape through tiny gaps barely larger than their eye. Each of their eight arms has its own cluster of nerves, so the arms can act almost on their own.

Pigs are very intelligent animals that can learn their names, play simple video games with a joystick, and remember things for years. They use different sounds to talk to one another. Some scientists think pigs are smarter than dogs.

Ravens are clever enough to plan for the future, a skill once thought to be human only. They can save a tool to use later for a reward and trade objects in fair swaps. They also play, sliding down snowy roofs seemingly just for fun.

Dolphins can recognize themselves in a mirror, which shows a sense of self that few animals have. They will turn and twist to look at marks on their bodies. Each dolphin also has its own signature whistle that works like a name.

Elephants seem to mourn their dead, gently touching the bones of relatives with their trunks and staying nearby. They have excellent memories and can recognize hundreds of other elephants and even old human friends after many years. A matriarch remembers where to find water in a drought.

Parrots can copy human words because they have a special voice box and a clever brain. Some African grey parrots learn hundreds of words and use them in the right situations, not just by accident. One famous parrot could even count and name colors.

Chimpanzees make and use tools, like stripping a twig to fish termites out of their mound. Different chimp groups have their own tool styles that they pass down, a kind of culture. They can also crack nuts using a stone like a hammer.

An earthworm does not have a true heart but has several pairs of muscular tubes near its head that pump blood, often counted as five pairs of hearts. It breathes through its moist skin and has no lungs. If its skin dries out, it cannot get oxygen.

A cockroach can survive for over a week without its head. It breathes through tiny holes along its body, not its mouth, and its simple nerves keep it moving. It eventually dies of thirst because it cannot drink without a mouth.

A tiny flatworm called a planarian can be cut into many pieces, and each piece can grow into a whole new worm, head and all. Even more strangely, some experiments suggest a regrown worm may keep memories from before it lost its head. Scientists are still studying how.

A green sea slug eats algae and keeps the algae's solar-powered parts alive inside its own body. This lets the slug make energy from sunlight, almost like a leaf. It can go a long time without eating by basking in the light.

The upside-down jellyfish rests on the seafloor with its tentacles pointing up toward the sun. Tiny algae living inside it use sunlight to make food, which the jellyfish shares. It farms its own food using the sun, so it barely needs to hunt.

On just a few nights each year, whole coral reefs release their eggs and sperm into the water all at the same time. Triggered by the moon and water temperature, this underwater snowstorm helps the tiny coral cells find each other. It is one of the largest synchronized events in nature.

The Surinam toad carries its eggs embedded in the skin of its back. The babies develop inside little pockets and then pop out fully formed, an eerie sight. The mother's back looks bumpy and full while the young grow safely inside her skin.

Emperor penguin fathers balance their single egg on their feet under a flap of warm skin through the brutal Antarctic winter. They huddle together and barely eat for around two months while the mothers feed at sea. When the chick hatches, the mother returns to take over.

Some birds called megapodes never sit on their eggs. Instead the male builds a giant mound of rotting leaves and soil, which heats up like a compost pile. He checks the temperature with his beak and adds or removes material to keep the eggs just right.

Some fish protect their young by carrying them in their mouths, a behavior called mouthbrooding. The parent holds dozens of eggs or babies safely inside and does not eat until they are ready to swim free. At the first sign of danger, the young dart back into the parent's mouth.

The cuckoo tricks other birds into raising its young. It lays its egg in another bird's nest, and the unsuspecting parents feed the cuckoo chick as their own. The cuckoo chick often pushes the other eggs out so it gets all the food.

Tiny shrimp-like animals called krill gather in swarms so huge they can be seen from space and weigh millions of tons. Despite being just a couple inches long, krill are food for the biggest animals on Earth, including blue whales. They glow with their own light at night.

Glowworms in New Zealand caves hang sticky glowing threads from the ceiling to catch insects. The blue-green glow lures bugs that fly toward it and get tangled in the lines. A cave full of them looks like a starry night sky underground.

Some tiny ocean creatures called plankton flash bright blue when the water is disturbed. On certain nights, breaking waves and swimming animals make the sea sparkle and glow. The flash may startle predators or attract bigger animals that will eat the plankton's enemies.

Some click beetles have glowing spots that shine like tiny headlights. The light helps them find mates in the dark. The click beetle can also flip itself upright with a loud snapping click if it lands on its back.

The railroad worm glows with two colors at once, with green spots down its sides and a red glow on its head. The rows of lights look like the windows of a tiny train at night. It is one of the only land animals that can make red light.

Lanternfish are small deep-sea fish covered in glowing spots that they can switch on and off. The lights help them hide by matching the faint glow from above, find mates, and confuse predators. They are among the most common fish in the deep ocean.

The vampire squid lives deep in dark water where it cannot flee fast. When threatened, it shoots out a cloud of glowing sticky mucus instead of ink. The glittering glob confuses predators while the squid slips away into the dark.

The small cookiecutter shark glows over most of its body except a dark collar. The dark patch looks like a tiny fish to big predators, luring them close. When a large animal comes to investigate, the shark bites out a round plug of flesh and swims away.

The flashlight fish has glowing organs under its eyes filled with light-making bacteria. It can blink the lights off by rolling the organ or covering it with a lid of skin. It uses the blinking glow to find food, signal mates, and confuse predators.

The deep-sea worm Tomopteris is one of the very few animals that glows yellow instead of the usual blue. Scientists are still puzzled by why it makes this rare color of light. It swims gracefully through the dark ocean like a glowing ribbon.

The atolla jellyfish flashes a spinning ring of blue light when it is attacked, like a burglar alarm. The light show attracts even bigger predators that may chase off whatever is bothering the jellyfish. It is a clever way to call for help with light.

A millipede called Motyxia glows greenish-blue in the dark hills of California. The glow is a warning that it can ooze toxic cyanide if attacked. It is the only millipede known to make its own light, and it is completely blind.

A deep-sea worm sometimes called the green bomber can release glowing globes from its body when threatened. The little green bombs flash brightly and distract predators while the worm escapes into the dark. The worm can grow replacement bombs afterward.

The tuatara, a lizard-like reptile from New Zealand, has a tiny third eye on top of its head. This pinhole eye can sense light and helps the young tuatara track the seasons, though it gets covered by scales as it ages. Tuataras can live over 100 years.

Frogs blink in an unusual way to help them swallow. They pull their eyeballs down into their heads, and the bulge pushes food down their throat. A see-through third eyelid also slides over each eye to keep it moist and protected.

Some caterpillars protect themselves by looking like a small snake. They puff up the front of their body to show fake eyes and even sway as if about to strike. Birds that see the snakelike shape often fly away in fear.

The viceroy butterfly looks almost exactly like the monarch butterfly, which tastes bad to birds. By copying the monarch's orange and black pattern, the viceroy warns predators to leave it alone too. Both butterflies actually taste unpleasant, so they protect each other.

Hoverflies are harmless flies that have no sting, but many are striped yellow and black to look like wasps or bees. Predators avoid them, fooled by the dangerous-looking disguise. You can spot the trick because hoverflies hover in midair and have only two wings instead of four.

The harmless scarlet kingsnake copies the bright red, yellow, and black bands of the venomous coral snake. Predators that have learned to fear the coral snake stay away from the lookalike too. The bands are in a slightly different order, which is how to tell them apart.

The margay, a small wild cat, can imitate the call of a baby monkey to lure curious adult monkeys closer. Once a monkey comes to investigate, the margay pounces. It is one of the few cats known to use a fake sound to hunt.

The zone-tailed hawk hides among harmless vultures by looking and flying just like them. Prey on the ground ignores the circling birds, thinking they only eat the dead. Then the disguised hawk suddenly drops out of the group to make a surprise attack.

Alligators can survive a pond freezing over by sticking just their nostrils above the surface and letting the ice trap them in place. They slow their bodies way down and barely move until the thaw. They can hold their breath for hours when relaxed underwater.

Baby painted turtles can survive being partly frozen in their nest through winter. Their bodies handle ice forming around their cells, and special chemicals protect them. In spring they thaw out and dig their way up to the surface.

The only insect that lives all year on the Antarctic mainland is a tiny wingless midge. It survives by drying out and letting itself freeze solid during the long winter. When summer comes, it thaws and finishes its short life cycle.

An Alaskan beetle can survive being chilled far below freezing without turning to ice. Its body fluids stay liquid using natural antifreeze, a trick called supercooling. It can endure temperatures cold enough to freeze most living things solid.

The desert pupfish lives in shallow desert pools that can get scalding hot and saltier than the sea. It survives in water that would kill most fish. Some pupfish live in a single warm pool found nowhere else on Earth.

The Greenland shark may be the longest-living animal with a backbone, possibly reaching 400 years old. It grows extremely slowly in the cold deep ocean, sometimes only about a centimeter a year. A shark alive today could have been born centuries ago.

A clam called the ocean quahog can live for centuries. One famous clam named Ming was found to be over 500 years old, making it the oldest known animal. Like a tree, you can count rings on its shell to learn its age.

Some deep-sea glass sponges may be among the oldest living animals, possibly thousands of years old. They grow incredibly slowly in cold, still water. Their bodies are built from delicate glassy spikes that can form beautiful lattice shapes.

Lobsters keep growing throughout their lives and do not seem to weaken much with age. To grow, a lobster sheds its hard shell and grows a bigger one, a process called molting. Some large lobsters are likely many decades old.

The bowhead whale is one of the longest-living mammals, possibly over 200 years old. Old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found in living whales. It has the thickest blubber of any animal to survive the icy Arctic seas.

Giant tortoises can live well over 100 years, and some have reached nearly 190. They grow and move slowly, and their bodies age very gently. A few famous tortoises were alive when explorers visited their islands long ago.

The hydra is a tiny freshwater animal that may not age at all. It constantly replaces its own cells, so it does not get weaker over time the way most animals do. Under good conditions, a hydra could in theory live almost forever.

Tiny spiders can fly through the air without wings using a trick called ballooning. They release strands of silk that catch the breeze and even ride on natural electric charges in the air. This lets young spiders drift for many miles to new homes.

Water striders skate across the surface of ponds without sinking. Tiny waterproof hairs on their legs trap air and let them rest on the water's skin-like surface tension. They feel the ripples made by struggling insects and zip over to grab them.

A small sea snail called the limpet has the strongest known natural material in its teeth. The teeth are tougher than spider silk and let the limpet scrape algae off hard rocks without wearing down. Engineers study them to make stronger materials.

The parrotfish bites off chunks of coral to eat the tiny plants on it, then grinds the coral in its gut and poops out fine white sand. A single big parrotfish can make hundreds of pounds of sand a year. Much of the white sand on tropical beaches is parrotfish poop.

Termites build tall mounds with clever tunnels that keep the inside cool and full of fresh air, like natural air conditioning. Warm air rises and escapes through the top while cool air is drawn in below. Engineers have copied this design to cool buildings.

Honeybees build their honeycomb out of perfect six-sided cells called hexagons. This shape stores the most honey using the least wax and leaves no wasted gaps. Bees create the strong, neat pattern without any measuring tools.

A spider's web can grab insects partly using static electricity. Flying bugs build up a charge, and the web stretches toward them as they approach. This electric pull may help the sticky strands snatch prey out of the air.

When oxygen runs low in their crowded tunnels, naked mole rats switch to burning a kind of sugar that plants use, fructose, for energy. This lets them survive with almost no oxygen for many minutes. Few other mammals can do anything close to this.

A woodpecker's tongue is so long it wraps all the way around the back of its skull when not in use. The tongue can shoot out far past the beak to spear insects deep inside trees. This wrapping also helps cushion the brain from all the hard pecking.

A giraffe's tongue can be nearly 20 inches long and is a dark purple-blue color. The dark color may protect it from sunburn while the giraffe spends all day reaching for leaves. The tough tongue can wrap around thorny branches without getting hurt.

The giant anteater has a sticky tongue around two feet long that it can flick in and out up to 150 times a minute. It has no teeth, so it slurps up tens of thousands of ants and termites every day. It eats quickly at each mound so the insects do not swarm it.

A chameleon can move each of its eyes in a different direction at the same time. One eye can look forward while the other looks backward, giving it almost a full view all around. When it spots prey, both eyes lock onto it together to judge the distance.

Birds have hollow bones filled with air pockets that make their skeletons very light for flying. The bones still stay strong thanks to crisscrossing struts inside, like the supports in a bridge. Some flying birds weigh less than their own feathers.

Male frigatebirds blow up a bright red throat pouch like a giant balloon to attract a mate. They sit in groups, inflate their pouches, and drum on them while calling to passing females. The biggest, reddest pouch usually wins the most attention.

Male sage grouse have air sacs on their chests that they puff out and pop to make a strange bubbling sound. They strut and bounce the sacs to impress watching females. Many males gather in one spot and compete to put on the best show.

The club-winged manakin sings with its wings instead of its voice. It rubs special wing feathers together more than 100 times a second to make a violin-like buzz. It is one of the only birds known to make courtship music with feathers.

The snipe makes an eerie drumming sound by diving through the air so its stiff outer tail feathers vibrate. The whistling hum, called winnowing, carries far across marshes during courtship. The bird makes the sound with its tail, not its throat.

The kakapo is a heavy, flightless parrot from New Zealand. Males dig a bowl in the ground and make a deep booming call that can travel for miles to attract a mate. It is one of the rarest and longest-living birds, sometimes reaching 90 years old.

Baby hoatzin birds have claws on their wings that they use to climb back into the nest if they fall into the water. The claws disappear as the bird grows up. Adult hoatzins digest leaves in a way more like a cow than a bird, which gives them a strong smell.

Besides its powerful shock, the electric eel also makes small electric pulses to sense the world around it. The pulses bounce off nearby objects and fish, helping the eel find its way and locate prey in dark, muddy rivers. It is like a built-in radar made of electricity.

Honeybees can sense Earth's magnetic field and use it to help build straight honeycomb and find their way home. Tiny magnetic bits in their bodies act like a built-in compass. This is one of the many tools bees use to navigate so well.

European robins may see Earth's magnetic field using special proteins in their eyes. Scientists think the magnetic compass appears as a kind of pattern over what the bird sees. This helps the robin fly the right way during migration, even at night.

The male platypus is one of the few venomous mammals. It has sharp spurs on its back legs that deliver venom strong enough to cause great pain to a person. It uses the spurs mostly to fight other males during breeding season.

The slow loris is the only venomous primate. It licks a gland on its arm to mix a toxin with its spit, then delivers a painful bite. It may also lick the venom onto its babies' fur to keep predators away.

A few shrews have venom in their saliva, making them rare venomous mammals. The venom can paralyze prey like insects and worms, letting the shrew store living food to eat later. Shrews must eat almost constantly to survive.

Caecilians are legless, worm-like amphibians that live underground. In some species, the babies eat their mother's outer layer of skin, which she grows extra thick just for them. The mother regrows the skin every few days to keep feeding her young.

The mudskipper is a fish that spends much of its time out of water, walking on its fins across muddy shores. It breathes through its skin and the lining of its mouth as long as it stays damp. It can even climb roots and skip across the mud to escape danger.

The climbing perch can survive out of water for days and wriggle across land to find a new pond. It gulps air using a special breathing organ above its gills. It uses its fins and gill covers to push itself along the ground.

The snakehead fish can breathe air and slither across land for short distances to reach another body of water. Young snakeheads can survive out of water for several days if they stay moist. This lets them spread into new ponds on their own.

The epaulette shark can walk along the seafloor and even across exposed reef using its fins like little legs. When tide pools run low on oxygen, it can slow its body and survive conditions that would suffocate other fish. It often hunts in shallow water other sharks avoid.

When an archerfish spits at a bug above the water, it must aim slightly off because light bends as it passes from air into water. The fish's brain automatically corrects for this so the jet hits the target. Young fish improve their aim with practice.

The spitting spider catches prey by spraying a zigzag of sticky, venomous silk to glue the victim down. It fires the gluey threads from its fangs while wagging its head side to side. The trapped insect is pinned in place before it can react.

The bolas spider hunts like a tiny cowboy. It dangles a single strand of silk with a sticky blob on the end and swings it at passing moths. It even releases a scent that copies a female moth's smell to lure males straight into its trap.

The pelican spider has a long neck and huge jaws that fold like a tiny grabbing arm. It hunts other spiders, stabbing them from a safe distance so it does not get bitten back. Its strange shape makes it look like a tiny pelican.

Jumping spiders have some of the best eyesight of any small creature, thanks to their large front eyes. They can see color and judge distance well enough to pounce precisely on prey. Before they leap, they attach a silk safety line in case they miss.

Many tarantulas defend themselves by flicking tiny barbed hairs off their bellies at attackers. The itchy hairs irritate the skin, eyes, and nose of predators, driving them away. The tarantula uses its back legs to kick the hairs into the air.

The vinegaroon, a kind of whip scorpion, defends itself by spraying a fine mist that smells strongly of vinegar. The sour spray comes from glands near its tail and stings the eyes of attackers. Despite its scary looks, it has no venomous sting.

Camel spiders are fast desert hunters with huge jaws for their size, though they are neither true spiders nor scorpions. They can run quickly to chase down insects and small lizards. Many stories exaggerate them, but they are not dangerous to people.

Centipedes are speedy hunters with a pair of venom-tipped claws right behind the head. Some giant centipedes are large enough to catch mice, lizards, and even bats. Each body segment carries one pair of legs, and they can have dozens of them.

The Argentine tegu is a lizard that can warm its own body above the surrounding air during breeding season. Most reptiles rely fully on the sun, so this part-time warm blood is very unusual. It helps the tegu stay active when it needs energy most.

Bluefin tuna can keep parts of their body warmer than the water around them, which is rare for a fish. The extra warmth powers their muscles, letting them swim fast and migrate across whole oceans. They are some of the fastest and most powerful swimmers in the sea.

The opah, or moonfish, is the only fish known to keep its whole body warm. Special blood vessels in its gills work like a heat exchanger, trapping warmth from its muscles. This warm body lets it stay active in the cold deep ocean where other fish slow down.

During a drought, the African lungfish slows its heart and body almost to a stop inside a mud cocoon, a state called estivation. It can stay like this for years, barely using any energy. When water returns, it wakes up and swims off as if nothing happened.

Antarctic fish make special antifreeze proteins in their blood that stop ice crystals from growing inside them. Without it, they would freeze solid in the icy seas. This is one of nature's best tricks for living in water below the normal freezing point.

Tiny springtails called snow fleas hop around on top of snow in winter without freezing. They make a special antifreeze protein that keeps ice from forming in their bodies. You can sometimes see them as little dark specks bouncing on a snowy day.

Camels have a stomach with several chambers and chew their food twice to get every bit of nutrition from dry desert plants. This careful digestion lets them survive on tough, thorny shrubs that other animals avoid. It also helps them go a long time between meals.

Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves that are poisonous to most animals. A special part of their gut and helpful bacteria break down the toxins so they can survive on this risky diet. The leaves give little energy, so koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day.

Giant pandas eat mostly bamboo even though their bodies are built for meat. They have a special wrist bone that works like an extra thumb to grip the stalks. Because bamboo gives so little energy, a panda must eat for many hours every day.

Vultures can safely eat rotting meat that would make other animals sick. Their stomach acid is so strong it destroys deadly germs like those that cause anthrax. By cleaning up carcasses, vultures help stop diseases from spreading.

A bird called the honeyguide leads people to wild beehives by chattering and flying ahead. After the humans crack open the hive and take the honey, the bird feasts on the leftover wax and grubs. It is one of the only wild birds that teams up with humans on purpose.

Clownfish live safely among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones that would harm most other fish. A special coating of mucus protects the clownfish from the stings. In return, the clownfish helps clean the anemone and chases away its enemies.

The cleaner wrasse runs a kind of cleaning station on the reef. Bigger fish line up and let the little wrasse swim into their mouths and gills to nibble off parasites and dead skin. The big fish get cleaned and the wrasse gets a meal, so neither one eats the other.

Oxpecker birds ride on the backs of rhinos, zebras, and buffalo, eating ticks and other pests from their skin. They also screech loudly to warn the big animals when danger is near. The birds get food, and the animals get cleaned and an early alarm.

The aye-aye, a strange lemur, has a long, thin middle finger it uses to tap on trees and listen for hollow tunnels where grubs hide. When it hears one, it gnaws a hole and fishes out the grub with that same skinny finger. It is the only primate that hunts this way.

A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its whole body and is rooted deep near its pelvis rather than in its mouth. It uses the long, sticky tongue to slurp ants and termites out of their nests. A pangolin can eat tens of thousands of insects in a single night.

The star-nosed mole can smell underwater, which scientists once thought was impossible for a mammal. It blows out tiny air bubbles and quickly sniffs them back in to catch scents in the water. This helps it find food while swimming in dark, murky streams.

Elephants may have the best sense of smell of any animal, with far more smell genes than a dog or a human. They can sniff out water from miles away and tell different groups of people apart by scent. Their trunk is both a nose and a hand.

Bears have an incredible sense of smell, far stronger than a bloodhound's. A bear can detect food or another animal from miles away, even across water. Much of its brain is devoted to smell, which it relies on more than its eyesight.

The kiwi is one of the only birds with nostrils at the very tip of its long beak. It pokes its beak into the soil and sniffs out worms and bugs hiding underground. With weak eyesight, the kiwi relies mostly on smell and touch to find food at night.

Breathing a little helium makes your voice sound high and squeaky. That's because sound travels much faster through light helium gas than through normal air, which changes the pitch of your voice. The size of your voice box stays the same, but the gas around your vocal cords speeds the sound up.

keywords: metal that melts in your hand
facts.answer: Gallium is a metal that stays solid at room temperature but melts in your warm hand at about 30 degrees Celsius. A gallium spoon would slowly turn into a puddle if you stirred a hot drink with it. It's not poisonous to touch, but it stains skin and sticks to other metals.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, which is why it was once called quicksilver. It is so dense that a cannonball can float on top of it. Mercury is poisonous, so scientists no longer use it the way they used to.

Diamonds and pencil 'lead' are both made of pure carbon, just arranged differently. In diamond the carbon atoms lock into a super-strong 3D grid, making it the hardest natural material. In graphite the atoms form slippery sheets that slide off onto paper, which is why it writes.

Most things shrink when they get cold, but water expands when it freezes into ice. The water molecules lock into an open, six-sided pattern that takes up more space than liquid water. That's why ice floats and why frozen water pipes can burst.

Gold is a 'noble' metal, meaning it almost never reacts with air or water, so it never rusts or tarnishes. Gold jewelry found in 3,000-year-old tombs still shines like new. That's part of why gold has been treasured for so long.

Fire is a chemical reaction that needs oxygen from the air to keep going. When you smother a candle with a glass, the flame uses up the trapped oxygen and goes out. This is why blowing on a campfire helps it grow: you're feeding it fresh oxygen.

Table salt is made of two dangerous elements joined together: sodium, a metal that explodes in water, and chlorine, a poisonous gas. But when they bond into sodium chloride, they become the harmless white crystals we sprinkle on food. Chemical bonds can completely change how elements behave.

Water is made of tiny molecules, each with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, which is why it's written H2O. Both hydrogen and oxygen are gases on their own, but combined they make a liquid we drink. Almost two-thirds of your body is water.

Hydrogen is the lightest and simplest element, with just one proton and one electron. It is also the most common element in the whole universe, making up most stars including our Sun. On Earth it's usually locked up inside water and other molecules.

Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon almost never react with other elements because their atoms already have a full, stable set of electrons. This makes them very calm and safe. Neon's lack of reactions is exactly why it can glow steadily inside light tubes.

Neon signs glow because electricity is passed through neon gas trapped in glass tubes, making the gas give off a bright orange-red light. Other colors in 'neon' signs actually come from different gases or coatings, not neon itself. Each gas glows its own special color.

Rust forms when iron reacts slowly with oxygen and water in the air, making a flaky reddish-brown coating called iron oxide. Unlike a protective layer, rust keeps eating deeper into the metal. That's why we paint or oil iron to keep air and water away from it.

Aluminum reacts with air too, but instead of flaky rust it forms a thin, tough, invisible layer of aluminum oxide that protects the metal underneath. This shield stops air from reaching deeper, so aluminum stays strong. That's why soda cans and airplanes don't fall apart.

Copper slowly reacts with air and rain to form a greenish coating called patina. The Statue of Liberty is made of copper and was once shiny brown, but over decades it turned its famous green color. The patina actually protects the copper underneath.

Acids are sour-tasting substances like lemon juice and vinegar, while bases are bitter and slippery, like soap and baking soda. When an acid and a base mix in the right amounts, they cancel each other out in a reaction called neutralization. Scientists measure how acidic something is using the pH scale.

keywords: why vinegar and baking soda bubble
facts.answer: When you mix baking soda (a base) with vinegar (an acid), they react and make bubbles of carbon dioxide gas. That fizzing gas is what makes toy volcanoes erupt. The same gas is what makes bread rise and fizzy drinks bubbly.

Fizzy drinks get their bubbles from carbon dioxide gas dissolved in the liquid under pressure. When you open the can, the pressure drops and the gas escapes as bubbles. That's also why a warm, shaken soda fizzes over so dramatically.

keywords: dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide
facts.answer: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, and it's far colder than normal ice. Instead of melting into a liquid, it turns straight into gas in a process called sublimation, which makes that spooky fog. You should never touch it with bare hands because it can give you frostbite.

Sublimation is when a solid turns straight into a gas without becoming a liquid first. Dry ice does this, and so does snow that vanishes on a sunny but freezing day. The opposite, gas turning straight into a solid, is called deposition, like frost forming on a window.

The three most common states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas. In a solid the particles are packed tightly and hold their shape; in a liquid they slide around and take the shape of the container; in a gas they fly around freely and spread out. A fourth state, plasma, is found in stars and lightning.

Plasma is a super-hot state of matter where atoms get torn apart into charged particles. It might sound rare, but plasma is actually the most common state of matter in the universe because stars are made of it. On Earth you can see plasma in lightning, neon signs, and flames.

Atoms are almost entirely empty space. The tiny nucleus in the center holds nearly all the mass, while electrons zip around far away. If an atom were the size of a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea in the middle and the rest would be empty.

An atom has three main parts: protons with a positive charge, neutrons with no charge, and electrons with a negative charge. Protons and neutrons sit in the center, called the nucleus, while electrons whiz around the outside. The number of protons decides which element an atom is.

The periodic table is a chart that organizes all the known chemical elements by their properties. Elements in the same column behave in similar ways, which lets scientists predict how they'll react. It was designed by Dmitri Mendeleev, who even left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

When Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table in 1869, he left empty gaps where he believed undiscovered elements should fit. He even predicted what those missing elements would be like. Years later scientists found them, and they matched his guesses almost perfectly.

There are 118 known chemical elements on the periodic table. About 90 of them occur naturally on Earth, and the rest are made by scientists in laboratories. Everything you can see and touch is built from combinations of these elements.

keywords: oxygen most common in earth crust
facts.answer: Oxygen is the most common element in Earth's crust, making up almost half of it by weight. It isn't floating around as gas there; instead it's locked inside rocks and minerals combined with other elements like silicon. Silicon is the second most common element in the crust.

Silicon is one of the most common elements on Earth and is found in sand and rocks. Purified silicon is used to make the tiny computer chips inside phones, laptops, and game consoles. So the same stuff in a sandcastle helps power your video games.

Glass is made mostly by melting sand at very high temperatures, around 1,700 degrees Celsius. The melted sand cools into a clear, hard material that we shape into windows and bottles. Glass isn't quite a normal solid; its particles are jumbled like a frozen liquid.

Glass is see-through because its particles are arranged so that visible light passes straight through without bouncing back to your eyes. Many solids block light because their particles scatter it, but glass lets it slip by. That's why you can see clearly through a clean window.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, around 3,400 degrees Celsius. That's why it's used for the glowing filament inside old-style light bulbs, where it gets white-hot without melting. Its name comes from Swedish words meaning 'heavy stone.'

In old-style incandescent bulbs, electricity flows through a thin tungsten wire and heats it until it glows white-hot, giving off light. The bulb is filled with gas that won't burn the wire away. Most of the energy turns into heat, which is why these bulbs feel hot.

Chlorine is added to swimming pools to kill germs and keep the water safe to swim in. That sharp pool smell often comes not from clean chlorine but from chlorine reacting with sweat and other stuff swimmers bring in. A clean, well-balanced pool actually smells very little.

Fluoride is added to toothpaste and some drinking water because it helps make tooth enamel stronger and more resistant to cavities. It bonds with the surface of your teeth to repair tiny weak spots. That's why dentists recommend brushing with fluoride toothpaste.

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. It works like a helper that makes the reaction easier to happen. Your body uses catalysts called enzymes to digest food quickly at normal body temperature.

Enzymes are special proteins in your body that act as catalysts, speeding up the chemical reactions that keep you alive. They help break down the food you eat into pieces small enough for your body to use. Without enzymes, digesting a single meal could take ages.

Metals conduct electricity well because some of their electrons are loosely held and free to move around. When you connect a battery, these free electrons flow through the metal, carrying the electric current. Copper and silver are especially good conductors, which is why wires are often made of copper.

Silver is the best electrical conductor of all metals, even better than copper. But silver is expensive, so most wires use copper instead, which is almost as good and much cheaper. Silver is still used in special electronics where top performance matters.

Rubber is an insulator, meaning electricity can't flow through it easily because its electrons are tightly held in place. That's why electrical wires are wrapped in rubber or plastic, to keep the current safely inside. Insulators are the opposite of conductors like metal.

Soap cleans because each soap molecule has one end that grabs onto water and another end that grabs onto oil and grease. This lets soap surround dirt and oil and wash them away with water. Plain water alone can't wash off greasy stuff, but soap makes it possible.

keywords: oil and water do not mix
facts.answer: Oil and water don't mix because water molecules are attracted to each other but not to oil. The oil clumps together and floats on top because it's less dense than water. Shaking them just makes tiny droplets that separate again once you stop.

Whether something floats or sinks depends on its density, which is how much mass is packed into its size. Objects less dense than water float, and denser ones sink. A heavy steel ship floats because its shape holds lots of air, making the whole ship less dense than water overall.

Helium balloons float because helium gas is much lighter than the air around them, so the air pushes the balloon up like a cork in water. Over a day or two the tiny helium atoms slip out through the balloon, and it sinks. Helium is the second-lightest element after hydrogen.

Metals look shiny because their loose surface electrons bounce light back at your eyes instead of letting it pass through or soak in. This bouncing-back is called luster. A freshly cut or polished metal reflects light almost like a mirror.

An alloy is a mix of two or more metals, or a metal with another element, made to get better properties. For example, bronze is copper mixed with tin, and it's harder than copper alone. Mixing metals lets us design materials that are stronger, lighter, or more rust-proof.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin that's much harder and stronger than copper by itself. It was so important to early people that an entire period of history is called the Bronze Age. Bronze tools and weapons gave a big advantage to those who could make them.

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, known for its golden color and bright sound. It's used to make musical instruments like trumpets and trombones, as well as door handles and decorations. Brass doesn't rust the way iron does, so it stays attractive for years.

Steel is an alloy made mostly of iron with a small amount of carbon added. That little bit of carbon makes the iron far stronger and harder, which is why steel is used to build bridges, cars, and skyscrapers. Adding other metals creates special steels that resist rust or extreme heat.

Stainless steel resists rust because it contains the metal chromium, which forms a thin invisible protective layer on the surface. Even if you scratch it, the layer quickly heals itself by reacting with air. That's why kitchen sinks and cutlery made of stainless steel stay shiny.

Titanium is a metal that is both very strong and surprisingly light, and it doesn't rust easily. These qualities make it perfect for airplanes, spacecraft, and even medical implants placed inside the body. It's also used in eyeglass frames because it's tough but barely felt.

Most metals look silvery, but gold has a warm yellow color because of how its electrons absorb and reflect light. Tiny effects from Einstein's theory of relativity change how gold's electrons behave, shifting the color we see. Copper's reddish tint comes from a similar cause.

Lead is a soft, very heavy metal that was once used in pipes, paint, and even gasoline. We now know lead is poisonous, especially for children, so it has been removed from most products. Its heaviness still makes it useful for blocking harmful radiation.

Uranium is a heavy metal whose atoms are unstable and slowly break apart, releasing energy as radiation. This energy can be used in nuclear power plants to make electricity. Because its radiation is dangerous, uranium must be handled with great care.

Radioactivity happens when the nucleus of an unstable atom breaks down and shoots out energy or tiny particles. Some elements like uranium and radium are naturally radioactive. The radiation can be harmful in large amounts, but small, controlled doses are used in medicine to see inside the body.

Marie Curie was a scientist who discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium. She won two Nobel Prizes, in physics and chemistry, which almost no one has ever done. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they must be stored in special protective boxes.

Scientists figure out the age of old bones and plants using carbon dating. Living things absorb a tiny amount of radioactive carbon, which slowly breaks down after they die. By measuring how much is left, scientists can estimate how long ago something lived, up to about 50,000 years.

A cut apple turns brown because the inside reacts with oxygen in the air, a process called oxidation. Squeezing lemon juice on the slices slows it down because the acid blocks the reaction. The same kind of browning happens to bananas and avocados.

Coins and silverware go dull and dark because the metal slowly reacts with chemicals in the air, especially tiny amounts of sulfur. This dark coating is called tarnish. Polishing rubs off the tarnish and brings back the shine, but it slowly returns over time.

In a physical change, a substance changes its form but stays the same material, like ice melting into water. In a chemical change, substances turn into entirely new ones, like wood burning into ash and smoke. A chemical change usually can't be easily reversed.

An atom is the smallest piece of an element, while a molecule is two or more atoms joined together. For example, a single oxygen atom is tiny, but in the air oxygen travels as molecules of two atoms bonded together. Water is a molecule made of three atoms: two hydrogen and one oxygen.

An element is made of just one kind of atom, while a compound is made when different elements bond together to form a new substance. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, and salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine. Compounds have totally different properties from the elements inside them.

A mixture is when substances are simply mixed together without bonding, like sand and water or salt stirred into soup. Unlike a compound, the parts of a mixture keep their own properties and can usually be separated again. You can filter sand out of water or boil salt water to get the salt back.

When you make ice cream by hand, you pack ice with salt around the bowl. Salt lowers the temperature at which ice melts, so the ice gets even colder than usual as it melts. That extra-cold mixture freezes the cream into ice cream.

People spread salt on icy roads because salt lowers the freezing point of water, making the ice melt even when it's below freezing. This helps keep roads and sidewalks safer in winter. It works best when it's not too far below freezing.

Cars use a liquid called antifreeze in their engines to stop the water inside from freezing in winter or boiling in summer. Antifreeze lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the engine's cooling liquid. This keeps the engine working safely in hot and cold weather.

When water boils, it gets hot enough to turn into gas called water vapor right inside the liquid. Those bubbles rising up are pockets of water vapor, not air. At sea level water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, but it boils at a lower temperature high up on mountains.

Water boils at a lower temperature high up on a mountain because the air pressure is lower there. With less air pushing down, water turns to vapor more easily. This means food can take longer to cook at high altitudes, since the boiling water isn't as hot.

Evaporation is when a liquid slowly turns into a gas even without boiling. A puddle dries up in the sun because its water evaporates into the air. Evaporation happens faster when it's warm, windy, or dry, which is why wet clothes dry quickest on a breezy sunny day.

Condensation is when water vapor in the air cools down and turns back into liquid water. That's why a cold glass of lemonade gets wet on the outside on a hot day. The same process forms dew on grass in the morning and clouds in the sky.

Water constantly travels in a cycle: it evaporates from oceans and lakes into vapor, rises and cools to form clouds, then falls back as rain or snow. This is called the water cycle. The water you drink today might have been part of a cloud or a dinosaur's drink long ago.

Bread rises because tiny living yeast in the dough eat sugar and give off carbon dioxide gas. The gas gets trapped as bubbles in the stretchy dough, making it puff up. Baking then sets the dough in its risen shape and gives bread its airy texture.

When sugar is heated, it melts and then breaks down into new compounds that are brown and rich-tasting, turning into caramel. This is a chemical change, not just melting. The same kind of browning gives toast, roasted marshmallows, and seared food their delicious flavor.

The browning and tasty smell of toast, grilled meat, and baked cookies comes from the Maillard reaction. It happens when heat makes the sugars and proteins in food react and form hundreds of new flavor compounds. This reaction is a big reason cooked food tastes so good.

Different metals burn with different colored flames, a trick scientists call a flame test. Copper turns a flame green or blue, sodium turns it bright yellow, and lithium turns it red. By looking at the flame color, chemists can tell which metal is present.

keywords: why fire is hot and bright
facts.answer: Fire is hot and bright because burning is a fast chemical reaction that releases lots of energy as heat and light. The glowing flame is made of hot gases and tiny glowing bits of fuel. The color of a flame tells you how hot it is: blue flames are hotter than yellow ones.

A blue flame is usually hotter than a yellow or orange one. Blue means the fuel is burning cleanly and completely with plenty of oxygen, releasing more heat. Yellow flames have tiny unburned bits of soot glowing inside them, and they burn cooler.

Smoke appears when something burns without enough oxygen to burn completely. The leftover tiny bits of unburned material float up as smoke and soot. A clean-burning fire with lots of air makes very little smoke.

Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no color or smell, made when fuel burns without enough oxygen. It's dangerous because your body absorbs it instead of oxygen. That's why homes have carbon monoxide detectors to warn people before it builds up.

Diamonds sparkle because they bend and bounce light around inside before sending it back out, splitting it into rainbow flashes. Cutters carefully shape each diamond's many flat faces to catch and reflect as much light as possible. The clearer and better cut the diamond, the more it sparkles.

Graphene is a material made of carbon arranged in a single layer just one atom thick, yet it's one of the strongest materials known. It conducts electricity and heat extremely well. Scientists are excited about using it in faster electronics and lighter, tougher products.

Charcoal is mostly pure carbon left behind when wood is heated without much air so it doesn't fully burn. It's black because carbon absorbs almost all the light that hits it. Charcoal is full of tiny holes, which is why it's used in filters and to soak up smells.

Activated charcoal is treated so it has millions of tiny holes, giving it a huge hidden surface area. Bad-tasting chemicals and impurities stick to all that surface, which is why it's used in water filters and air purifiers. A single gram can have the surface area of a football field.

Bleach removes stains and color by chemically breaking apart the molecules that give things their color. Once those color molecules are broken, the stain can't reflect color anymore, so it looks white. Bleach is strong, which is why it can also kill germs.

Batteries make electricity through chemical reactions inside them. Different materials at the two ends react and push electrons through a wire, creating an electric current. When the chemicals are used up, the battery goes dead, though rechargeable batteries can reverse the reaction.

Rechargeable batteries work like normal ones, but their chemical reaction can run backward. When you plug them in to charge, electricity reverses the reaction and restores the chemicals to their starting state. This lets the same battery be used hundreds of times before wearing out.

Phones can get warm while charging because pushing electricity through the battery's chemicals creates some heat as a side effect. A little warmth is normal, but too much heat can damage a battery. That's why phones are designed to slow charging if they get too hot.

Metals expand a little when heated because their atoms jiggle harder and push slightly farther apart. This is why bridges have special gaps so they don't buckle on hot days. A tight metal jar lid often loosens after running it under hot water for the same reason.

Most materials grow a little bigger when heated and shrink when cooled, because heat makes their tiny particles move more and spread apart. Engineers must plan for this when building railroads, bridges, and roads. Thermometers work using this idea, as liquid expands up a tube when warm.

Hot air rises because heating makes air expand and become less dense than the cooler air around it, so it floats upward. This movement of warm and cool air is called convection. It's why the upstairs of a house is often warmer and how hot air balloons fly.

Hot air balloons fly because heating the air inside the balloon makes it lighter than the cooler air outside. The lighter air lifts the balloon up, just like a bubble rising in water. The pilot controls height by heating the air to rise or letting it cool to descend.

Water puts out most fires by cooling the burning fuel below the temperature it needs to keep burning, and by blocking oxygen. But you should never use water on a grease or electrical fire, because it can make those worse. Different fires need different ways to put them out.

keywords: why grease fire spreads with water
facts.answer: Pouring water on a burning pan of oil is very dangerous because the water instantly turns to steam and blasts the burning oil everywhere. Since oil floats on water, the fire spreads instead of stopping. Smothering the flames with a lid is much safer.

Many fire extinguishers spray a powder or gas that smothers a fire by cutting off its oxygen supply or cooling it down. Without oxygen, the fire can't keep its chemical reaction going. Different types are made for different fires, like burning liquids or electrical fires.

The air around us is mostly nitrogen gas, about 78 percent, with only about 21 percent oxygen. Nitrogen is calm and doesn't react easily, which is good because it dilutes the oxygen so things don't burn too quickly. We breathe in nitrogen but our bodies mostly breathe it right back out.

Liquid nitrogen is nitrogen gas cooled until it becomes a liquid at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, which is extremely cold. Scientists and chefs use it to freeze things almost instantly. Touching it without protection can cause serious frostbite, so it must be handled carefully.

Plants take in carbon dioxide gas from the air and, using sunlight, turn it into food and release oxygen. This process is called photosynthesis. So while we breathe out carbon dioxide, plants breathe it in, making them and us perfect partners.

The ozone layer is a band of special oxygen molecules high in the sky that blocks most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays. Without it, life on Earth would be badly damaged by too much radiation. People once made a hole in it with certain chemicals, but it's slowly healing now they're banned.

Only a few metals, like iron, nickel, and cobalt, are strongly magnetic. That's because their atoms can line up so their tiny magnetic fields point the same way. Most metals, like gold and aluminum, are not magnetic at all even though they're shiny.

Old thermometers used liquid mercury because it expands evenly as it gets warmer, climbing up a thin tube to show the temperature. Since mercury is poisonous, most modern thermometers use a safer liquid or electronics instead. Mercury thermometers are now being phased out.

Permanent markers use ink that contains stuff that doesn't dissolve in water once it dries. The ink also soaks slightly into surfaces and grips them. That's why it shrugs off water but can sometimes be removed with rubbing alcohol, which can dissolve it.

A pencil writes by leaving tiny flakes of graphite on the paper's surface. An eraser works by gently grabbing and lifting those flakes off, while crumbling away to take the smudge with it. That's why erasers leave little crumbs behind.

Glow sticks light up when you snap them, breaking an inner tube so two chemicals mix and react. The reaction releases energy as light instead of heat, which is why glow sticks stay cool. This is called chemiluminescence, the same trick fireflies use.

Fireflies make light through a chemical reaction in their bodies, using a substance called luciferin and oxygen. Almost all the energy becomes light with hardly any heat, so it's sometimes called cold light. This natural glow is known as bioluminescence.

keywords: why some animals glow in deep sea
facts.answer: Many deep-sea creatures glow using chemical reactions in their bodies, since sunlight can't reach those dark depths. They use the light to attract prey, scare enemies, or find mates. This living light, called bioluminescence, can be blue, green, or even red.

Milk goes sour when bacteria in it turn the milk's sugar into lactic acid. The acid changes the taste and makes the milk's proteins clump, which is why old milk smells bad and gets lumpy. Keeping milk cold slows the bacteria down.

Cheese is made by adding things to milk that make its proteins clump together into solid curds. The watery part, called whey, is drained away, and the curds are pressed and aged into cheese. Different methods and aging times create hundreds of cheese flavors.

Vinegar tastes sour because it contains acetic acid, which forms when bacteria turn the alcohol in things like wine or cider into acid. Acids generally taste sour, which is why lemons and vinegar both pucker your mouth. Vinegar is also used to clean and preserve food.

Lemons taste sour because they're full of citric acid. Your tongue has special taste sensors that detect acids and send a sour signal to your brain. Many sour candies coat themselves in citric acid to give that mouth-puckering zing.

keywords: why baking powder makes cakes rise
facts.answer: Baking powder makes cakes and muffins rise because it releases carbon dioxide gas when it gets wet and hot. The gas forms tiny bubbles in the batter that puff it up as it bakes. Unlike yeast, baking powder works fast and doesn't need time to rest.

Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases a chemical that floats up and reacts with the water in your eyes to make a mild acid. Your eyes water to wash the stinging acid away. Chilling the onion first or cutting it under running water can reduce the tears.

Chili peppers feel hot because they contain a chemical called capsaicin, which tricks the pain sensors in your mouth into thinking they're being burned. There's no real heat, just a fooled nerve signal. Drinking milk helps more than water because the spicy chemical dissolves in fat, not water.

Mint feels cool in your mouth because it contains a chemical called menthol that activates the same nerves that sense cold. Your mouth isn't actually getting colder; the menthol just tricks those nerves. This is the opposite of how chili peppers fool your heat sensors.

Sugar dissolves in water because water molecules surround each sugar particle and pull it away from the others until it's spread evenly through the liquid. Warm water dissolves sugar faster because its molecules move quicker. The sugar isn't gone; it's just hidden among the water molecules.

Most solids dissolve faster in hot water because the heat makes the water molecules move quicker and bump into the solid more often. That's why sugar disappears faster in hot tea than in iced tea. Stirring also speeds dissolving by bringing fresh water to the solid.

Water can only dissolve so much of something before it can't hold any more, at which point the solution is saturated. Add extra sugar to a saturated cup and it just sits at the bottom. Heating the water lets it dissolve more, which is how you can grow sugar crystals.

Rock candy forms when you dissolve lots of sugar in hot water, then let it cool slowly. As the water cools and evaporates, it can't hold all that sugar, so the sugar slowly builds back into crystals on a string. Growing big crystals can take a week or more.

Crystals form when atoms or molecules line up in a neat, repeating pattern as a liquid cools or evaporates. This orderly stacking gives crystals their flat faces and sharp edges. Salt crystals are cubes and snowflakes are six-sided because of how their particles connect.

Salt crystals form tiny cubes because sodium and chlorine atoms stack in a neat, box-like grid. If you look at table salt under a magnifying glass, you can spot the little cube shapes. The orderly stacking of atoms is what gives many crystals their geometric shapes.

Gemstones get their colors from tiny amounts of certain elements mixed into their crystals. For example, a bit of chromium turns a clear mineral into a red ruby, while the same mineral with iron and titanium becomes a blue sapphire. Pure crystals with no extras are often colorless.

Rubies and sapphires are actually the same mineral, called corundum, just with different impurities. A trace of chromium makes corundum red, creating a ruby, while iron and titanium make it blue, creating a sapphire. So these two famous gems are really chemical cousins.

Emeralds are green because their crystals contain small amounts of the elements chromium or vanadium. These trace elements absorb certain colors of light and let green through to your eyes. Without them, the same mineral, called beryl, would be colorless.

Diamond is the hardest natural material, which means it can scratch almost anything but is very hard to scratch itself. Scientists rank hardness on the Mohs scale from 1 to 10, and diamond sits at the very top, 10. That's why diamonds are used on cutting and drilling tools.

Talc is the softest mineral, scoring a 1 on the Mohs hardness scale, so soft you can scratch it with your fingernail. Ground-up talc makes the smooth, slippery powder used in baby powder and makeup. Its softness comes from layers that slide past each other easily.

Glass shatters into sharp pieces because it's brittle, meaning it can't bend or stretch to absorb a sudden force. When hit hard enough, the energy races through it as cracks. Special tempered glass is treated so it breaks into small, dull cubes that are safer.

Car side windows are made of tempered glass, which is treated with heat so it's stronger and breaks into tiny dull cubes instead of sharp shards. This makes it much safer in a crash. Front windshields use a different design with a plastic layer that holds broken glass together.
