Plastic lasts a very long time because it's made of strong human-made molecules that natural microbes don't know how to break down. While a banana peel rots in weeks, a plastic bottle can last hundreds of years. That's a big reason littered plastic is such a problem.

Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas, which come from deep underground. Factories link tiny molecules from these fuels into long chains that can be molded into almost any shape. That's why plastic is in so many things, from toys to water bottles.

Styrofoam is mostly air trapped inside a lightweight plastic foam. All that trapped air makes it float and also makes it a great insulator, slowing heat from moving through it. That's why it keeps drinks hot or cold and protects fragile packages.

Metals can be recycled over and over because melting them down doesn't ruin them; they can be reshaped into new things. Recycling an aluminum can uses far less energy than making one from raw materials. That's why recycling metal is so good for the planet.

Aluminum cans are valuable to recycle because making a new can from recycled aluminum uses about 95 percent less energy than making one from scratch. A recycled can be back on a shelf as a new can in as little as 60 days. Aluminum can be recycled endlessly without losing quality.

keywords: why paper is made from trees
facts.answer: Paper is made from tiny wood fibers from trees. The wood is mashed into a wet pulp, spread thin, pressed, and dried into sheets. Paper can be recycled by soaking it back into pulp, though the fibers get shorter each time and eventually wear out.

Oil is slippery because its molecules slide past each other and don't stick to surfaces the way water does. This is why oil is used to lubricate machines, letting metal parts glide instead of grinding. The slipperiness reduces friction and wear.

Soap lets water form bubbles by making a thin, stretchy film that can trap air inside. Plain water can't hold a bubble because its surface pulls too tightly and pops. Soap loosens that pull just enough so the film can stretch around a pocket of air.

Water molecules pull on each other so strongly that the surface acts like a thin stretchy skin, called surface tension. This is why water forms rounded drops and why some bugs can walk on a pond. A gentle paperclip can even float on water if you place it carefully.

keywords: why some bugs walk on water
facts.answer: Some insects, like water striders, can walk on water because of surface tension, the stretchy skin on the water's surface. Their light bodies and water-repelling legs spread out their weight so they don't break through. To them, the pond surface feels like a trampoline.

Ice is slippery partly because a thin layer of liquid water sits right on its surface, even when it's freezing. Pressure and movement, like an ice skate gliding, can help create this slick film. The water layer lets things slide easily across the ice.

Putting metal in a microwave is dangerous because the metal can build up electric charge at its edges until it sparks. Microwaves heat food by shaking water molecules, but metal reflects and concentrates the energy instead. Those sparks can start a fire or damage the microwave.

Microwave ovens heat food by sending invisible waves that make the water molecules inside the food jiggle very fast. All that jiggling creates heat, cooking the food from the inside out. Dry foods with little water heat up slowly, while watery foods get hot quickly.

keywords: why nonstick pans do not stick
facts.answer: Nonstick pans are coated with a special slippery material that food can't grip onto. The coating's molecules are so slick that almost nothing sticks to them. This lets you cook eggs with little oil, though you need to avoid scratching the coating with metal tools.

keywords: why metal gets a static shock
facts.answer: You get a static shock when extra electric charge builds up on your body, often from rubbing your feet on carpet. When you touch metal, the charge suddenly jumps across as a tiny spark you feel as a zap. Dry air makes static shocks more common in winter.

Rubbing a balloon on your hair gives it an electric charge by moving tiny electrons. The charged balloon then attracts the opposite charge in a wall and sticks to it. The same static makes your hair stand up and follow the balloon.

Lightning is a giant spark of electricity. Inside storm clouds, ice and water crashing around build up huge electric charges. When the charge gets strong enough, it leaps as lightning, heating the air so fast it explodes with a boom we call thunder.

Thunder happens because a lightning bolt heats the air around it to thousands of degrees in an instant. The air expands so violently that it makes a loud bang, which we hear as thunder. Since light travels faster than sound, we see the flash before we hear the boom.

Tall metal objects can attract lightning because metal lets electric charge flow easily, giving lightning an easy path. Buildings use lightning rods, metal poles that safely carry a strike's electricity down into the ground. This protects the building from catching fire.

Every magnet has two ends called the north pole and the south pole. Opposite poles attract each other, while two of the same poles push apart. Even if you cut a magnet in half, each piece still has its own north and south pole.

Earth acts like a giant magnet because of swirling melted metal deep in its core. This creates a magnetic field that stretches into space and points roughly north and south. A compass needle lines up with this field, which is how it helps people find their way.

A compass works because its needle is a small magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field. One end always swings to point toward the north. People have used compasses for navigation for nearly a thousand years, long before satellites and maps on phones.

keywords: why iron filings show magnetic field
facts.answer: When you sprinkle tiny iron pieces near a magnet, they line up along invisible lines showing the magnet's field. Each little piece becomes a mini magnet and points the way the field goes. This makes the hidden magnetic field visible in a beautiful curved pattern.

An electromagnet is a magnet you can turn on and off using electricity. Wrapping wire around an iron core and running current through it makes it magnetic, and cutting the power makes the magnetism stop. Giant electromagnets are used in junkyards to lift and drop cars.

keywords: why some things are heavy for their size
facts.answer: Some materials feel heavy for their size because they're very dense, meaning lots of mass is packed into a small space. A small lump of lead or gold weighs much more than the same size piece of wood or plastic. Density depends on how heavy the atoms are and how tightly they're packed.

Osmium is the densest natural element, packing more mass into a given space than any other. A small block of osmium would feel surprisingly heavy in your hand. It's a hard, bluish metal sometimes used to make the tough tips of fountain pens.

Metals like gold, silver, and platinum are called precious because they're rare, beautiful, and resist rusting or tarnishing. Their rarity and lasting shine have made them valuable for money and jewelry for thousands of years. Platinum is even rarer than gold.

Platinum is a shiny, silvery metal that is even rarer than gold. It doesn't rust or tarnish and can speed up chemical reactions, so it's used in jewelry and in car parts that clean exhaust. All the platinum ever mined could fit in a small room.

Cars have a part called a catalytic converter that uses rare metals like platinum to turn harmful exhaust gases into safer ones. The metals act as catalysts, speeding up reactions that clean the fumes before they leave the tailpipe. This greatly reduces air pollution from cars.

Rust doesn't just look bad; it actually eats into iron and steel, making them weaker and flaky. Over time enough rust can make a structure crumble, which is why bridges and ships are carefully protected from it. Painting and coating keep air and water away from the metal.

keywords: why salt water rusts metal faster
facts.answer: Salt water makes metal rust faster than fresh water because the salt helps electricity flow, which speeds up the rusting reaction. That's why boats, piers, and seaside structures rust quickly. Engineers use special coatings and metals to fight this ocean corrosion.

keywords: why nails are coated with zinc
facts.answer: Galvanized metal is steel coated with a layer of zinc to stop it from rusting. The zinc reacts with the air instead of the steel, protecting it like a shield, and even keeps working if scratched. That's why galvanized nails and fences last longer outdoors.

keywords: why some metals react with acid
facts.answer: Many metals react with acids, fizzing as they release hydrogen gas and slowly dissolve. For example, dropping zinc into acid makes bubbles of hydrogen. Some metals like gold and platinum barely react, which is one reason they're considered noble metals.

keywords: why some metals explode in water
facts.answer: Certain soft metals like sodium and potassium react violently with water, fizzing, catching fire, and sometimes exploding. They react so fast that they release hydrogen gas and lots of heat. Because of this, these metals are stored in oil to keep them away from any water or air.

keywords: why helium is used in balloons not hydrogen
facts.answer: Both helium and hydrogen are lighter than air, but balloons use helium because it doesn't burn, while hydrogen catches fire easily. A famous airship called the Hindenburg, filled with hydrogen, caught fire in 1937. Helium is safer even though it's more expensive.

keywords: why deep voice with heavy gas
facts.answer: Breathing a heavy gas like sulfur hexafluoride makes your voice sound deep and low, the opposite of helium. Sound travels slower through heavy gas, which lowers the pitch. It's risky to breathe, though, because the heavy gas can settle in your lungs and push out oxygen.

keywords: why some elements are gases at room temperature
facts.answer: Some elements are gases at room temperature because their tiny molecules barely stick together and zip around freely. Oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen are all gases for this reason. Whether an element is a solid, liquid, or gas depends on how strongly its particles attract each other.

keywords: why some metals are liquid or low melting
facts.answer: A few metals melt at low temperatures because their atoms aren't held together very tightly. Gallium melts in your hand, and mercury is liquid at room temperature. Most metals, though, have strong bonds and need very high heat to melt.

keywords: why diamonds are made of carbon under pressure
facts.answer: Natural diamonds form deep underground where intense heat and crushing pressure squeeze carbon atoms into a super-tight crystal structure. This takes place over millions of years, far below the surface. Volcanic eruptions sometimes carry these diamonds up to where people can find them.

Scientists can now make real diamonds in laboratories by recreating the high heat and pressure found deep in the Earth, or by growing them from carbon gas. These lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical to natural ones. They're often cheaper and don't require mining.

Coal is a black rock made mostly of carbon, formed from ancient plants buried and squeezed underground for millions of years. Burning coal releases the energy those plants once captured from sunlight. Because burning it also pollutes the air, the world is moving toward cleaner energy.

keywords: why oil is called fossil fuel
facts.answer: Oil, coal, and natural gas are called fossil fuels because they formed from the remains of tiny ancient plants and animals buried for millions of years. The energy in them originally came from sunlight. Burning fossil fuels releases that stored energy but also adds carbon dioxide to the air.

keywords: why burning fossil fuels warms earth
facts.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in Earth's atmosphere like a blanket. As more builds up, the planet slowly warms. This is why scientists encourage cleaner energy sources like solar and wind power that don't release this gas.

Natural gas is mostly methane, a fuel that burns cleaner than coal or oil. It's used to heat homes and cook food on gas stoves. Methane has no smell, so a stinky chemical is added to it so people can notice leaks and stay safe.

Natural gas is naturally odorless, so a smelly chemical is added that makes it smell like rotten eggs. This is a safety trick so people can quickly notice a gas leak. If you ever smell that strong rotten-egg odor, it means gas might be escaping.

keywords: why hydrogen could be clean fuel
facts.answer: Hydrogen can be used as a clean fuel because when it burns or powers a fuel cell, it mainly produces water, not pollution. Scientists are working on cars and trucks that run on hydrogen. The challenge is making and storing hydrogen cheaply and safely.

Solar panels make electricity from sunlight using special materials, usually made of silicon. When sunlight hits the panel, it knocks tiny electrons loose, and that flow of electrons becomes electric current. No fuel is burned, so solar power doesn't pollute the air.

Old or dead batteries can leak because the chemicals inside slowly eat through the casing. The leaked goo is often a crusty white substance that can damage devices and irritate skin. That's why you should remove old batteries and never mix old and new ones.

Waterproof materials either have no gaps for water to slip through, or they're coated so water beads up and rolls off instead of soaking in. Raincoats and umbrellas use this trick. Some leaves in nature are naturally waterproof, which inspired human-made coatings.

Lotus leaves stay clean because their surface is covered in tiny bumps too small to see, which make water roll off in beads and carry dirt away. Scientists copied this 'lotus effect' to make self-cleaning paints and waterproof fabrics. Nature often inspires new materials.

Concrete is made by mixing cement, sand, gravel, and water, which then harden through a chemical reaction into a rock-hard material. Adding steel bars inside makes it even stronger for buildings and bridges. Concrete actually keeps getting harder for years after it's poured.

Cement hardens not by drying out but through a chemical reaction with water called curing. The water and cement powder react to form crystals that lock everything together into a solid. That's why concrete can even harden underwater.

Bricks are made by shaping clay and then baking it in a very hot oven called a kiln. The heat causes a chemical change that makes the clay hard, strong, and waterproof. This is why fired bricks last for centuries while raw clay would crumble in the rain.

Pottery starts as soft clay that's shaped and then fired in a hot kiln. The intense heat changes the clay's structure permanently, turning it into hard ceramic that won't dissolve in water. A glaze can be added to give pottery a smooth, glassy, colorful surface.

A glaze is a glassy coating put on pottery before its final firing. In the kiln's heat, the glaze melts into a smooth, glassy layer that makes the pot waterproof, shiny, and colorful. Different minerals in the glaze create different colors and finishes.

keywords: why some materials are see through
facts.answer: Materials are see-through, called transparent, when light passes straight through them, like clear glass. Translucent things like frosted glass scatter light so you see only blurry shapes. Opaque things like wood block light completely, so you can't see through them at all.

A mirror is usually glass with a thin shiny metal coating on the back. Light bounces off that smooth metal layer in an orderly way, sending an image straight back to your eyes. Because the surface is so flat and smooth, you see a clear reflection.

Smooth, polished metal reflects light because its free electrons bounce light right back instead of letting it pass through. The smoother the surface, the clearer the reflection. That's why a polished metal spoon can act a bit like a mirror, even bending your reflection.

A prism splits white light into a rainbow because different colors bend by different amounts as they pass through the glass. Red bends the least and violet the most, spreading the colors apart. This proves that white light is actually all the colors mixed together.

keywords: why white light contains all colors
facts.answer: White light, like sunlight, is actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow combined. When it passes through a prism or raindrops, the colors spread apart so we can see them separately. Isaac Newton first proved this with a prism over 350 years ago.

Smells happen when tiny molecules float off an object and into your nose, where special sensors recognize their shapes. Different molecules trigger different smell signals to your brain. That's why a flower and a stinky sock smell so different; they release different molecules.

Perfume smells fade as the scented molecules slowly evaporate into the air and drift away from your skin. Lighter molecules float off first, which is why a perfume can smell different after a few hours. Warmth speeds up the evaporation, so scents fade faster on hot days.

keywords: why food smells stronger when hot
facts.answer: Warm food smells stronger because heat makes its scent molecules evaporate and float into the air faster. More molecules reaching your nose means a stronger smell. That's why a hot pizza smells amazing, but a cold leftover slice smells much fainter.

Disinfectants kill germs by chemically damaging the germs' outer coverings or insides so they can't survive. Some break apart the germ's protective layer, while others scramble the chemicals germs need to live. This is why cleaning with disinfectant helps stop the spread of sickness.

Hand sanitizer works mainly because of the alcohol in it, which destroys the outer coating of many germs and kills them. It needs to be strong enough, usually at least 60 percent alcohol, to work well. Washing with soap and water is still best when hands are visibly dirty.

Soap bubbles are round because the soapy film pulls itself as tight as possible, and a sphere is the shape that holds the most air with the least surface. Even if you blow a wobbly bubble, it quickly snaps into a ball. Nature loves spheres for this reason.

Soap bubbles show rainbow swirls because light bounces off both the front and back of the thin soap film, and the two reflections mix. Depending on the film's thickness, different colors get brighter or cancel out. As the film thins and shifts, the colors keep changing.

keywords: why iron is in your blood
facts.answer: Your blood contains iron inside a substance called hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. The iron is what helps grab the oxygen. It's also part of why blood looks red and why eating iron-rich foods keeps you healthy.

Blood is red because of iron-containing hemoglobin in red blood cells, which turns bright red when it carries oxygen. Blood low on oxygen looks darker red, not blue, even though veins can look bluish through your skin. Some animals have blue or green blood from different chemicals.

keywords: why some animals have blue blood
facts.answer: Some animals, like horseshoe crabs and octopuses, have blue blood because they use copper instead of iron to carry oxygen. The copper-based substance turns blue when carrying oxygen, just like our iron-based one turns red. Their blood is blue for the same reason ours is red, just a different metal.

Your bones are strong partly because they're packed with the mineral calcium. Calcium combines with other elements to form a hard material that supports your body. Drinking milk and eating leafy greens gives your body calcium to keep your bones strong as you grow.

The outer layer of your teeth, called enamel, is the hardest substance your body makes, even harder than bone. It's made mostly of tightly packed mineral crystals. But unlike bone, enamel can't repair itself if it gets a cavity, which is why brushing matters.

Salt preserves food by pulling water out of it and out of any germs trying to grow on it. Without water, bacteria and mold can't survive and multiply. That's why salted meat and fish could be stored for long voyages before refrigerators existed.

Sugar helps preserve jams and jellies the same way salt preserves meat, by tying up water so germs can't grow. The high sugar amount makes it hard for mold and bacteria to survive. That's why a jar of jam lasts much longer than fresh fruit.

Cold temperatures in a refrigerator slow down the chemical reactions and the bacteria that make food spoil. The germs don't die, they just grow much more slowly when chilled. That's why milk and leftovers stay fresh longer in the fridge but spoil fast when left out.

Freezing food preserves it because at very cold temperatures the bacteria and chemical reactions that cause spoilage nearly stop. The germs aren't all killed, just paused, so food keeps for months. When you thaw it, the germs can wake up again, which is why thawed food should be eaten soon.

keywords: why metal spoons conduct heat in soup
facts.answer: Leave a metal spoon in hot soup and its handle soon feels hot too, because metal conducts heat very well. The heat travels quickly up the metal from the soup to the handle. A wooden or plastic spoon stays cool longer because those materials don't conduct heat well.

Wooden spoons stay cool to hold even while stirring hot food because wood is a poor conductor of heat. The heat barely travels up the handle, unlike with metal. That's why cooks often prefer wooden spoons for stirring hot pots.

keywords: why metal is used in cookware
facts.answer: Pots and pans are made of metal because metal conducts heat quickly and evenly, helping food cook fast. Copper and aluminum are especially good at spreading heat. Often the handles are made of plastic or wood so they stay cool enough to hold.

Aluminum foil is shiny, which lets it reflect heat and light. Wrapping food in foil can help keep it warm by bouncing escaping heat back. The foil also blocks air, which is why it's handy for covering leftovers and cooking food on a grill.

keywords: why salt makes water boil differently
facts.answer: Adding salt to water raises its boiling point slightly, so it gets a tiny bit hotter before bubbling. The change is small, so people mostly add salt to pasta water for flavor, not to cook faster. The salt also seasons the food as it cooks.

keywords: why eggs turn solid when cooked
facts.answer: A raw egg is runny, but heat changes its proteins so they unfold and link together, turning the egg solid and white. This change can't be undone; you can't un-cook an egg. The same protein change firms up meat and fish when they cook.

Popcorn pops because each kernel holds a tiny bit of water inside a hard shell. When heated, the water turns to steam and builds up pressure until the kernel bursts and turns inside out into a fluffy puff. Only special corn with the right shell pops well.

Bread goes stale as its starches slowly change shape and the bread loses softness, even more than from drying out. Surprisingly, bread goes stale faster in the fridge than at room temperature. Warming stale bread can briefly reverse some of the change and soften it again.

Many metals can be bent and hammered into new shapes without breaking because their atoms can slide past one another and still hold together. This property is called being malleable. It's why gold can be pounded into sheets thin enough to see light through.

Gold is so soft and bendable that it can be hammered into sheets called gold leaf, thinner than a human hair and almost see-through. A single gram of gold can be flattened to cover a whole square meter. This thin gold is used to decorate art and fancy buildings.

keywords: why wires can be pulled thin
facts.answer: Metals like copper can be pulled into long thin wires without snapping, a property called being ductile. The metal's atoms slide along and stretch out while staying connected. This is why electrical wires can be made so long and thin from a chunk of metal.

Glass can be recycled endlessly because melting it down and reshaping it doesn't lower its quality. The same glass could become a bottle, then a jar, then a window, over and over. Recycling glass also saves energy compared to making new glass from raw sand.

keywords: why some rocks fizz with acid
facts.answer: Some rocks, like limestone and chalk, fizz when acid is dripped on them because they contain a mineral that releases carbon dioxide gas when it meets acid. Geologists use this fizz test to identify rocks in the field. The same reaction happens slowly when acid rain wears down stone buildings.

Underground caves often form in limestone because slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the rock over thousands of years. Tiny cracks widen into tunnels and huge chambers. The dripping mineral-rich water then builds the pointy stalactites and stalagmites you see inside caves.

Stalactites hang from cave ceilings and stalagmites rise from the floor, both formed by dripping mineral-rich water. As each drop hangs or lands, it leaves behind a tiny bit of mineral that slowly stacks up over thousands of years. A way to remember: stalactites cling 'tight' to the ceiling.

Acid rain forms when pollution mixes with rainwater, making it slightly acidic. This acid slowly eats away at stone statues and buildings made of limestone or marble, blurring their carved details over decades. Reducing air pollution helps protect old monuments.

keywords: why marble is used in statues
facts.answer: Marble is a beautiful stone formed when limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground. It's smooth, fairly soft to carve, and can be polished to a lovely shine, which is why famous sculptors have used it for thousands of years. But acid rain can slowly wear it away.

Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth, made of silicon and oxygen. It's hard, comes in many colors, and is found in sand, granite, and many gemstones like amethyst. Quartz crystals can even vibrate steadily, which is how some watches keep accurate time.

Quartz watches keep time using a tiny quartz crystal that vibrates a precise number of times each second when electricity passes through it. The watch counts these steady vibrations to track seconds. This makes quartz watches very accurate and cheap to make.

Amethyst is a purple type of quartz that gets its color from tiny amounts of iron inside the crystal plus natural radiation over time. Heating amethyst can change its color to yellow, turning it into a gem called citrine. They're really the same mineral in different colors.

Opals shimmer with rainbow colors because they're made of tiny spheres stacked in a pattern that bends light into different colors as you tilt the stone. This flashing color is called play-of-color. Unlike most gems, opals also contain a surprising amount of water.

A pearl forms when something irritating, like a tiny grain, gets stuck inside an oyster or mussel. To protect itself, the animal coats the irritant with smooth layers of the same shiny material that lines its shell. Over years, those layers build up into a pearl.

Seashells are hard because sea animals build them from a mineral called calcium carbonate, the same stuff found in chalk and limestone. The animal pulls the minerals from seawater and lays them down in tough layers. The shell protects the soft creature living inside.

Chalk is a soft white rock made from the tiny crushed shells of ancient sea creatures, mostly calcium carbonate. It's soft enough that rubbing it on a board leaves a powdery trail of itself. The famous White Cliffs of Dover are made of this very chalk.

Sand comes in many colors depending on what rocks and minerals it formed from. Most beaches have tan sand from quartz, but some have black sand from volcanic rock, white sand from coral and shells, or even green and pink sand. The color is a clue to what's nearby.

Rock from volcanoes is often dark or black because it's rich in iron and magnesium and cooled quickly from lava. This common volcanic rock is called basalt. Some black beaches near volcanoes are made of basalt ground into sand by the waves.

Pumice is a rock that can float on water because it's full of tiny air bubbles, making it lighter than water. It forms when frothy lava cools quickly, trapping gas inside. People use rough pumice stones to scrub dry skin off their feet.

Obsidian is a natural glass made when lava cools so fast that crystals don't have time to form. It's shiny, dark, and can be chipped into edges sharper than a steel knife. Ancient people used obsidian to make cutting tools and arrowheads.

keywords: why some metals are colored not silver
facts.answer: Most metals look silvery-gray, but a few have their own colors: gold is yellow, copper is reddish, and freshly cut cesium is golden. These colors come from the special way those metals' electrons absorb and reflect light. They're rare exceptions among the silvery crowd.

Iron is one of the most useful metals because it's strong, common, and cheap, and it can be turned into steel. We use it in buildings, cars, tools, and machines. Iron is even at the center of our planet, forming most of Earth's hot metal core.

Earth's center, called the core, is made mostly of iron and nickel. The inner core is solid because of crushing pressure, while the outer core is molten and flowing. The swirling liquid metal there creates Earth's magnetic field that compasses point to.

keywords: why some metals are needed by your body
facts.answer: Your body actually needs tiny amounts of certain metals to work properly. Iron carries oxygen in your blood, calcium builds bones, and zinc helps you heal and taste food. You get these helpful metals in small, safe amounts from the food you eat.

keywords: why too much of an element can be harmful
facts.answer: Even helpful elements can be harmful in large amounts; the amount, or dose, is what matters. Your body needs a little iron, but too much is toxic. Even water can be dangerous if you drink way too much. Scientists say the dose makes the poison.

Plants need nitrogen to grow strong and green, but they can't use the nitrogen gas floating in the air directly. Instead they get it from the soil, often added by fertilizers. Certain bacteria and lightning can also turn air nitrogen into a form plants can use.

Bean and pea plants have a special trick: tiny bacteria living on their roots can grab nitrogen from the air and turn it into food the plants can use. When these plants die, they leave the soil richer in nitrogen. Farmers plant them to naturally feed the soil.

The element phosphorus got its name from Greek words meaning light-bearer because some forms of it glow in the dark when exposed to air. Phosphorus is also vital for life, found in your bones, teeth, and even your DNA. The first person to isolate it did so from urine long ago.

keywords: why glow in the dark stickers work
facts.answer: Glow-in-the-dark items contain materials that soak up light energy, then slowly release it as a soft glow in the dark. The longer you charge them under a bright light, the longer and brighter they glow. The glow fades as the stored energy runs out.

keywords: why some clothes glow under black light
facts.answer: Some materials glow brightly under a black light because they absorb the light's invisible ultraviolet rays and re-emit them as visible light. This is called fluorescence. White clothes often glow because laundry detergents add fluorescent chemicals to make whites look brighter.

Highlighter ink looks super bright because it's fluorescent, meaning it soaks up invisible ultraviolet light from sunlight and gives it back as extra visible color. This makes the marked words seem to glow on the page. The same trick makes safety vests so eye-catching.

Pure water barely conducts electricity, but adding salt changes that. The salt splits into charged particles that can carry an electric current through the water. This is one reason it's dangerous to use electrical devices near water, especially salty water.

Distilled water is made by boiling water into steam and then cooling the steam back into liquid, leaving minerals and impurities behind. The result is very pure water with nothing dissolved in it. It's used in science experiments, irons, and car batteries where minerals could cause problems.

Hard water contains dissolved minerals like calcium and magnesium. When it dries or is heated, it leaves behind white mineral spots and crusty buildup called limescale on faucets and kettles. This is why some areas have water that makes soap lather less easily.

keywords: why soap works less in hard water
facts.answer: Soap doesn't lather well in hard water because the dissolved minerals react with the soap and form a sticky scum instead of bubbles. That's the gray ring you sometimes see in a bathtub. Soft water, with fewer minerals, makes soap foam up much more easily.

keywords: why ice melts faster in salt water
facts.answer: Salt makes ice melt faster because it lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so the ice can't stay frozen as easily. This is the same reason salt is spread on icy roads and used to make ice cream. The salty water around the ice keeps eating into it.

keywords: why a penny can turn green
facts.answer: Old copper coins can turn greenish over time as the copper reacts with air, moisture, and other chemicals to form a green coating. It's the same reaction that turns the copper Statue of Liberty green. A quick dip in vinegar and salt can clean a dull copper penny shiny again.

Vinegar with a little salt cleans dull copper pennies because the acid dissolves the dark layer of copper oxide on the surface. Underneath, the shiny copper is revealed again. It's a fun, safe science experiment you can do at home with a few coins.

keywords: why some metals are used in fireworks colors
facts.answer: Fireworks makers add specific metal compounds to create different colors when they burn. Strontium gives red, copper gives blue, barium gives green, sodium gives yellow, and titanium adds bright white sparks. Mixing these is like painting with chemistry in the sky.

Sparklers burn slowly along a coated wire, throwing off tiny bright sparks. Those sparks are little bits of metal, often iron or aluminum, that heat up and glow as they burn in the air. The fuel keeps the wire burning steadily so the sparks keep flying.

Metals can ring with clear musical tones because they're stiff and bounce vibrations back and forth for a long time. Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, is especially good for bells and cymbals. The size and shape of the metal decide the pitch of the sound.

keywords: why bells are made of bronze
facts.answer: Bells are often made from a special bronze called bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. This mix rings clearly and loudly for a long time without cracking easily. The exact recipe and shape are carefully chosen to give each bell its musical tone.

Cymbals are made from metal alloys, usually based on copper, because metal vibrates and rings loudly when struck. Drummers crash them together or hit them with sticks to make bright, splashy sounds. The metal's stiffness lets the sound ring out and slowly fade.

keywords: why ice is clear or cloudy
facts.answer: Ice cubes often look cloudy in the middle because tiny air bubbles and minerals in the water get trapped as it freezes. Water freezes from the outside in, pushing impurities toward the center. Slowly frozen, filtered water makes the clear ice you see at fancy restaurants.

keywords: why hot water can freeze faster sometimes
facts.answer: Surprisingly, hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water under the right conditions, a puzzle called the Mpemba effect. Scientists still debate exactly why, but evaporation and dissolved gases may play a role. It doesn't always happen, but it's a famous chilly mystery.

Point Nemo is the spot in the Pacific Ocean that is farthest from any land, about 1,670 miles from the nearest coast. The closest humans are often astronauts on the Space Station passing overhead, because they are nearer than anyone on land. Because it is so remote, space agencies steer old satellites and spacecraft to crash there.

Lake Titicaca sits high in the Andes between Peru and Bolivia at about 12,500 feet above sea level, making it the highest large lake big boats can sail on. People there have lived on floating islands made of reeds for centuries. The reed islands can be moved if the people want to relocate.

The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest dry land on Earth, sitting about 1,400 feet below sea level. The water is so salty that people float on top of it without trying to swim. Almost nothing can live in it, which is why it is called the Dead Sea.

Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, and it is slowly getting taller. India is pushing into Asia, crumpling the land and lifting the Himalayas a few millimeters every year. So the mountain you climb today is a tiny bit shorter than the one your grandchildren might climb.

If you measure from its base on the ocean floor to its top, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the tallest mountain on Earth, over 33,000 feet. Most of it is hidden underwater, so we only see the part poking above the sea. Everest is taller above sea level, but Mauna Kea wins from bottom to top.

Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador is the spot on Earth that is closest to outer space. Earth bulges out at the equator, so even though Everest is taller, Chimborazo's peak sticks out farthest from the planet's center. Standing on its top puts you nearer to the stars than any other place.

The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth and is roughly the size of the entire United States. It stretches across North Africa through more than ten countries. Long ago it was green with lakes and rivers, and you can still find ancient cave paintings of animals that lived there.

The biggest desert on Earth is not the Sahara but Antarctica. A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not by heat, and Antarctica gets almost no precipitation. So this frozen continent is the largest and driest desert of all.

Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall in the world, dropping about 3,212 feet from a flat-topped mountain. The water falls so far that much of it turns to mist before reaching the bottom. It was named after a pilot named Jimmie Angel who flew over it in the 1930s.

The Nile in Africa is usually called the longest river in the world at about 4,130 miles, though some scientists argue the Amazon may be longer. The Nile flows north, which surprises many people who expect rivers to flow south. Ancient Egypt grew up along its banks because it flooded each year and made the soil rich for farming.

The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth, more than the next several biggest rivers combined. During the rainy season parts of it can swell to over 20 miles wide. It pours so much fresh water into the ocean that you can still find drinkable water more than 100 miles out to sea.

Russia is the largest country on Earth and spans 11 time zones. When people are waking up for breakfast on one side, others are getting ready for bed on the other side of the same country. It is so big that it borders both Europe and Asia and touches more countries than almost any other nation.

On many flat maps Greenland looks as big as Africa, but Africa is actually about 14 times larger. Flat maps stretch out the areas near the poles to fit a round Earth onto a flat page. This is why countries near the top and bottom of maps look much bigger than they really are.

The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean has the deepest known spot on Earth, called the Challenger Deep, almost 36,000 feet down. If you dropped Mount Everest into it, the peak would still be more than a mile underwater. Only a few people have ever traveled to the very bottom.

The Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic Ocean is the only sea on Earth with no land coastline. Instead, it is bordered by ocean currents that circle around it. It is named after the floating sargassum seaweed that drifts there and gives baby sea turtles a place to hide.

Istanbul, Turkey, is the only major city that sits on two continents at once, split between Europe and Asia by a narrow waterway called the Bosphorus. People can cross from one continent to the other on a ferry in just a few minutes. Bridges and a tunnel now connect the two sides.

Lesotho is a small country in southern Africa that is completely surrounded by just one other country, South Africa. You cannot reach Lesotho without traveling through South Africa first. It is also one of the few countries where all the land sits above 3,200 feet, earning it the nickname the Kingdom in the Sky.

San Marino, a tiny country surrounded by Italy, claims to be the oldest republic in the world, founded in the year 301. It sits on top of a mountain and has its own laws and government even though it is smaller than many cities. Legend says a stonemason named Marinus started it to escape persecution.

Nauru is the world's smallest island country, only about 8 square miles, and you can drive all the way around it in less than half an hour. It has no official capital city. The island was once rich from mining phosphate, a mineral made from ancient bird droppings.

Tuvalu in the Pacific Ocean is one of the lowest countries in the world, with its highest point only about 15 feet above the sea. Rising oceans threaten to cover it someday. Its government has even made a digital copy of the whole country online so its culture can survive if the land disappears.

The Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the world's largest salt flat, covering more than 4,000 square miles. After it rains, a thin layer of water turns it into a giant mirror that reflects the sky so perfectly you cannot tell up from down. It holds a huge share of the world's lithium, the metal used in batteries.

The Aral Sea in Central Asia was once one of the largest lakes on Earth, but rivers feeding it were diverted for farming and it nearly dried up. Old fishing boats now sit rusting in the middle of a desert where water used to be. It is one of the saddest examples of how people can change the land.

Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world at over a mile deep, and also the oldest at about 25 million years. It holds around one-fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet. It is home to a freshwater seal found nowhere else on Earth.

In the United States, the Four Corners is the only place where four states touch at a single point: Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah. Visitors love to stand on the spot so they can be in four states at the same time. You can put a hand or foot in each state at once.

La Paz in Bolivia is the highest capital city in the world, sitting around 11,900 feet up in the Andes mountains. The air is so thin there that visitors often feel out of breath just walking around. Sports teams visiting from lower places sometimes struggle to play because there is less oxygen.

Oymyakon in Siberia, Russia, is one of the coldest places where people live year-round, with temperatures that have dropped to about minus 90 degrees Fahrenheit. Cars are sometimes left running all day so the engines do not freeze. Schools stay open until it gets shockingly cold.

Death Valley in California holds the record for the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth, about 134 degrees Fahrenheit in 1913. The valley is below sea level and surrounded by mountains that trap the heat. Despite the name, plants and animals still find ways to survive there.

Mawsynram in northeast India is the wettest place on Earth, receiving around 467 inches of rain a year. People there make raincoats and shelters out of bamboo and grass to stay dry. The rain comes from moist air sweeping in off the Bay of Bengal and dumping its water on the hills.

The Atacama Desert in Chile is the driest non-polar place on Earth, and some weather stations there have never recorded a single drop of rain. Parts of it are so dry and Mars-like that scientists test space rovers there. Yet rare flowers sometimes bloom after a surprise sprinkle.

Singapore has grown about 25 percent bigger since the 1960s by adding new land along its coast, a process called land reclamation. Workers pile sand and rock into the sea to create more space for the crowded city. The country has imported so much sand that some neighbors stopped selling it.

About a quarter of the Netherlands sits below sea level, kept dry by walls called dikes and pumps that push water away. Much of this land was once underwater and was reclaimed by the Dutch over centuries. The famous windmills were originally built to pump water off the land.

Many people think rivers always flow south, but rivers flow downhill no matter which direction that is. The Nile in Africa flows north for thousands of miles, and so does part of the St. Johns River in Florida. Water simply follows gravity toward lower ground.

Africa is the only continent that lies in all four hemispheres at once: north, south, east, and west. Both the equator and the prime meridian pass through it. This makes it possible to stand in places where these famous imaginary lines cross African soil.

China is so wide it should span five time zones, but the whole country uses a single time zone set to Beijing's clock. This means in the far west the sun can rise around 10 in the morning by the official clock. Many people there quietly follow an unofficial local time instead.

keywords: country first to see new year
facts.answer: Kiribati is a Pacific nation spread across so many islands that it touches three time zones, and it moved the international date line to keep its country on the same calendar day. Because of this, one of its islands is among the first places on Earth to greet each new day and new year. Its sunrise happens before almost anyone else's.

The International Date Line is an imaginary line in the Pacific Ocean where the date changes by one day. Cross it heading west and you skip ahead a day; cross it going east and you live the same day twice. It zigzags around islands so neighboring places can share the same date.

Mount Thor on Baffin Island in Canada has the tallest purely vertical cliff on Earth, a sheer drop of about 4,100 feet. The rock actually leans inward, overhanging like a frozen wave. Climbers travel from around the world to test themselves against it.

Spotted Lake in British Columbia, Canada, is full of so many minerals that in summer it dries into dozens of separate colorful pools that look like polka dots. The colors change depending on which minerals are most concentrated. Local Indigenous people have long considered the lake sacred and healing.

The Danakil Depression in Ethiopia is one of the hottest and strangest places on Earth, with bright yellow sulfur springs, salt flats, and even a bubbling lava lake. It sits below sea level where three pieces of Earth's crust are slowly pulling apart. Despite the harsh heat, people there still mine salt by hand.

Socotra, an island off Yemen, has plants found nowhere else, including the dragon's blood tree shaped like an upside-down umbrella that oozes red sap. Because the island has been cut off from the mainland for millions of years, life there evolved on its own. People sometimes call it the most alien-looking place on Earth.

Lake Hillier in Australia is bright bubblegum pink, and it stays pink even when you scoop the water into a glass. Scientists think tiny algae and salt-loving microbes give it the color. It sits right next to the blue ocean, separated only by a thin strip of land, so from above the two colors sit side by side.

In Turkmenistan there is a giant pit called the Darvaza gas crater, or Door to Hell, that has been on fire for decades. Geologists are believed to have lit the leaking natural gas to burn it off, expecting it to stop in a few days, but it never went out. At night the glowing crater attracts curious visitors from far away.

Over Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, lightning flashes almost every night for much of the year in a phenomenon called Catatumbo lightning. Some storms produce hundreds of flashes an hour, making it the lightning capital of the world. Sailors once used the glow to navigate at night.

In Namibia's desert, mysterious bare patches called fairy circles dot the grass in neat polka-dot patterns stretching for miles. Scientists have argued for years about what makes them, blaming termites, thirsty competing plants, or both. Local legends say they are the footprints of gods.

The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is a stretch of about 40,000 stone columns, most of them shaped like neat six-sided hexagons. They formed when hot lava cooled and cracked into regular shapes long ago. Legend says a giant built it as a path across the sea to fight another giant.

Pamukkale in Turkey looks like a frozen white waterfall, with terraces of bright white stone and warm pools of water. The name means cotton castle. The terraces formed over thousands of years as mineral-rich hot springs left behind layers of white calcium.

The Zhangye Danxia mountains in China look like they were painted with rainbow stripes of red, orange, and yellow. The colors come from layers of different minerals laid down over millions of years and then tilted and worn down. Sunset light makes the colors glow even brighter.

Lake Natron in Tanzania is so full of harsh minerals that its water can be as caustic as ammonia, and it sometimes turns blood red from algae. Yet millions of flamingos nest there because few predators can survive the conditions. Animals that die in the lake can become coated in hard minerals.

Dallol in Ethiopia has some of the most colorful and bizarre hot springs on Earth, with neon green and yellow pools bubbling up from underground. The water is acidic and extremely salty, yet scientists have still found tiny life forms surviving there. It is one of the closest things to an alien world on our planet.

In the Sahara Desert of Mauritania there is a giant bullseye pattern in the rock about 25 miles wide called the Eye of the Sahara. It is so big that astronauts use it as a landmark from space. Scientists think it formed when a dome of rock slowly eroded into rings, not from a meteor as once believed.

In the Nazca Desert of Peru, ancient people scraped huge drawings into the ground, including a hummingbird, a monkey, and a spider, some longer than a football field. They are so large that the full shapes can only be seen clearly from the sky. People still debate exactly why they made them about 2,000 years ago.

Uluru, also called Ayers Rock, is a giant sandstone formation rising from the flat Australian desert. Most of the rock is actually hidden underground, like an iceberg, with only the top showing. It glows fiery red at sunrise and sunset and is a sacred site to the Aboriginal Anangu people.

Wave Rock in Western Australia is a granite cliff shaped exactly like a giant ocean wave about to crash, standing nearly 50 feet tall. Rainwater running down the rock over millions of years carved the curved shape and left colorful mineral streaks. People love taking photos that make it look like they are surfing it.

Antelope Canyon in Arizona is a narrow slot canyon with swirling orange walls carved by rushing flood water over time. At certain times of day, sunbeams shine straight down through the narrow opening like spotlights. The Navajo people consider the canyon a spiritual place.

Plitvice Lakes in Croatia is a chain of 16 turquoise lakes that flow into one another over natural stone dams in a stair-step pattern. The bright blue-green color comes from minerals and sunlight in the clear water. The dams are made by mosses and bacteria that slowly turn into rock.

keywords: why you float in dead sea
facts.answer: The Dead Sea between Jordan and Israel is one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth, almost ten times saltier than the ocean. All that salt makes the water dense, so people bob on top like corks without sinking. The mud along its shores is sold as a beauty treatment.

The Bermuda Triangle is an area of the Atlantic Ocean between Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico where some ships and planes have gone missing over the years. People have invented spooky stories about it, but scientists say bad weather and human mistakes explain most cases. It is not actually marked on official maps.

Even the scorching Sahara Desert has had snow a few times in recent years, surprising people in towns like Ain Sefra in Algeria. Cold air and just enough moisture combined to dust the orange sand dunes with white. The snow usually melts within hours once the sun comes up.

Wind carries millions of tons of dust from the Sahara Desert across the Atlantic Ocean to the Amazon rainforest every year. This dust is full of a mineral called phosphorus that helps the rainforest plants grow. So one of the driest places on Earth helps feed one of the wettest.

The Caspian Sea touches five countries: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, and Azerbaijan. It is landlocked, meaning it has no connection to the open ocean. The countries spent years arguing about how to share its fish and the valuable oil and gas beneath it.

Lake Retba in Senegal, also called Lac Rose, can turn a strawberry-milk pink color thanks to salt-loving microbes. Workers wade into the water to collect salt by hand, coating their skin in shea butter to protect it from the strong brine. It is so salty that people float easily, just like in the Dead Sea.

Long ago the River Thames in London froze solid enough in some winters that people held festivals on the ice called frost fairs. They set up market stalls, lit fires, and even paraded an elephant across the river. The river no longer freezes like that because the climate warmed and the river was made to flow faster.

The Puerto Princesa Underground River in the Philippines flows for miles through a dark limestone cave before reaching the sea. Visitors ride boats deep into the cave past giant rock formations and colonies of bats. It is one of the longest navigable underground rivers in the world.

In Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula there are thousands of natural water-filled sinkholes called cenotes. They formed when underground caves collapsed, revealing crystal-clear pools below. The ancient Maya believed cenotes were gateways to the underworld and used some for ceremonies.

The Great Blue Hole off the coast of Belize is a huge round sinkhole in the ocean, more than 400 feet deep and so big it can be seen from above as a dark blue circle. It formed when a cave roof collapsed long ago when sea levels were lower. Divers explore its underwater rock formations.

The Lofoten Islands in Norway sit above the Arctic Circle, yet they stay surprisingly mild thanks to a warm ocean current called the Gulf Stream. This makes them much warmer than other places at the same far-north latitude. Fishermen there dry cod on wooden racks in the cool sea air.

In places near the North and South Poles, the sun stays up all day and night during summer, a phenomenon called the midnight sun. In parts of Norway you can play soccer at midnight in full daylight. In winter the opposite happens and the sun never rises at all.

During winter in the far north and far south, the sun never climbs above the horizon for weeks, a period called the polar night. The town of Utqiagvik in Alaska can go more than two months without a true sunrise. People use bright lamps and community gatherings to stay cheerful through the long darkness.

A hill in New Zealand has one of the longest place names in the world, with 85 letters, often shortened to Taumata. The full Maori name tells a story about a chief who played a flute to his loved one. Locals are proud of it and tourists try to read the whole thing on a sign.

Some towns have names with just a single letter, like the village of A in Norway and another A in Sweden. Their tiny names make great photo spots for visitors. There is also a town in France once written as simply Y.

Algeria is the largest country in Africa, with most of its land covered by the Sahara Desert. It became the biggest after South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011. Even though it is huge, most of its people live near the cooler northern coast.

Greenland is the largest island in the world that is not a continent, covering about 836,000 square miles. Most of it is buried under a thick sheet of ice. Despite its name, it is mostly white with snow, while Iceland is actually quite green.

Australia is unusual because it is both a country and the smallest continent, and it is sometimes called the world's largest island. It is so big that it is the only continent governed by a single nation. The middle of the country, called the outback, is dry desert with very few people.

Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands scattered across the sea, though people live on only a fraction of them. Some islands are so remote that they were not even named or mapped until recently. The country stretches so far that flying from one end to the other takes hours.

Sweden actually has more islands than any other country, with around 270,000, though the vast majority are tiny and uninhabited. Many are just bare rocks poking out of the cold sea. The capital, Stockholm, is built across 14 islands connected by bridges.

The Sutter Buttes in California are sometimes called the world's smallest mountain range, rising suddenly from a flat valley and stretching only about 10 miles across. They are the remains of an old volcano. From a distance they look like a lonely island of peaks in a sea of farmland.

The Andes in South America form the longest mountain range on land, running about 4,300 miles down the western edge of the continent through seven countries. The longest mountain range of all is actually underwater, snaking around the globe on the ocean floor. The Andes hold many of the world's highest volcanoes.

keywords: mid ocean ridge longest mountain range
facts.answer: The longest mountain range on Earth is hidden under the ocean, called the mid-ocean ridge, stretching about 40,000 miles around the globe. It forms where Earth's crust pulls apart and new seafloor is created. Most people never see it because it lies deep beneath the waves.

The Congo River in Africa is the deepest river in the world, plunging to depths of over 720 feet in places. It is so deep and dark down there that fish living in those waters have evolved to survive in conditions found nowhere else. It is also the only major river to cross the equator twice.

The Yangtze in China is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world, flowing about 3,900 miles to the sea. It is home to the giant Three Gorges Dam, one of the largest dams ever built. Endangered animals like the finless porpoise still swim in its waters.

The Volga in Russia is the longest river in Europe, winding about 2,300 miles before emptying into the Caspian Sea. So many Russians feel connected to it that they call it Mother Volga. Much of the country's freight and farming has depended on it for centuries.

Lake Superior, one of North America's Great Lakes, is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area. It holds enough water to cover all of North and South America in about a foot of water. Its name comes from being the highest and largest of the Great Lakes.

keywords: which sea has no land coastline
facts.answer: The Sargasso Sea is special because it is bounded not by land but by four giant ocean currents that swirl in a loop. Inside this loop the water is calm, clear, and a deep blue. Eels travel thousands of miles to lay their eggs there before they die.

The Maldives is the flattest country in the world, with its highest natural point only about 8 feet above the sea. Its hundreds of islands are spread across the Indian Ocean like sprinkles. Because the land is so low, the country is very worried about rising oceans.

Bhutan in the Himalayas is one of the highest countries on Earth, with much of its land in steep mountains. It measures its success not just in money but in something called Gross National Happiness. Television was not even allowed in the whole country until 1999.

Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania sits near the warm equator, yet its peak is so high and cold that it has glaciers and snow on top. Climbers pass through several climate zones, from hot grasslands at the bottom to icy air at the summit. Sadly, the famous snow is slowly melting away.

keywords: equator passes through how many countries
facts.answer: The equator, the imaginary line around the middle of Earth, passes through 13 countries, including Ecuador, Kenya, and Indonesia. Places on the equator have roughly 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night all year. The country Ecuador is even named after the Spanish word for equator.

The prime meridian is the imaginary line at zero longitude that the world agreed to measure east and west from, and it runs through Greenwich, England. Visitors can stand with one foot in the eastern hemisphere and one in the west. World time zones are counted starting from this line.

Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth, where the lowest natural temperature ever recorded reached about minus 128 degrees Fahrenheit. It is also the windiest and one of the driest continents. Almost no people live there permanently, just visiting scientists and lots of penguins.

The Cape of Good Hope near the bottom of Africa is a famous point where sailors used to round the continent on long voyages. Many believe it is where the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet, though the true meeting point is a bit farther east at Cape Agulhas. Sailors once feared its rough, stormy waters.

Norway is famous for its fjords, deep narrow inlets where the sea reaches far inland between tall cliffs. They were carved by massive glaciers grinding through the land during the ice ages. The Sognefjord is over 100 miles long and more than 4,000 feet deep.

Iceland is called the land of fire and ice because it has both active volcanoes and huge glaciers, sometimes right next to each other. Heat from underground volcanoes warms water that heats homes and fills outdoor pools. The country sits where two of Earth's plates are pulling apart.

At Thingvellir in Iceland you can walk in a valley between two of Earth's tectonic plates, one belonging to North America and one to Europe. The plates pull apart a little each year, slowly widening the gap. Divers can even swim in a crack filled with crystal-clear water between the two continents.

Cerro Blanco in Peru is one of the tallest sand dunes in the world, rising over 3,800 feet from its base. People climb it for the thrill of sandboarding back down the slopes. It would take hours to walk to the top, so most riders ride part way up in special vehicles.

Some sand dunes around the world hum, boom, or sing when sand slides down their slopes. The sound can be loud enough to be heard miles away and last for minutes. Scientists think the rounded, dry grains rubbing together create the strange musical noise.

White Sands in New Mexico is a desert of brilliant white dunes made of gypsum, the same mineral used in chalk. The sand stays cool to the touch even on hot days because it reflects so much sunlight. Some animals there have turned pale white to blend in with the bright dunes.

Lake Taupo in New Zealand fills the crater of an ancient supervolcano that erupted thousands of years ago. The blast was so powerful that ash from it reddened skies on the other side of the world. Today the calm blue lake is a peaceful spot for fishing and boating.

Yellowstone National Park sits on top of a giant supervolcano, which powers its bubbling hot springs and erupting geysers. The most famous geyser, Old Faithful, shoots boiling water high into the air about every 90 minutes. Underneath the park, a huge pool of magma keeps everything warm.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is about a mile deep and up to 18 miles wide, carved over millions of years by the Colorado River. The colorful rock layers in its walls record nearly two billion years of Earth's history. Standing at the rim, the bottom looks tiny and far away.

The deepest part of the ocean, the Mariana Trench, is so deep that you could drop Mount Everest into it and the mountain's peak would still be more than a mile underwater. The pressure down there is crushing, more than a thousand times the pressure at the surface. Only special submarines can reach the bottom.

The Tree of Tenere in Niger was once the most isolated tree on Earth, the only one for about 250 miles in the Sahara. Travelers used it as a landmark for crossing the desert. Sadly a truck driver crashed into it in 1973, and a metal sculpture now stands in its place.

The Chocolate Hills on Bohol Island in the Philippines are more than a thousand grassy mounds that turn brown in the dry season, like rows of chocolate drops. They formed from old coral reefs and limestone shaped by weather over time. From a viewpoint they look almost too neat to be natural.

The Stone Forest in Yunnan, China, is a maze of tall gray limestone pillars that look like petrified trees. They formed over millions of years as rainwater slowly dissolved the soft rock. Visitors wander narrow paths between stone columns that tower overhead.

In Madagascar there is a landscape called the Tsingy, made of razor-sharp limestone spikes so dangerous that walking across them barefoot is impossible. The name means where one cannot walk barefoot. Rain carved the soft rock into a forest of stone knives, with caves and animals hidden inside.

In Cappadocia, Turkey, soft rock has been shaped by wind and rain into tall cone-shaped towers called fairy chimneys. People long ago carved homes, churches, and even entire underground cities right into the rock. Today hot air balloons drift over the magical landscape at sunrise.

Mount Roraima is a flat-topped mountain at the meeting point of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana, with sheer cliffs rising thousands of feet on every side. Its top is often wrapped in clouds and is home to plants found nowhere else. These tabletop mountains, called tepuis, are among the oldest rock formations on Earth.

The Sahel is a wide band of dry grassland that stretches across Africa just south of the Sahara Desert, acting like a doorway between desert and greener lands. Countries there are planting a Great Green Wall of trees to stop the desert from spreading. Many animals migrate across it following the seasonal rains.

Thousands of years ago the Sahara was not a desert but a green land full of lakes, rivers, and animals like hippos and crocodiles. Ancient cave paintings show people swimming and hunting where only sand sits today. The land dried out as Earth's tilt slowly changed how much rain fell there.

Gaet'ale Pond in Ethiopia is the saltiest body of water in the world, even saltier than the Dead Sea. Its water is so dense that almost nothing can live in it, and dangerous gases sometimes bubble up nearby. The harsh, colorful landscape around it looks like another planet.

The largest waterfall on Earth is hidden underwater in the Denmark Strait between Greenland and Iceland. Cold, dense water sinks and flows downward in a huge underwater cascade nearly two miles tall. It moves far more water than any waterfall you can see on land.

Fly Geyser in Nevada is a colorful, bumpy geyser that humans created by accident when drilling a well let hot water escape. Over the years minerals and algae built up into red and green mounds that keep growing. It looks like something from another world rising out of the desert.

Devils Tower in Wyoming is a flat-topped column of rock rising about 1,267 feet, with deep grooves running up its sides. It formed when underground magma cooled and the softer rock around it wore away. It became the very first national monument in the United States in 1906.

Some of the highest roads in the world climb through the Andes and Himalayas to over 18,000 feet, far higher than many airplanes fly at takeoff. Drivers can feel dizzy from the thin air. These roads connect remote mountain villages that would otherwise be cut off from the world.

The Panama Canal lets ships cut through Central America instead of sailing all the way around South America. Surprisingly, because of the shape of the land, a ship heading from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travels from west to east. The canal uses giant water-filled locks to lift ships over a hill.

The Suez Canal in Egypt connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, saving ships from sailing all the way around Africa. Thousands of ships pass through each year carrying goods between Europe and Asia. In 2021 a single stuck cargo ship blocked the whole canal for almost a week.

The Strait of Gibraltar is a narrow stretch of water separating Europe from Africa, only about 8 miles wide at its tightest point. On a clear day you can see one continent from the other. Long ago the strait dried up and refilled, and the Mediterranean Sea behind it has refilled in a dramatic flood.

The border between Spain and Portugal is one of the oldest unchanged borders in the world, set in place around the year 1297. It stretches about 750 miles and has stayed nearly the same for over 700 years. There is even a quiet zigzag border town with houses in both countries.

The town of Baarle on the border of Belgium and the Netherlands is split into a confusing patchwork, with the border zigzagging right through streets and even houses. Some homes have the line painted on the floor, so you can stand in two countries while sitting at your kitchen table. Which country your front door is in even decides your address.

For a long time the border between India and Bangladesh near Cooch Behar was the most tangled in the world, with pockets of one country inside the other, and even a piece of India inside Bangladesh inside India. People living there sometimes could not easily reach their own country. The two nations finally swapped the confusing pockets in 2015.

Mount Augustus in Western Australia is often called the largest single rock in the world, even bigger than Uluru. It rises about 2,300 feet above the surrounding plain and stretches for miles. Because it is so remote, far fewer visitors see it than its famous cousin Uluru.

Some rivers flow along the surface and then suddenly vanish underground into caves and cracks in soft rock, sometimes reappearing miles away. These are common in limestone areas where water dissolves the rock. The Danube River even loses some of its water to an underground path that pops out in a different river system.

keywords: two oceans meet gulf of alaska
facts.answer: In places like the Gulf of Alaska, water from different sources can meet and create a visible line where the colors do not mix right away. The difference comes from things like how much mud, salt, or melted glacier water each carries. Eventually the waters do blend together, despite the dramatic line.

Lake Assal in Djibouti is the lowest point in Africa, sitting about 509 feet below sea level. Its shores glitter with white salt, and the water is among the saltiest on Earth. People have harvested salt there to trade across the region for centuries.

Badwater Basin in Death Valley is the lowest point in North America, about 282 feet below sea level. It is a flat field of cracked white salt left behind when ancient lakes dried up. A sign high up on a nearby cliff marks where sea level actually is, far above your head.

The land around the northern Caspian Sea, called the Caspian Depression, is the lowest point in Europe at about 92 feet below sea level. This flat, dry region stretches across parts of Russia and Kazakhstan. The Volga River drains into the sea here after its long journey.

In some rivers, an incoming tide is so strong it pushes a wave upstream against the current, called a tidal bore. The Qiantang River in China has one of the most powerful bores, drawing crowds who watch the wall of water rush in. Surfers sometimes ride these waves for miles.

Saltstraumen in Norway has one of the strongest natural whirlpools in the world, formed when huge amounts of seawater squeeze through a narrow channel with the changing tides. The swirling water can spin in vortexes several feet wide. Fish gather there, making it a favorite fishing spot despite the danger.

Sometimes dust from the Sahara Desert is blown high into the sky and carried far away, then falls mixed with rain, leaving cars and snow tinted orange or red in places like Europe. People long ago called it blood rain and thought it was a bad sign. It is really just desert sand hitching a ride on the wind.

Lake Nyos in Cameroon is a dangerous lake that can release a huge cloud of carbon dioxide gas from deep underwater. In 1986 such a release tragically harmed people and animals nearby. Engineers now use pipes to slowly let the gas out safely before it builds up.

Dominica in the Caribbean has a Boiling Lake where the water actually bubbles and steams because it is heated by molten rock below. The water can reach temperatures hot enough to cook in. Hikers must trek for hours through rainforest to reach the edge of the misty, churning lake.

Five Flower Lake in Jiuzhaigou, China, is famous for water so clear and colorful you can see fallen tree trunks resting on the bottom. Minerals and water plants give it shifting shades of turquoise, green, and gold. The valley is fed by mountain snowmelt that keeps the water crystal clear.

On some beaches, the waves glow blue at night because of tiny living things in the water that light up when disturbed. In the Maldives, this can make the shoreline look like it is full of stars. The same magic glow can appear when boats stir up the sea.

The Red Beach in Panjin, China, turns a brilliant red each autumn, not from sand but from a special seaweed that changes color. From above it looks like a giant scarlet carpet stretching toward the sea. Rare birds nest in the marshes there.

Papakolea Beach in Hawaii is one of the few green sand beaches in the world, colored by a green mineral called olivine left behind by a volcano. The greenish crystals are heavier than regular sand, so waves wash the lighter sand away and leave the green behind. Reaching it requires a long hike along the coast.

Iceland has dramatic black sand beaches like Reynisfjara, where the sand is dark because it came from cooled volcanic lava. Tall black rock columns and powerful waves make the scenery look otherworldly. Visitors are warned to keep back because sudden sneaker waves can be dangerous.

A few beaches around the world have pink sand, including one near Komodo in Indonesia. The pink color comes from tiny bits of crushed red coral mixing with the white sand. Each wave washes a soft rosy tint across the shore.

Glass Beach in California is covered with smooth, colorful pebbles of sea glass instead of plain sand. It formed because people once dumped trash there, and decades of waves tumbled the broken glass into rounded gems. Now visitors are asked to look but not take any home so it can last.

keywords: which country has no rivers saudi arabia
facts.answer: Saudi Arabia is one of several countries with no permanent rivers at all, because the land is mostly hot desert. To get fresh water, the country turns salty seawater into drinking water using huge factories. Ancient dry riverbeds called wadis only fill with water after rare heavy rains.

Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined, with over two million of them. They formed when giant glaciers scraped out hollows in the land during the ice ages and then melted. Some are so small they do not even have names.

Finland is nicknamed the land of a thousand lakes, but it actually has around 188,000 of them. Many Finnish families have a cabin by a lake where they relax and take saunas. In winter, some of the lakes freeze solid enough to drive a car across.

keywords: lake with thousands of islands lake huron
facts.answer: Lake Huron, one of the Great Lakes, contains Manitoulin Island, the largest island in a freshwater lake in the world. Manitoulin itself has more than a hundred lakes on it, and some of those lakes have their own islands. So there are islands within lakes within an island within a lake.

keywords: lake on an island on a lake
facts.answer: In the Philippines there used to be a tiny island in a lake, on an island, in a lake, on an island, called Vulcan Point. This nesting-doll arrangement made it one of the most unusual spots on Earth. A volcanic eruption in 2020 changed the area and the famous point.

Mont Saint-Michel in France is a rocky island topped by an ancient abbey, and the tides around it are so dramatic that at low tide you can walk to it across the sand. When the tide rushes back in, it surrounds the island again, sometimes faster than a person can run. For centuries this protected the abbey from attackers.

Many people call the country Holland, but Holland is really just two provinces within the larger country called the Netherlands. It would be like calling the whole United States Texas. The mix-up happened because Holland was the most powerful and famous region long ago.

keywords: why is it called turkey country
facts.answer: The country Turkey shares its English name with the bird, which causes some confusion. The bird was named after the country because Europeans first got it through Turkish traders. In 2022 the country asked the world to use its own spelling, Turkiye, partly to avoid the mix-up.

There are two famous places called Georgia: a state in the United States and a country in the Caucasus region between Europe and Asia. The country is much older and is known for its mountains and ancient way of making wine. The American state was named after a British king named George.

About a third of the world drives on the left side of the road, including the United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, and India. Most of these places were once connected to Britain, which kept the old custom of riding horses on the left. The rest of the world mostly drives on the right.

keywords: country with most neighbors china russia
facts.answer: China and Russia are tied for sharing borders with the most countries, each touching 14 different neighbors. That means a single road trip could pass through many different cultures and languages. Such long borders are hard to guard and have led to many historical disputes.

Only two countries in the world are doubly landlocked, meaning all their neighbors are also landlocked: Liechtenstein in Europe and Uzbekistan in Central Asia. To reach the ocean from these places, you must cross at least two other countries. Liechtenstein is so small it has no airport of its own.

A landlocked country is one with no coastline touching the ocean, and there are over 40 of them in the world. Africa and Europe have the most. Some landlocked countries, like Bolivia, even keep a navy and dream of one day reaching the sea.
