Bolivia has a navy even though it has no coastline, because it lost its access to the ocean in a war with Chile in the 1800s. The navy patrols rivers and Lake Titicaca instead of the sea. Each year Bolivians celebrate a Day of the Sea, hoping to one day regain their coast.

The Caspian seal is one of the only seals in the world that lives in a lake instead of the open ocean. It is found nowhere else but the salty Caspian Sea. Scientists think its ancestors swam in from the Arctic long ago when the waterways were connected.

Lake Baikal in Siberia is home to the nerpa, the world's only seal that lives entirely in fresh water. How its ancestors reached this lake far from any ocean is still a bit of a mystery. The chubby seals have learned to find air holes in the thick winter ice.

Son Doong Cave in Vietnam is the largest cave in the world, big enough to hold an entire city block with skyscrapers inside. It even has its own jungle, river, and clouds that form near the ceiling. It stayed hidden until a local man stumbled upon its entrance in 1991.

The Waitomo Caves in New Zealand glow with thousands of tiny glowworms clinging to the ceiling, looking like a starry night sky underground. The glowworms make light to lure insects into their sticky threads. Visitors float quietly through the cave on boats to see the magical blue glow.

Sumidero Canyon in Mexico has walls that tower up to about 3,000 feet, nearly straight up from the river below. Crocodiles and monkeys live along its banks, which visitors see from boats. A waterfall there leaves mineral deposits shaped like a giant Christmas tree on the rock wall.

Longyearbyen in Norway's Svalbard islands is one of the northernmost towns in the world where people live year-round. It is so far north that polar bears roam nearby, and a law there once said you could not be born or buried in the town because the cold ground does not let bodies decay. The sun does not set for months in summer.

keywords: city at the end of the world
facts.answer: Ushuaia in Argentina is one of the southernmost cities in the world and is nicknamed the End of the World. From there, ships set off toward Antarctica. Surrounded by snowy mountains and cold seas, it is the last stop before the great frozen continent.

keywords: most remote inhabited island tristan da cunha
facts.answer: Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic is the most remote inhabited island in the world, more than 1,500 miles from the nearest land. Fewer than 300 people live there, and the only way to reach it is a multi-day boat trip, since there is no airport. Everyone on the island shares just a handful of last names.

Pitcairn Island in the Pacific is one of the least populated places with a permanent community, home to only a few dozen people. Most of them are descendants of sailors who rebelled on a ship called the Bounty in 1789 and hid there. The island is so remote it takes days by boat to reach.

Easter Island in the Pacific Ocean is famous for nearly a thousand giant carved stone heads called moai, made by the Rapa Nui people. The statues actually have buried bodies beneath the giant heads. The island is one of the most isolated inhabited places on Earth, far from any mainland.

Far beneath the ice of Antarctica lies Lake Vostok, a huge lake that has been sealed off from the surface for millions of years. The thick ice above keeps the water liquid and dark. Scientists are curious whether unique tiny life forms might survive in this hidden world.

Blood Falls in Antarctica is a waterfall that pours out bright red water onto the white ice. The color comes from iron in salty water that has been trapped under a glacier for over a million years, rusting as it meets the air. From a distance it really does look like the glacier is bleeding.

The Dry Valleys of Antarctica are among the driest places on Earth, with some areas that may not have seen rain or snow for millions of years. Fierce winds blow away any snow before it can pile up. The barren ground is so much like Mars that scientists study it to imagine life on other planets.

Mount Erebus in Antarctica is the southernmost active volcano on Earth, and it holds a rare lake of bubbling lava at its summit. Fire and ice meet there as the hot volcano sits surrounded by snow. Strange ice towers form where warm volcanic gas freezes in the cold air.

The Great Rift Valley runs for thousands of miles down eastern Africa, where the continent is slowly tearing apart. In millions of years, the crack may grow wide enough for the ocean to flow in and split off a new piece of land. Many of the oldest human fossils were found in this valley.

The border between Canada and the United States is the longest border between two countries in the world, stretching about 5,525 miles. Much of it runs in a perfectly straight line along a line of latitude. In some places a single building or even a library sits in both countries at once.

The Haskell Free Library sits right on the border between the United States and Canada, with a line on the floor marking which country you are standing in. People from both countries can use it, and books are kept in one country while the reading area is in another. It was built on purpose to be shared by both nations.

Hidden beneath the Pacific Ocean lies Zealandia, a mostly sunken continent that some scientists call the eighth continent. Only the tops poke above the water as New Zealand and a few islands. Almost all of it broke away from a giant ancient supercontinent and slowly sank.

Long ago all of Earth's continents were joined into one giant landmass called Pangaea. Over millions of years it slowly broke apart and the pieces drifted to where they are today. That is why the coastlines of Africa and South America look like they could fit together like puzzle pieces.

The continents are still slowly moving, drifting about as fast as your fingernails grow, around an inch or two a year. This happens because Earth's outer shell is broken into giant plates that float on hotter rock below. Over millions of years this movement builds mountains and opens new oceans.

Lake Malawi in Africa is home to more fish species than any other lake in the world, with hundreds of types of colorful fish called cichlids found nowhere else. Explorer David Livingstone nicknamed it the Lake of Stars because lantern lights on fishing boats looked like stars on the water. Many of its fish are popular in home aquariums.

Lake Tanganyika in Africa is the second deepest and one of the longest freshwater lakes in the world, stretching about 420 miles. It is so old and deep that strange creatures evolved there over millions of years. The lake touches four countries: Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Zambia.

keywords: caspian sea biggest below sea level
facts.answer: The surface of the Caspian Sea sits about 92 feet below the level of the world's oceans, making it the largest body of water on land that is below sea level. It has slowly shrunk and grown over the centuries. Its level still rises and falls depending on rainfall and rivers feeding it.

When Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in 1815, it was one of the most powerful eruptions in recorded history. So much ash filled the sky that the next year was called the year without a summer, with snow falling in June in some places. Crops failed far away, all because of one volcano.

When the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, it made what may be the loudest sound in recorded history. The boom was heard nearly 3,000 miles away, and the shock wave circled the Earth several times. The eruption was so powerful it lowered temperatures around the world for a while.

In winter, Lake Baikal in Siberia freezes into ice so clear you can see right through it to the water below, sometimes looking like turquoise glass. Cracks and bubbles trapped in the thick ice make beautiful patterns. The ice gets strong enough that people have driven trucks across it.

At Lake Abraham in Canada, frozen bubbles can be seen stacked inside the clear winter ice, looking like jellyfish frozen mid-float. The bubbles are methane gas released by plants rotting at the bottom of the lake. As the gas rises in the cold, it gets trapped layer by layer in the freezing water.

Aogashima is a small Japanese island that is actually a volcano inside a larger volcano, with a village built right inside the outer crater. Around 150 people live there, surrounded by green volcano walls. The island is so remote it can only be reached by boat or helicopter, and weather often cancels trips.

Surtsey is one of the newest islands on Earth, formed off Iceland's coast by an undersea volcano that erupted from 1963 to 1967. Scientists protect it so they can watch how plants and animals naturally arrive on brand-new land. Birds, seeds, and insects slowly turned the bare rock into a living place.

Lake Tahoe, between California and Nevada, is one of the clearest large lakes in the world, with water so transparent you can see objects dozens of feet below the surface. It is also one of the deepest lakes in the United States. It formed in a basin between mountains and is fed by mountain streams and snowmelt.

The Roe River in Montana is one of the shortest rivers in the world, running only about 200 feet from a spring to a larger river. It once held a world record for shortest river. You could walk its entire length in less than a minute.

keywords: river splits two oceans continental divide
facts.answer: Along a line called the continental divide in North America, rain that falls on one side eventually flows to the Atlantic Ocean, while rain on the other side flows to the Pacific. In rare spots, a single stream actually splits and sends water to both oceans. You can stand on the divide with each foot draining to a different sea.

Isa Lake in Yellowstone sits right on the continental divide and is one of the few lakes that drains into two different oceans. Strangely, its eastern side flows toward the Pacific and its western side toward the Atlantic, the opposite of what you might expect. It only flows when snow melts in spring.

The Danube River flows through or borders ten countries in Europe, more than any other river in the world. It passes by four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. People have traveled and traded along it for thousands of years.

Lake Eyre in Australia is usually a dry, cracked salt pan, but every few years heavy rains far away flow in and fill it with water. When it fills, millions of birds suddenly appear to feed and breed, and the desert bursts to life. It is also the lowest point in Australia.

keywords: world's largest island in a river
facts.answer: Marajo Island sits at the mouth of the Amazon River in Brazil and is one of the largest islands surrounded by river water, roughly the size of Switzerland. Water buffalo roam there, and the local police even ride them on patrol. During the rainy season much of the island floods.

Majuli in India's Brahmaputra River has been called one of the largest river islands in the world. Sadly, it is slowly shrinking each year as the powerful river erodes its banks. People there live closely with the river, which both nourishes and threatens their homes.

Mount Kelimutu in Indonesia has three crater lakes that can be different colors, sometimes red, green, blue, or black, all next to each other. The colors change over time as minerals and gases in the water shift. Local people believe the lakes hold the souls of the departed.

The Bisti Badlands in New Mexico look like an alien planet, full of strange mushroom-shaped rocks called hoodoos and colorful mounds of clay. Wind and water carved these shapes from soft rock over millions of years. Fossils of dinosaurs and ancient creatures have been found there.

Thor's Well on the Oregon coast is a hole in the rocky shore that seems to swallow the ocean as waves pour into it. At high tide, water shoots up and then drains away as if down a giant sink. It is beautiful but dangerous, so visitors keep a safe distance.

keywords: great barrier reef largest living structure
facts.answer: The Great Barrier Reef off Australia is the largest living structure on Earth, stretching over 1,400 miles and made by billions of tiny coral animals. It is so big it can be seen from space. Thousands of kinds of fish, turtles, and other creatures make their homes there.

Even at the very bottom of the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the ocean, scientists have found living creatures like tiny shrimp-like animals and strange fish. Life survives there in total darkness and crushing pressure. Sadly, plastic trash has even been found at the deepest point.

Surprisingly, only about a fifth of the Sahara Desert is actually sandy dunes; the rest is rocky plains and gravel. The big seas of sand dunes are called ergs, and some have dunes hundreds of feet tall. Wind constantly reshapes them, so the desert is always slowly changing.

keywords: world's largest waterfall by volume inga
facts.answer: The Inga Falls on the Congo River move more water than almost any waterfall on Earth, though it is more like a series of huge rapids than a single tall drop. The river there carries an enormous amount of water rushing through narrow channels. Engineers dream of one day using its power to make electricity for much of Africa.

Iguazu Falls on the border of Argentina and Brazil is one of the largest waterfall systems in the world, made of about 275 separate falls spread across nearly two miles. The biggest part is a roaring U-shaped drop called the Devil's Throat. When a former first lady of the United States saw it, she reportedly exclaimed about how much bigger it was than Niagara.

Victoria Falls between Zambia and Zimbabwe forms the largest single sheet of falling water in the world, over a mile wide and 350 feet tall. The local name means the smoke that thunders, because the mist rises high and can be seen for miles. Brave visitors can swim in a natural pool right at the edge of the falls when the water is low.

In 1969, engineers actually turned off part of Niagara Falls by building a dam to study the rock underneath. For months, the American side of the falls was completely dry. They wanted to see if loose rock should be removed, but in the end they let the water flow again.

keywords: sahara desert below sea level qattara
facts.answer: The Qattara Depression in Egypt is a huge desert valley that dips down to about 436 feet below sea level. It is so low that engineers have dreamed of digging a canal from the sea to fill it and make electricity. For now it remains a vast, sandy bowl with quicksand and salt marshes.

The Taklamakan Desert in China is one of the largest sandy deserts in the world and is nicknamed the Sea of Death because it is so hard to cross. Its name is said to mean you can go in but you cannot come out. Ancient mummies thousands of years old have been preserved in its dry sands.

The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China is a cold desert where temperatures can swing from very hot to freezing. It is one of the best places in the world to find dinosaur fossils, and the first dinosaur eggs ever discovered were found there. Sandstorms there can be fierce enough to darken the sky.

The Lut Desert in Iran has recorded some of the hottest surface temperatures ever measured on Earth, with the ground reaching around 159 degrees Fahrenheit. It is so harsh that some areas have almost no living things, not even bacteria. Wind has sculpted its sand into giant ridges seen from space.

The Sahara Desert is so enormous that it spreads across parts of 11 countries in northern Africa, including Egypt, Libya, Algeria, and Chad. Despite its harshness, around two million people call the desert home. They include nomads who travel with camels between oases.

An oasis is a green spot in a desert where water reaches the surface, allowing plants and palm trees to grow. The water usually comes from underground sources that bubble up or are reached by digging wells. For thousands of years, oases have been lifesaving rest stops for desert travelers.

Long ago, salt mined in the Sahara Desert was so valuable that it was traded for nearly its weight in gold. Camel caravans carried huge slabs of salt across the desert to cities like Timbuktu. Salt was precious because people needed it to keep food from spoiling before refrigerators existed.

Timbuktu is a real city in the African country of Mali, not just a made-up far-away place. Long ago it was a rich center of trade and learning, with libraries full of thousands of handwritten books. People still use its name today to mean somewhere extremely remote.

Each year, winds form an invisible highway carrying Saharan dust across the entire Atlantic Ocean. Besides feeding the Amazon, this dust can affect weather and even reach the United States, sometimes making sunsets extra colorful. Scientists track these dust clouds using satellites.

Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, is the coldest capital city in the world, with winter temperatures often dropping far below zero. Many residents heat their round tents, called gers, with stoves through the long winter. The cold air combined with smoke sometimes makes the city quite hazy in winter.

Wellington, the capital of New Zealand, is the southernmost capital city of any independent country. It is also famous for being one of the windiest cities in the world. Sitting near where two tectonic plates meet, it experiences plenty of small earthquakes.

Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland, is the northernmost capital of any independent country, located very close to the Arctic Circle. Hot water from underground volcanoes heats most of the city's homes and pools. In summer the sky barely gets dark at night.

keywords: world's largest gulf gulf of mexico
facts.answer: The Gulf of Mexico is one of the largest gulfs in the world, bordered by the United States, Mexico, and Cuba. It was likely shaped long ago partly by the same giant meteor impact thought to have ended the dinosaurs. Warm water from the gulf helps power hurricanes and a current called the Gulf Stream.

The Sundarbans, spread across India and Bangladesh, is the largest mangrove forest in the world, where trees grow with their roots in salty water. It is one of the few places where tigers have learned to swim and hunt in the watery forest. The tangled roots protect the coast from storms and waves.

The Pantanal in South America is the largest tropical wetland in the world, much bigger than the more famous Amazon for spotting wildlife. During the rainy season much of it floods, turning the land into a giant water world. Jaguars, caimans, and huge flocks of birds thrive there.

The Okavango River in Africa is unusual because instead of flowing to the ocean, it spreads out and disappears into the Kalahari Desert, forming a lush green delta. This watery oasis attracts elephants, lions, and hippos, especially during the dry season. It is one of the few large deltas that never reaches the sea.

In a part of the Egyptian desert called the Valley of the Whales, scientists have found fossils of ancient whales that lived there about 40 million years ago when the area was underwater. These whales still had tiny back legs, showing how they evolved from land animals. The skeletons sit out in the open sand.

Many mountains contain seashells and fossils of sea creatures because the rock formed at the bottom of ancient oceans. When Earth's plates pushed up the land, those old seafloors became mountaintops. You can even find marine fossils high up on Mount Everest.

On the island nation of Palau there is a lake filled with millions of golden jellyfish that follow the sun across the water each day. Over thousands of years, with no predators around, these jellyfish lost most of their sting. Snorkelers can gently swim among them safely.

The Maldives is the flattest country in the world, while large flat regions also exist in places like the vast plains of Central Asia and the prairies of North America. Flat land often forms from ancient seabeds or from rivers spreading mud over wide areas. The flatness can make these places very prone to flooding.

The Carcross Desert in Canada is sometimes called the smallest desert in the world, covering only about one square mile. It is really the sandy remains of an ancient lake, left behind by glaciers. Though tiny, it has real dunes where people sandboard, surrounded by northern forest.

The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta in India and Bangladesh is the largest river delta in the world, where huge rivers fan out and drop their mud before meeting the sea. The rich soil makes it one of the most fertile farming areas on Earth, feeding hundreds of millions of people. It is also home to the Sundarbans mangrove forest.

keywords: amazon rainforest oxygen lungs of the earth
facts.answer: The Amazon rainforest is often called the lungs of the Earth because its plants produce a lot of oxygen, though it also uses up much of that oxygen itself. More importantly, it stores huge amounts of carbon and helps control the world's weather. It is home to one in ten of all known species on the planet.

The Congo Basin in central Africa holds the world's second largest rainforest, after the Amazon. Forest elephants, gorillas, and the rare okapi live there. The forest takes in so much carbon that it is sometimes called one of the planet's lungs, just like the Amazon.

The taiga, also called the boreal forest, is the largest forest on Earth, ringing the cold northern parts of the world like a green belt. It stretches across Russia, Canada, and Scandinavia, filled mostly with evergreen trees. It holds more trees than any other forest type and stores enormous amounts of carbon.

In Utah there is a forest of about 47,000 quaking aspen trees called Pando that are actually all one single living organism, sharing one giant root system underground. It is considered one of the heaviest and oldest living things on Earth, perhaps thousands of years old. What looks like a forest is really one enormous connected plant.

The tallest known living tree on Earth is a coast redwood named Hyperion in California, standing about 380 feet tall, higher than the Statue of Liberty. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it from too many visitors. Redwoods can live for over two thousand years.

In a few places the Sahara Desert reaches all the way to the Atlantic Ocean, so towering sand dunes sit right next to crashing waves. In Namibia's desert farther south, the same thing happens along a famous foggy coast. The mix of dry sand and ocean spray creates dramatic scenery.

The Skeleton Coast in Namibia is a foggy, dangerous shoreline where the desert meets the cold ocean. Many ships have wrecked there over the centuries, and their rusted hulls still poke out of the sand. The bones of whales and seals once littered the beach, giving the coast its eerie name.

Deadvlei in Namibia is a white clay pan surrounded by some of the tallest sand dunes in the world. Dead camel thorn trees still stand there, blackened by the sun, even though they died around 900 years ago. The dry air keeps them from rotting away, like a frozen scene from the past.

Lencois Maranhenses in Brazil looks like a desert of white sand dunes, but each rainy season the valleys between the dunes fill with crystal-clear blue and green lagoons. Fish somehow appear in the pools, possibly carried by birds or surviving in the mud. It is not officially a desert because it gets too much rain.

Off the coast of Norway, the Moskstraumen is a famous and powerful tidal whirlpool that has inspired scary sea legends for centuries. Strong currents and fierce tides create swirling waters dangerous to small boats. Writers like Jules Verne and Edgar Allan Poe wrote stories about being caught in such whirlpools.

Wadi Rum in Jordan is a vast desert of red sand and towering sandstone cliffs, nicknamed the Valley of the Moon because it looks so otherworldly. Its dramatic scenery has been used to film many movies set on Mars. The Bedouin people have lived in this desert for thousands of years.

Tugela Falls in South Africa is one of the tallest waterfalls in the world, tumbling down a mountain in several leaps. It is fed by a small stream high in the Drakensberg mountains and can freeze in winter. After heavy rain, it roars to life with mist visible from far away.

Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps, sits right on the border between France and Italy. The two countries have politely disagreed for years about exactly where the boundary runs across the snowy summit. Climbers from around the world come to reach its icy peak.

The Alps are the highest and largest mountain range fully in Europe, curving through eight countries including France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Their snowy peaks feed major rivers and are popular for skiing. The famous explorer Hannibal once led an army with elephants across them.

The Ural Mountains in Russia mark the traditional dividing line between the continents of Europe and Asia. They are very old and worn down, so they are not as tall as ranges like the Alps. A traveler crossing them moves from one continent to another without leaving Russia.

Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus Mountains of Russia is the highest peak in Europe, standing about 18,510 feet tall. It is actually a dormant volcano with two snowy summits. Climbers consider it one of the seven summits, the highest peak on each continent.

K2, on the border of Pakistan and China, is the second highest mountain in the world but is considered far more dangerous to climb than Everest. It is nicknamed the Savage Mountain because of its steep ice and unpredictable weather. For every few people who reach the top, many never make it.

Denali in Alaska is the tallest mountain in North America, rising about 20,310 feet. Its native name means the high one or the great one. Because it rises so steeply from low surrounding land, it actually looks taller from base to peak than even Everest does.

Aconcagua in Argentina is the highest mountain in both South America and the entire western and southern hemispheres, at about 22,837 feet. Despite its great height, it can be climbed without ropes on the easiest route, though the thin air makes it very hard. It is one of the famous seven summits.

In a flat part of Death Valley called Racetrack Playa, large rocks slowly move across the ground on their own, leaving long trails behind them. For years it was a mystery, but scientists finally discovered that thin sheets of ice push the rocks along when conditions are just right. No one had ever seen them move because it happens so slowly and rarely.

Nettilling Lake on Baffin Island in Canada is the largest lake on any island in the world. It freezes for much of the year in the cold Arctic climate. Only hardy fish and birds make their home around its chilly shores.

During some volcanic eruptions, lightning crackles right inside the ash cloud, a stunning event called a dirty thunderstorm. The ash particles rub together and build up electric charge, just like in a regular thunderstorm. The result is bolts of lightning flashing through clouds of glowing ash.

Beneath the Caspian Sea lies one of the world's oldest and largest collections of oil and natural gas. People have collected oil there for thousands of years, and the city of Baku in Azerbaijan grew rich from it. Long ago, eternal flames where gas seeped out of the ground were considered sacred.

Azerbaijan is nicknamed the Land of Fire partly because of places like Yanar Dag, a hillside where natural gas seeping from the ground has been burning for centuries. The flames never go out, even in rain or snow. Ancient travelers were amazed by the fires springing from the earth.

Parts of the Sahara Desert were once covered by an ancient ocean called the Tethys Sea millions of years ago. That is why fossils of sea creatures, including ancient sharks and giant sea reptiles, turn up buried in the dry sand. The desert holds clues to a watery past hidden beneath the dunes.

Beneath the dry Sahara Desert lies a huge supply of ancient underground water called fossil water, trapped there from a much wetter time thousands of years ago. Some countries pump it up to grow crops and supply cities. Once used up, this old water cannot easily be replaced.

keywords: worlds largest waterfall vertical drop kaieteur
facts.answer: Kaieteur Falls in Guyana is one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, plunging about 741 feet in one fall, nearly five times higher than Niagara. It is surrounded by untouched rainforest. Tiny golden frogs live their whole lives inside giant plants near the misty falls.

The Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon in Tibet is one of the deepest canyons in the world, in some places more than three miles deep, far deeper than the Grand Canyon. The river roars through it on its way down from the high Himalayas. Parts of it are so remote that few people have ever explored them.

Colca Canyon in Peru is one of the deepest canyons in the world, about twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. Giant Andean condors, among the largest flying birds, soar on the warm air rising from the canyon. Visitors gather at dawn to watch the huge birds glide overhead.

Fingal's Cave on a Scottish island is made of the same kind of six-sided basalt columns as the Giant's Causeway, formed from cooled lava. Waves echoing inside create eerie musical sounds, which once inspired a famous piece of music. You can only reach it by boat, then walk along a natural rock walkway inside.

The Marble Caves in Chile are swirling caverns of smooth marble that glow blue from the reflection of a turquoise lake. The colors change with the seasons depending on the water level and how much light comes in. Visitors paddle right inside the caves in small boats.

keywords: sea of galilee lowest freshwater lake
facts.answer: The Sea of Galilee in Israel is the lowest freshwater lake in the world, sitting about 700 feet below sea level. Despite its name, it is really a lake, fed by the Jordan River. It provides much of the drinking water for the surrounding region.

The wheel was likely invented around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia, but surprisingly it was first used for making pottery, not for transportation. Only centuries later did people put wheels on carts. The hardest part wasn't the wheel itself but the axle that lets it spin smoothly.

The first true writing system, called cuneiform, was invented by the Sumerians in Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE. They pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay tablets using a reed stylus. It started mostly as a way to keep track of trade, like counting sheep and grain.

The plow was one of farming's most important early inventions, appearing in Mesopotamia around 4000 BCE. It let farmers turn over soil far faster than digging by hand. A later improvement, the heavy moldboard plow, helped Europeans farm thick, wet northern soils in the Middle Ages.

Soap-like substances were made by the ancient Babylonians around 2800 BCE by boiling fats with ashes. The ashes contain a chemical that reacts with fat to form soap. For a long time soap was used more for cleaning cloth and treating skin than for washing the whole body.

The abacus is one of the oldest calculating tools, used in Mesopotamia thousands of years ago and perfected in China. By sliding beads along rods, a skilled user can add, subtract, multiply, and divide very quickly. Some abacus experts can still beat electronic calculators on certain math problems.

Bronze was one of the first metals people learned to make, around 3300 BCE, by mixing copper with a little tin. The mix is much harder than copper alone, so it made better tools and weapons. This invention was so important that a whole period of history is called the Bronze Age.

People learned to smelt iron from rock around 1200 BCE, kicking off the Iron Age. Iron is harder than bronze and the ore is far more common, so tools and weapons became cheaper and more widespread. Getting iron out of rock needs very high heat, which is why it was invented later than bronze.

Movable type, where individual letters can be arranged to print a page, was actually invented in China by Bi Sheng around 1040 CE using baked clay characters. Korea later made movable metal type. Gutenberg invented his version independently in Europe about 400 years later.

The modern pencil came from a discovery of pure graphite in England in the 1500s, which people first thought was a type of lead. Graphite is messy, so it was wrapped in string or wood. Pencils still don't actually contain any lead at all, just graphite mixed with clay.

The fountain pen, which holds its own supply of ink inside, was perfected by Lewis Waterman in 1884. Earlier pens leaked badly because of trapped air, but he designed a channel that let air in as ink flowed out. Before fountain pens, writers had to constantly dip a pen into an inkwell.

The ballpoint pen was invented by Hungarian journalist Laszlo Biro in the 1930s. He noticed that newspaper ink dried fast and wanted a pen that used it, so he put a tiny rolling ball in the tip to control the flow. In some countries ballpoint pens are still called 'biros' after him.

The first commercially successful typewriter was made by Christopher Sholes in 1868. He also created the QWERTY keyboard layout, supposedly arranging letters to keep the metal keys from jamming. That same QWERTY layout is still on computer keyboards and phones today.

Braille, the system of raised dots that blind people read by touch, was invented by Louis Braille in 1824 when he was only 15 years old. He had lost his sight in an accident as a small child. He based his system on a military code of raised dots used for reading messages in the dark.

The first sticky postage stamp, the Penny Black, was introduced in Britain in 1840. Before it, the person receiving a letter had to pay, and the price depended on distance. The stamp let the sender pay a single flat price, which made mail cheap and popular almost overnight.

Morse code was developed in the 1830s and 1840s by Samuel Morse and his partners for sending messages over the telegraph. It turns letters into patterns of short dots and long dashes. The famous distress signal SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots, chosen because it's easy to remember.

Shorthand is a fast way of writing using symbols instead of full letters, and systems for it go back to ancient Greece and Rome. A popular modern version was created by Isaac Pitman in 1837. Skilled shorthand writers could keep up with someone speaking, which made them valuable in courts and offices.

Mechanical clocks driven by weights and gears appeared in European monasteries around 1300, used to ring bells for prayer times. Early clocks had no hands or face at all, just a bell. The minute hand didn't become common until clocks got much more accurate centuries later.

The pendulum clock was invented by Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens in 1656. A swinging pendulum keeps very steady time, so his clock was the most accurate the world had seen, losing only about a minute a day. Pendulum clocks remained the most precise timekeepers for nearly 300 years.

Sundials, which tell time by the shadow the sun casts, were used by the ancient Egyptians over 3500 years ago. As the sun moves across the sky, the shadow of a raised piece sweeps across marked hours. The big drawback is obvious: they don't work at night or on cloudy days.

Water clocks, which measure time by water dripping steadily from one container to another, were used in ancient Egypt, Babylon, and China. They had a big advantage over sundials because they worked at night. Some elaborate Chinese water clocks were huge mechanical towers with moving figures.

Watches were worn in pockets for centuries before they moved to the wrist. Wristwatches became popular with soldiers in World War One, who needed to check the time without fumbling for a pocket watch in battle. After the war, wristwatches became fashionable for everyone.

Quartz watches, introduced by Seiko in 1969, keep time using a tiny quartz crystal that vibrates exactly 32,768 times every second when electricity passes through it. They are far more accurate and cheaper than spring-and-gear watches. This 'quartz revolution' nearly wiped out the traditional Swiss watch industry.

Early thermometers were built by several inventors in the early 1600s, including Galileo. Daniel Fahrenheit made the first reliable mercury thermometer with a numbered scale in 1714. A few decades later Anders Celsius created the scale based on water freezing at 0 and boiling at 100.

keywords: history of the ruler and standard measures
facts.answer: The metric system was created in France during the 1790s to replace a confusing mess of local measurements. The meter was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. Almost every country now uses the metric system for science and trade.

The barometer, which measures air pressure, was invented by Evangelista Torricelli in 1643. He filled a tube with mercury and turned it upside down in a dish, and the air pushing on the dish held the mercury up. Because air pressure changes with the weather, barometers became important tools for forecasting.

The magnetic compass was invented in China, where people noticed that a lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, would point north and south. By around 1000 CE the Chinese were using compasses for navigation. This let ships sail far from land without getting lost, even on cloudy days.

The first friction match that lights when struck was invented by English chemist John Walker in 1826, almost by accident, when he scraped a coated stick and it burst into flame. Early matches were dangerous and smelly. Safer 'safety matches' that only light on a special strip came later.

Oil lamps are among the oldest lighting inventions, with stone versions burning animal fat over 15,000 years ago. People later burned olive oil, fish oil, and whale oil. A big improvement came in the 1780s when the Argand lamp added a hollow wick and glass chimney for a much brighter, steadier flame.

Gas lighting lit up cities long before electricity, with whole streets and homes piped with coal gas starting around 1807 in London. For the first time, cities could stay bright at night, which changed how people lived and worked. Lamplighters walked the streets each evening to light the lamps by hand.

Fluorescent lights, the long glowing tubes common in schools and offices, were developed by General Electric and shown off in 1939. They work by exciting gas inside the tube, which makes a coating glow. They use far less electricity than old-style bulbs to make the same amount of light.

The first practical visible LED, or light-emitting diode, was made by Nick Holonyak in 1962 and glowed red. For decades there was no bright blue LED, which was needed to make white light. Three scientists finally cracked the blue LED in the 1990s and won a Nobel Prize, opening the door to today's LED bulbs.

The portable electric flashlight appeared around 1899, once batteries and small lightbulbs were good enough to combine. Early batteries were weak, so people could only flash the light on briefly, which is how it got its name. The British call it a 'torch.'

Neon signs were created by French inventor Georges Claude, who showed the first one in 1910. They glow when electricity passes through neon gas sealed in glass tubes, which gives off a bright reddish-orange light. Other gases and coatings produce the rainbow of colors seen in old signs.

The first true battery was invented by Italian scientist Alessandro Volta in 1800. He stacked discs of copper and zinc with soggy cardboard between them, and the pile produced a steady flow of electricity. The unit of electrical push, the volt, is named after him.

Michael Faraday demonstrated the principle of the electric motor in 1821, showing that electricity and magnetism could create spinning motion. Practical motors strong enough to run machines came in the following decades. Electric motors now power everything from fans and trains to the tiny vibration in a phone.

Michael Faraday discovered in 1831 that moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces electricity, the principle behind every generator. This is the reverse of a motor. Almost all the electricity in the world today, whether from coal, water, or wind, is made by spinning a generator.

In the late 1880s there was a 'war of the currents' between Thomas Edison, who backed direct current, and George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, who backed alternating current. AC won because it can be sent over long distances much more cheaply. That's why power lines carry AC to our homes today.

The transformer, a device that changes the voltage of alternating current, was developed in the 1880s and made the modern power grid possible. It steps voltage way up to send electricity efficiently over long distances, then steps it back down for safe use in homes. The gray cans on power poles are small transformers.

The world's first central power stations opened in 1882, including Edison's Pearl Street Station in New York City, which lit up part of Manhattan. Before this, anyone wanting electricity needed their own generator. The idea of sharing electricity through a network of wires is now called the grid.

The first hydroelectric power plant began running in 1882 in Appleton, Wisconsin, using a river to spin a generator. Flowing water has powered mills for thousands of years, but now it could make electricity. Today huge dams like the Hoover Dam use the same basic idea on a giant scale.

The first practical solar cell that turned sunlight into useful electricity was made at Bell Labs in 1954. Early cells were very expensive, so they were first used to power satellites in space. Over the decades they became dramatically cheaper, and now they power homes and entire towns.

keywords: history of wind turbines for electricity
facts.answer: While windmills ground grain for centuries, the first windmill built to make electricity was set up by Charles Brush in Ohio in 1888. It was a giant wooden machine that charged batteries in his home. Modern wind turbines are sleek, towering machines that can power thousands of homes.

keywords: history of the electric eel battery inspiration
facts.answer: Alessandro Volta got part of his inspiration for the battery from studying electric animals and a debate about 'animal electricity.' He proved that the spark came from the contact between different metals, not from living tissue. His electric pile launched the modern study of electricity.

The fuel cell, which makes electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen with only water as waste, was invented by William Grove in 1839. The idea was ahead of its time and largely ignored for over a century. NASA later used fuel cells to power spacecraft, and they may help power clean cars in the future.

The electric telegraph, perfected in the 1830s and 1840s, was the first technology to send messages almost instantly over long distances using electric signals on wires. Before it, the fastest news traveled only as fast as a horse or ship. It used Morse code to spell out words in dots and dashes.

The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic Ocean was laid in 1858, connecting Europe and North America. The first cable failed after a few weeks, but a successful one in 1866 worked for years. A message that once took ten days by ship could now cross the ocean in minutes.

Early telephones could only connect two fixed points, so the telephone exchange was invented in 1878 to link many callers. Human operators sat at switchboards and physically plugged cables to connect calls. Automatic dial systems gradually replaced them, but for decades you had to ask an operator to connect you.

Guglielmo Marconi sent the first long-distance radio signals in the late 1890s and famously transmitted across the Atlantic Ocean in 1901. Radio sends sound through the air using invisible waves, with no wires needed. Inventors like Nikola Tesla also did key early work on the technology.

The first regularly scheduled commercial radio broadcasts began in 1920, with station KDKA in Pittsburgh airing election results. Suddenly families could gather around a radio to hear news, music, and shows from far away. Radio became the first electronic mass medium that reached into the home.

Color television broadcasts began in the United States in the 1950s, though it took years to catch on because color sets were expensive. The clever trick was making color signals that old black-and-white TVs could still show in black and white. By the late 1960s color TV was becoming the standard.

The fax machine is older than you might think: Alexander Bain patented an early version in 1843, decades before the telephone. A fax scans a page and sends the image over a wire. Fax machines became common in offices in the 1980s before email slowly replaced them.

Telstar, launched in 1962, was the first satellite to relay live television, phone calls, and pictures across the Atlantic. Before satellites, live TV couldn't cross the ocean at all. Today thousands of communication satellites carry phone calls, internet, and TV around the planet.

The first steam locomotive to haul a load on rails was built by Richard Trevithick in 1804. George Stephenson's famous locomotive, the Rocket, won a contest in 1829 and helped launch the railway age. Trains let people and goods travel overland faster than ever before.

The first public railway to carry passengers with steam locomotives opened in England in 1825. Railways spread quickly because they could move huge loads cheaply over long distances. They shrank travel times so much that towns far apart suddenly felt close together.

The penny-farthing, with its huge front wheel and tiny back wheel, was popular in the 1870s and 1880s. The big wheel let riders go faster, but mounting it was tricky and falls could be nasty. It got its nickname because the two wheels looked like a large penny next to a small farthing coin.

Henry Ford's Model T, introduced in 1908, was the first car ordinary families could afford. Ford perfected the moving assembly line in 1913, where the car moved past workers who each did one job. This made cars so cheap and fast to build that they spread across the world.

Henry Ford popularized the moving assembly line in 1913 for building cars, cutting the time to make one from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes. Instead of workers walking to the car, the car moved past workers who each repeated one task. This idea of mass production reshaped factories everywhere.

The air-filled rubber tire, called the pneumatic tire, was reinvented for bicycles by John Dunlop in 1888 to give his son a smoother ride. The cushion of air made vehicles far more comfortable and faster. The same idea was soon used on cars and is on most vehicles today.

An early gas-powered traffic signal was installed in London in 1868, but it exploded and injured a policeman. Electric traffic lights appeared in the United States in the 1910s as cars multiplied. Garrett Morgan patented an improved three-position signal in 1923.

Sails were one of the earliest ways to harness wind, with Egyptians sailing boats on the Nile over 5000 years ago. A sail catches the wind to push a boat without rowing. Clever sail shapes later let ships sail even when the wind wasn't blowing the direction they wanted to go.

Robert Fulton built the first commercially successful steamboat, the Clermont, in 1807, paddling up the Hudson River. Steamboats could travel against the current and the wind, which sailing ships could not. They opened up rivers as busy two-way highways for trade and travel.

An early working submarine, a wooden rowboat covered in greased leather, was built by Cornelius Drebbel around 1620 and tested in the River Thames. Military submarines were used as early as the American Revolution. Modern submarines can stay underwater for months thanks to nuclear power.

keywords: history of the hot air balloon
who invented the hot air balloon
facts.answer: The Montgolfier brothers launched the first hot air balloon to carry people in France in 1783. Hot air is lighter than cool air, so it lifts the balloon. The very first passengers on a test flight weren't people but a sheep, a duck, and a rooster.

Igor Sikorsky built the first practical helicopter in 1939. Unlike a plane, a helicopter's spinning rotor lets it take off straight up, hover in place, and land in tight spaces. Leonardo da Vinci had sketched a flying screw idea centuries earlier, but the engines to make it work didn't exist yet.

The jet engine was invented separately by Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany in the 1930s. Instead of a propeller, a jet engine shoots out a high-speed blast of hot gas to push the plane forward. Jets fly much faster and higher than propeller planes.

Leonardo da Vinci sketched a pyramid-shaped parachute around 1485, but the first successful jumps came in the late 1700s using balloons. Andre-Jacques Garnerin made a famous jump from a balloon in 1797. Parachutes work by trapping air to slow a falling person down to a safe speed.

Rigid airships called zeppelins, named after Count von Zeppelin, carried passengers across the Atlantic in the early 1900s. These giant floating ships were filled with lighter-than-air gas. Their golden age ended after the famous Hindenburg disaster in 1937, when a hydrogen-filled airship caught fire.

The first rockets were invented in China around 1200 CE, using gunpowder to launch arrows and fireworks. Modern liquid-fueled rockets were pioneered by Robert Goddard, who launched the first one in 1926. Rockets are the only engines that work in the vacuum of space, where there's no air.

Ada Lovelace, working with Charles Babbage in the 1840s, wrote what many consider the first computer program, even though no computer existed yet to run it. She realized a computing machine could do more than math, perhaps even create music. A computer programming language is named Ada in her honor.

The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley. It's a tiny switch that controls electric current, and it replaced bulky, hot, fragile vacuum tubes. Transistors are the basic building blocks inside every computer and phone, with billions packed onto a single chip today.

The integrated circuit, or microchip, was invented around 1958 by Jack Kilby and independently by Robert Noyce. The breakthrough was putting many transistors and connections onto a single small piece of silicon. This let electronics shrink from room-sized machines down to devices that fit in a pocket.

The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was released in 1971 and put a whole computer's brain on a single chip the size of a fingernail. It had about 2,300 transistors, while modern chips have billions. This invention made personal computers and smartphones possible.

The personal computer era took off in the mid-1970s with kits like the Altair 8800, which hobbyists assembled themselves. Soon companies like Apple and others sold ready-to-use home computers. For the first time, ordinary people could own a computer instead of renting time on a huge machine.

The computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart in the 1960s, and the first one was a small wooden box with a single button and two metal wheels. He demonstrated it in 1968 in a famous presentation later called 'the mother of all demos.' It got its name because the cord looked like a tail.

The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed in the 1870s for typewriters, and a popular story says the letters were arranged to slow typists down and stop the keys from jamming. Even though computers don't jam, QWERTY stuck because everyone already knew it. Faster layouts exist but never caught on.

The floppy disk was developed by IBM in the early 1970s as a way to load and store data. Early versions were 8 inches across and truly floppy, but later 3.5-inch disks had a hard plastic case. A whole floppy held less data than a single phone photo does today.

Wi-Fi, which connects devices to the internet without wires, became a common standard in the late 1990s. Part of the technology came from Australian scientists, including work by John O'Sullivan, who originally developed signal-processing methods while studying black holes. Today Wi-Fi is found in homes, schools, and cafes everywhere.

Bluetooth, the short-range wireless tech that connects headphones and speakers, was developed in the 1990s. It's named after a medieval Danish king, Harald Bluetooth, who united warring tribes, just as the tech unites different gadgets. The Bluetooth symbol is actually his initials in old Norse runes.

USB, short for Universal Serial Bus, was introduced in the mid-1990s to replace the confusing jumble of different plugs computers used. The goal was one simple connector for keyboards, printers, and more. A running joke is that it takes three tries to plug in a USB the right way up.

IBM made the first computer hard drive in 1956, and it was the size of two refrigerators yet held less data than a single song does today. Hard drives store information on spinning magnetic disks. Over the decades they shrank enormously while holding millions of times more.

The compact disc, or CD, was developed by Philips and Sony and went on sale in 1982. It stores music as tiny pits read by a laser, with no needle touching it. CDs could hold about 74 minutes of music, reportedly chosen so a famous symphony would fit on one disc.

The DVD arrived in the late 1990s and looked just like a CD but held much more data, enough for a whole movie. The same-sized disc could store about seven times more by using a finer laser and smaller pits. DVDs replaced bulky videotapes before streaming took over.

The QR code was invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at a Japanese company to track car parts in factories. Unlike a regular barcode, it stores information both across and up-and-down, holding much more data. Phones can read them instantly, which is why they're now on menus, tickets, and posters.

The first text message was sent in 1992 and simply read 'Merry Christmas.' Early texts had a strict limit of 160 characters, which is why people invented short forms like 'lol.' Texting was almost an afterthought built into phone networks, but it became wildly popular.

Sony released the Walkman in 1979, the first truly portable personal cassette player with headphones. For the first time people could carry their own music anywhere and listen privately while walking around. It was a global sensation and added the idea of a personal soundtrack to daily life.

The MP3, a way of shrinking music files so they take up much less space, was developed by German researchers led by Karlheinz Brandenburg in the early 1990s. By cleverly removing sounds the ear barely notices, it made files small enough to store and share easily. This paved the way for digital music players and downloads.

Apple released the first iPod in 2001 with the slogan '1,000 songs in your pocket.' Its scroll wheel made flipping through music easy. The iPod helped change how people bought music, shifting from buying whole albums to downloading single songs.

The first commercial camera phone was sold by Sharp in Japan in the year 2000. Combining a camera and phone seemed strange at first, but it meant people always had a camera with them. This eventually made standalone cameras rare and turned billions of people into casual photographers.

Touchscreens were invented decades before smartphones, with early versions appearing in the 1960s and 1970s for things like air traffic control. Self-capacitive multi-touch, which lets you pinch and zoom with fingers, became popular on phones in the late 2000s. Now touchscreens are on phones, tablets, cars, and fridges.

Pagers, also called beepers, were small devices that buzzed to alert someone to call back, and they became popular in the 1980s and 1990s. They were widely used by doctors who needed to be reachable at all times. Mobile phones eventually made most pagers obsolete.

The telephone answering machine, which records a message when you can't pick up, used tape recorders and became common in homes in the 1980s. Electronic voicemail stored on phone company computers came soon after. Both meant a caller no longer needed to keep ringing until someone answered.

The oldest surviving photograph was taken by Joseph Nicephore Niepce around 1826, and the exposure took about eight hours. Soon after, Louis Daguerre made much sharper photos called daguerreotypes. Early photos required people to sit perfectly still for a long time, which is why old portraits look so serious.

The first color photograph was made in 1861 by combining three black-and-white images taken through red, green, and blue filters. The idea came from physicist James Clerk Maxwell. Practical color film for everyday use didn't arrive until the 1930s with products like Kodachrome.

George Eastman made photography easy for everyone with his Kodak camera in 1888 and the slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest.' It came loaded with roll film, and you mailed the whole camera back to get prints. This freed people from messy plates and chemicals.

Edwin Land invented the instant camera, sold as the Polaroid in 1948, which developed a photo right inside the camera in about a minute. The idea reportedly came when his young daughter asked why she couldn't see a photo right away. People loved watching the picture slowly appear before their eyes.

The first digital camera was built by Steven Sasson at Kodak in 1975, and it was the size of a toaster and took 23 seconds to record one black-and-white photo onto a cassette tape. Kodak worried digital would hurt its film business, a fear that later came true. Digital cameras eventually replaced film almost completely.

Early motion pictures were created in the 1890s by inventors including Thomas Edison's lab and the Lumiere brothers in France. The Lumieres held some of the first public film screenings in 1895. Legend says a film of a train rushing toward the camera made some early viewers jump from their seats.

Movies were silent for their first few decades, with live musicians playing along in theaters. The Jazz Singer in 1927 became the first major film to feature synchronized spoken dialogue, ending the silent era. These new films with sound were nicknamed 'talkies.'

The videocassette recorder, or VCR, let people record TV shows and watch rented movies at home, becoming popular in the late 1970s and 1980s. There was a famous format war between Betamax and VHS, which VHS won. Families could finally watch movies on their own schedule.

The microwave oven was discovered by accident in 1945 when engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melted in his pocket while he worked near radar equipment. He realized the microwaves were heating it. The first microwave ovens were nearly six feet tall before they shrank to fit on a counter.

The first electric toasters appeared around 1909, but you had to watch them and flip the bread by hand. The pop-up toaster that automatically ejects toast when it's done was invented by Charles Strite in 1919. Sliced bread arrived later, in 1928, making toast even easier.

The first practical dishwasher was invented by Josephine Cochrane in 1886, reportedly because she was tired of servants chipping her fine china. Her machine used water pressure to clean dishes held in racks. Dishwashers didn't become common in homes until decades later.

Canning food to keep it from spoiling was invented around 1810 by Nicolas Appert in France, who sealed food in jars and heated them. The metal can came soon after. Strangely, the can opener wasn't invented until about 50 years later, so early cans were opened with hammers and chisels.

Canned food existed for about 50 years before a proper can opener was invented in 1858 by Ezra Warner. Early cans were so thick that instructions said to open them with a hammer and chisel. The familiar rotating-wheel can opener came along in 1870.

The vacuum flask, sold as the Thermos, was invented by scientist James Dewar in 1892 to keep substances very cold in his lab. It has two walls with a vacuum between them that blocks heat from moving. The same design keeps your drinks hot or cold for hours.

The zipper took decades to perfect, with Gideon Sundback creating the modern reliable design in 1913. At first people didn't trust it and used it mainly for boots and tobacco pouches. The name 'zipper' came from a boot company that liked the 'zip' sound it made.

Velcro was invented by Swiss engineer George de Mestral in the 1940s after he noticed how burrs stuck to his dog's fur on a walk. He studied the tiny hooks on the burrs under a microscope and copied the idea. The name combines the French words for velvet and hook.

The safety pin, with its clever clasp that covers the sharp point, was invented by Walter Hunt in 1849. The story goes he designed it in a few hours to pay off a debt, then sold the rights for a small sum. It hasn't changed much in over 170 years.

Eyeglasses were invented in Italy around 1286 by an unknown craftsman who put two curved lenses in a frame. They were a huge help to scholars and monks whose eyesight had blurred with age. Benjamin Franklin later invented bifocals, which combine two lens strengths in one pair.

Paper made specially for the bathroom was first sold in the United States in 1857 by Joseph Gayetty. The roll of toilet paper that fits on a holder came in the 1880s. Before then, people used whatever was handy, including leaves, corncobs, and old newspapers.

The flush toilet was greatly improved by Thomas Crapper and others in the late 1800s, though earlier flushing designs existed. The key was the S-shaped pipe that traps water and blocks sewer smells from coming up. Good plumbing and sewers did more to improve health than almost any medicine.

Modern air conditioning was invented by Willis Carrier in 1902, but not to cool people. He designed it to control humidity in a printing plant where damp air was ruining the paper. Cooling people turned out to be a popular bonus, and it changed where people could comfortably live and work.

The electric fan was invented by Schuyler Wheeler in 1882, soon after electric motors became practical. Early fans had exposed metal blades with no protective cage, which was quite dangerous. Fans gave people relief from heat decades before air conditioning existed.

The stethoscope was invented by French doctor Rene Laennec in 1816. He felt awkward pressing his ear against patients' chests, so he rolled up a paper tube to listen instead and found it worked even better. The stethoscope let doctors hear the heart and lungs clearly for the first time.

X-rays were discovered by accident in 1895 by Wilhelm Rontgen while experimenting with electricity in glass tubes. He noticed a mysterious glow and found a ray that could pass through skin but not bone. One of his first X-ray images showed the bones in his wife's hand, complete with her ring.

The compound microscope, using more than one lens, was developed in the Netherlands around 1600. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built powerful single-lens microscopes in the 1670s and became the first person to see bacteria and tiny living creatures, which he called 'animalcules.' It revealed a whole hidden world.

The first vaccine was created by Edward Jenner in 1796 to fight smallpox, a deadly disease. He noticed that milkmaids who caught a mild cowpox seemed protected, so he used cowpox to make people immune. The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin word for cow.

Penicillin, the first true antibiotic, was discovered by accident in 1928 when Alexander Fleming noticed that mold growing on a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it. It took over a decade more to turn it into a usable medicine. Penicillin has since saved many millions of lives from infections.

Before the 1840s, surgery was done while patients were fully awake and in agony. Doctors began using ether and other gases as anesthesia to put patients to sleep during operations around 1846. This made longer, more careful surgeries possible for the first time.

The first practical medical thermometer was about a foot long and took 20 minutes to read a patient's temperature. In 1867 Thomas Allbutt invented a short 6-inch thermometer that gave a reading in about 5 minutes. Measuring body temperature became a quick, routine part of medical checkups.

Before electronics, people used ear trumpets, large funnel-shaped horns held to the ear to gather more sound. The first electric hearing aids appeared in the early 1900s but were large and clumsy. Transistors in the 1950s finally made hearing aids small enough to wear comfortably.

The idea of placing a lens directly on the eye goes back to a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci. The first contact lenses, made of glass, were created in the late 1880s and covered the whole front of the eye. Soft, comfortable plastic lenses didn't arrive until the 1960s and 1970s.

The pacemaker, a device that sends tiny electric pulses to keep a heart beating steadily, was developed in the 1950s. The first wearable battery-powered version was built by Earl Bakken in 1957. Soon after, pacemakers small enough to be placed inside the body were created, saving countless lives.

Gunpowder was invented in China around the 9th century, reportedly by alchemists who were actually trying to create a potion for living forever. Instead they made an explosive powder. It was first used for fireworks and signaling before becoming a weapon.

Dynamite was invented by Alfred Nobel in 1867 to make explosives safer to handle for mining and building. He soaked an unstable liquid explosive into a clay-like material to tame it. Troubled by how his invention was used in war, Nobel later left his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes.

Steel was rare and expensive until Henry Bessemer invented a fast, cheap way to make it in the 1850s by blasting air through melted iron. Suddenly steel was affordable enough to build railroads, bridges, and skyscrapers. The skylines of modern cities exist because of cheap steel.

The first fully synthetic plastic, Bakelite, was invented by Leo Baekeland in 1907. Unlike natural materials, it was made entirely from chemicals and could be molded into any shape, then hardened forever. It was used for radios, phones, and jewelry and kicked off the age of plastics.

Nylon, the first fully synthetic fiber, was created by a team at DuPont led by Wallace Carothers in the 1930s. It was strong, stretchy, and cheap. Nylon stockings were a sensation, but during World War Two the material was redirected to make parachutes and ropes.

Natural rubber was useless in heat and cold until Charles Goodyear discovered vulcanization in 1839, supposedly by accidentally dropping rubber mixed with sulfur onto a hot stove. The process made rubber strong and stable. This breakthrough made rubber tires, hoses, and waterproof goods possible.

The ancient Romans were master concrete makers, mixing volcanic ash with lime to build structures that have lasted 2,000 years. The recipe was lost for centuries after Rome fell. Modern Portland cement, the base of today's concrete, was patented in 1824.

keywords: who invented the three point seatbelt
facts.answer: The modern three-point seatbelt, the kind that crosses your chest and lap, was designed by Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin in 1959. Volvo made the patent free for all carmakers to use because it saved so many lives. It is considered one of the most important safety inventions ever.

Inventors patented inflatable car cushions in the 1950s, but airbags that reliably saved lives took decades to perfect. They had to inflate in a fraction of a second using a small chemical explosion, then deflate so they didn't suffocate anyone. Airbags became common safety equipment in cars by the 1990s.

Kevlar, a super-strong fiber used in bulletproof vests, was invented by chemist Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont in 1965. The cloudy liquid she made was so unusual that a colleague almost refused to test it. Woven into fabric, Kevlar is several times stronger than steel by weight and has saved many lives.

Isaac Newton built the first working reflecting telescope in 1668, using a curved mirror instead of lenses to gather light. Mirrors avoided color blurring that lenses caused and could be made much bigger. Nearly all giant telescopes today, including space telescopes, use mirrors based on his idea.

The sextant, invented around 1730, let sailors find their position by measuring the angle between a star or the sun and the horizon. It was a huge improvement for navigation at sea. Combined with an accurate clock, the sextant let ships figure out exactly where they were on the open ocean.

For centuries, sailors could not figure out their east-west position, called longitude, and many ships were lost. John Harrison spent decades building an incredibly accurate sea clock, the marine chronometer, finishing it around 1761. By keeping perfect time at sea, it finally solved the longitude problem.

GPS, the satellite system that tells you your exact location, was built by the U.S. military starting in the 1970s and opened to everyone in the 1980s and 1990s. It works by measuring how long signals take to reach you from several satellites. Surprisingly, it must account for Einstein's relativity to stay accurate.

Radar, which detects objects by bouncing radio waves off them and timing the echo, was developed by several countries in the 1930s. It played a huge role in World War Two by spotting incoming planes and ships. Today radar guides air traffic, tracks storms, and helps cars avoid crashes.

Sonar uses sound waves to detect objects underwater by listening for echoes, much like a bat or dolphin. It was developed in the early 1900s, spurred by the Titanic disaster and submarines in World War One. Sonar helps ships measure ocean depth and find shipwrecks and fish.

An early earthquake detector was built in China by Zhang Heng around 132 CE, a bronze jar that dropped a ball toward the direction of a distant quake. Modern seismographs, which record ground shaking on a moving chart, were developed in the late 1800s. They let scientists study earthquakes around the world.

The gyroscope, a spinning wheel that resists changes to its direction, was named and studied by Leon Foucault in 1852. Because it holds its orientation steady, it became vital for navigation. Gyroscopes help keep ships, planes, rockets, and even your phone's screen oriented correctly.

The spectroscope, developed in the 1800s, splits light into a rainbow of colors that reveals what something is made of. Each chemical element leaves its own pattern of colored lines. Astronomers use it to discover what distant stars are made of without ever traveling there.

The cotton gin, invented by Eli Whitney in 1793, quickly separated cotton fibers from their sticky seeds, a job that was painfully slow by hand. It made cotton hugely profitable. Sadly, this also greatly expanded slavery in the American South, showing that inventions can have harmful effects too.

The mechanical reaper, invented by Cyrus McCormick in 1831, cut grain crops far faster than workers swinging scythes by hand. One machine could do the work of many people. It helped farms grow much larger and feed booming cities.

Steam-powered farm machines came first, but the gasoline tractor was perfected in the early 1900s, with Henry Ford's affordable Fordson arriving in 1917. Tractors replaced horses and oxen for plowing and hauling. They let a single farmer work far more land than ever before.

The spinning jenny, invented by James Hargreaves around 1764, let one worker spin many threads at once instead of just one. It was a key machine of the Industrial Revolution in the textile industry. Some hand-spinners feared for their jobs and even destroyed the machines.

The power loom, invented by Edmund Cartwright in 1785, used machine power to weave cloth automatically instead of by hand. Combined with spinning machines, it moved cloth-making from homes into giant factories. This transformed the textile industry and the way people worked.

Refrigerated railroad cars, developed in the 1870s and 1880s, let fresh meat, fruit, and vegetables travel long distances without spoiling. Before this, people mostly ate food grown nearby. Refrigerated shipping changed diets by bringing distant foods to faraway markets year round.

Pasteurization, named after Louis Pasteur, is gently heating liquids like milk to kill harmful germs without ruining the taste. Pasteur developed it in the 1860s. This simple process made milk and many other foods far safer to drink and helped people understand that germs cause disease.

In the early 1900s, Fritz Haber found a way to pull nitrogen from the air to make fertilizer, a process later scaled up by Carl Bosch. Crops grew much more abundantly with this fertilizer. Scientists estimate this single invention helps feed billions of people who could not otherwise be fed.

Windmills that grind grain or pump water using sails caught in the wind appeared in Persia over a thousand years ago. They spread to Europe, where the tower windmill became a common sight, especially in the Netherlands. The Dutch used windmills to pump water and reclaim land from the sea.

Watermills, which use flowing water to turn a wheel and power machinery, were used by the ancient Greeks and Romans over 2000 years ago. For centuries they were the most powerful machines around, grinding grain and later sawing wood and forging iron. They were a major source of power before the steam engine.

Sputnik, launched by the Soviet Union in 1957, was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, and it was about the size of a beach ball. It simply beeped as it circled the planet, but it shocked the world and kicked off the Space Race. People could spot it crossing the night sky.

The first space station, the Soviet Salyut 1, launched in 1971, letting people live and work in space for longer stretches. The International Space Station, built by many countries starting in 1998, has been continuously occupied by people for over two decades. Astronauts there orbit Earth about 16 times a day.

The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits above Earth's blurry atmosphere to take incredibly sharp pictures of distant galaxies. At first its main mirror was flawed and images came out fuzzy, so astronauts flew up to fix it with a corrective device. It has since transformed our view of the universe.

The Space Shuttle, first launched in 1981, was the first spacecraft designed to be reused many times instead of being thrown away after one flight. It took off like a rocket but landed like a glider on a runway. Shuttles carried satellites and helped build the International Space Station.

The first rover to roam another planet was Sojourner, which explored Mars in 1997 and was about the size of a microwave oven. Later, much larger rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance have driven for years studying Martian rocks. They are controlled from Earth, with commands taking minutes to arrive.

The first successful weather satellite, TIROS-1, launched in 1960 and sent back the first television views of clouds from space. Before satellites, forecasters had to guess at storms over oceans they couldn't see. Weather satellites now track hurricanes and help give days of warning before they hit.

The Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft launched in 1977 to study the outer planets and have since traveled beyond our solar system into interstellar space. Each carries a golden record with sounds and images of Earth in case aliens ever find it. They are the most distant human-made objects in existence.

Spacesuits act like a tiny personal spaceship, providing air, pressure, and temperature control so astronauts survive in the vacuum of space. Early suits grew out of high-altitude pilot suits in the 1950s. A modern spacesuit is extremely complex and can cost millions of dollars.

The escalator, a moving staircase, was invented in the 1890s and first shown as an amusement park ride at Coney Island. The name 'escalator' was originally a brand name before it became the common word. Escalators let crowds move smoothly between floors in stores and subway stations.

Elevators existed before, but they were unsafe because the rope could break. Elisha Otis invented a safety brake in 1853 that stops the elevator from falling if the cable snaps. He proved it by having his own elevator cable cut on stage. This invention made tall skyscrapers practical.

The first skyscraper, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, was completed in 1885 and stood ten stories tall. The breakthrough was using a strong steel frame to hold the building up instead of thick stone walls. Safe elevators and steel frames together made ever-taller buildings possible.

Suspension bridges hang the roadway from huge cables draped over tall towers, letting them span very wide gaps. The Brooklyn Bridge, completed in 1883, was a famous early example and the longest of its time. The cables are made of thousands of steel wires bundled together.

One of the most famous early lighthouses was the Pharos of Alexandria, built around 280 BCE and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Lighthouses guide ships safely past dangerous rocks using a bright light, often made far brighter by special lenses. Many now run automatically without keepers.

The Fresnel lens, invented by Augustin Fresnel in 1822, focuses light into a powerful beam using rings of glass instead of a thick solid lens. It made lighthouse lights visible from far out at sea. The same flat-lens idea is now used in projectors and car headlights.

Early diving suits in the 1800s used a heavy metal helmet with air pumped down from a boat through a hose. This let people work deep underwater for the first time. The self-contained scuba gear that frees divers from hoses was co-invented by Jacques Cousteau in 1943.

The lawn mower was invented by Edwin Budding in 1830, inspired by a machine that trimmed cloth in textile mills. Before it, grass was cut slowly with hand scythes or grazed by animals. The mower made neat lawns possible for ordinary homes.

Surprisingly, an early chainsaw was invented in the late 1700s for use in medicine, to help with difficult births before it was ever used on trees. The tree-cutting chainsaw came later, in the early 1900s. Early logging chainsaws were so heavy they took two people to operate.

Mechanical adding machines existed for centuries, but the first electronic pocket calculators appeared around 1970. Early ones were expensive and could only add, subtract, multiply, and divide. Within a few years they became cheap enough that students could own one, changing how math was taught.

Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877, the first machine that could both record and play back sound. He recorded himself reciting 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' onto a tin-foil cylinder. People were amazed to hear a voice come out of a machine for the first time.

The gramophone, which played sound from flat discs instead of cylinders, was invented by Emile Berliner in the late 1880s. Flat records were easier to make copies of and store than Edison's cylinders. This disc format became the record album that ruled music for nearly a century.
